description: Authored curriculum baseline before the 2026-09-25 learning-system changes; excludes learner-owned state.

topics.title: Web3 / Solidity / DeFi
topics.description: Root of the Web3 learning path: fundamentals → Solidity → tooling → standards → gas → security → DeFi → EVM internals → frontier → full-stack. Code-first — every leaf has a Build task in the web3-practice repo and a Done-when gate; security threads from Phase 4 and is exhaustive in Phase 6. Study one leaf at a time.
topics.aiContext: path root, created 2026-07-07. Approach B (phased spiral, woven security). Toolchain: Foundry-primary + Hardhat 3 for TS deploy/full-stack. Extend via living-roadmap prompting.

topics.title: Phase 1 — Blockchain & Ethereum Fundamentals
topics.description: How Ethereum works: accounts, transactions, gas, the EVM, PoS consensus, L2s/rollups, account abstraction, and the 2025–26 protocol state (Pectra/Fusaka). Mostly theory; entry point.

topics.title: Phase 2 — Solidity Language
topics.description: The Solidity language end to end: types, storage, functions, inheritance, events, errors, low-level calls, ABI, signatures, assembly intro.

topics.title: Phase 3 — Tooling: Foundry & Hardhat
topics.description: Foundry (primary: test/fuzz/invariant/gas/security) and Hardhat 3 (secondary: TS deploy pipelines, full-stack), plus their interop.

topics.title: Phase 4 — Core Contract Patterns & Standards
topics.description: Token standards (ERC-20/721/1155/4626), proxies/upgradeability, access control, signatures/permit/meta-tx, airdrops, multisig, factories, DAOs — each with its threat model.

topics.title: Phase 5 — Gas Optimization
topics.description: Exhaustive gas: storage packing, warm/cold access, calldata, unchecked, bitmaps, custom errors, assembly, architecture.

topics.title: Phase 6 — Security & Auditing
topics.description: The full attack taxonomy + audit methodology, static analysis, fuzzing/invariants, report writing, wargames (Ethernaut, Damn Vulnerable DeFi v4), real-exploit replays, and CodeHawks First Flights.

topics.title: Phase 7 — DeFi Mechanics & From-Scratch Builds
topics.description: Build DeFi from scratch: AMMs, Uniswap V2→V3→V4, lending, stablecoins, oracles, staking/restaking, perps, vaults, flash loans.

topics.title: Phase 8 — EVM Internals & Advanced Solidity
topics.description: Opcodes, Yul/Huff, storage/memory/calldata at the bytecode level, proxies at bytecode level, formal verification.

topics.title: Phase 9 — Frontier Strands
topics.description: MEV, intents/ERC-7683, Uniswap V4 hooks, restaking, RWAs, ZK, L2 internals. Independently orderable after Phase 7.

topics.title: Phase 10 — Full-Stack dApp
topics.description: viem/wagmi, wallet connection, reading/writing contracts, events/indexing, Scaffold-ETH 2, the Speedrun Ethereum challenge ladder.

topics.title: Public-key cryptography & wallets
topics.description: An EOA is controlled by a keypair, while a wallet is the interface that manages signing authority: the private key signs, and the public key derives the 20-byte address (keccak of the pubkey, last 20 bytes). Losing an unbacked-up key means losing control; there is no protocol reset.
topics.aiContext: Build: run `cast wallet new` in web3-practice; in contracts/phase01/README.md explain, in your own words, how the address is derived from the public key and why the private key must never touch the chain. Done when: you can state the derivation (pubkey → keccak256 → last 20 bytes) without looking.

topics.title: SEC1 public-key serialization & address derivation
topics.description: A secp256k1 public key is a curve point (x,y), not an ECDSA operation. SEC1 encodes it as 33-byte compressed 02/03||x or 65-byte uncompressed 04||x||y; Ethereum derives an address from Keccak-256 of the raw 64-byte x||y, excluding 04, then keeps the final 20 bytes. Confusing bits with hex characters, SHA3-256 with Keccak-256, or hashing the SEC1 prefix produces the wrong address.
topics.aiContext: Build: in scripts/phase01/address-derivation.ts, use a fixed non-secret 32-byte scalar and an established secp256k1 primitive to emit compressed and uncompressed SEC1 keys, validate their 33/65-byte prefixes and lengths, strip 04, Keccak-hash x||y, and slice the final 20 bytes; compare with `cast wallet address --private-key`. Reject 0 and scalars >= curve order, and assert that SHA3-256 or hashing 04||x||y disagrees. Done when: one command runs deterministic assertions for the expected address, representations, invalid-scalar boundaries, and both deliberate wrong-hash cases.

topics.title: ECDSA signing, verification & recovery
topics.description: ECDSA signs a message digest with a private scalar and lets verifiers check authorization with the public point; Ethereum also carries recovery parity so the signer can be recovered. A valid signature proves authorization of exact bytes, not safety or intent. Nonce reuse, high-s malleability, missing domain separation, ambiguous message prefixes, and accepting a recovered zero address are practical failure modes.
topics.aiContext: Build: in scripts/phase01/sign-recover.ts, hash a fixed message with and without the EIP-191 prefix, sign locally, split r/s/recovery parity, recover the address, and verify it equals the address-derivation lab; mutate one message byte and assert failure. Add assertions for low-s normalization and domain separation, and never print a real secret. Done when: deterministic checks prove exact-byte authorization, recovery, mutation failure, prefix mismatch, and the low-s boundary.

topics.title: RLP & typed transaction serialization
topics.description: RLP encodes byte strings and nested lists with length prefixes; integers are minimally encoded big-endian byte strings, so zero is the empty byte string rather than byte 00. EIP-2718 typed transactions prepend a type byte to an opaque payload, and a type-2 signing hash covers 0x02||rlp(unsigned fields) while the broadcast form appends yParity, r, and s. One wrong field order, integer encoding, or signed/unsigned boundary changes the hash and signer.
topics.aiContext: Build: in scripts/phase01/type2-transaction.ts, implement the small RLP subset needed for one fixed EIP-1559 transaction using only byte/string primitives; encode its unsigned signing payload, Keccak-hash it, sign it, append yParity/r/s, and recover the sender. Compare every hex result with `cast mktx --offline` or a maintained client library. Done when: deterministic assertions cover single-byte, short-string, long-length, zero-integer, nested-list, type-byte, field-order, signing-hash, raw-transaction, and recovered-sender cases.

topics.title: Stack / memory / storage / calldata
topics.description: The EVM's working areas differ in lifetime, mutability, addressing, and cost: the stack is a 1024-word operand workspace, memory is byte-addressed and expansion-priced, storage is persistent 32-byte-slot state, and calldata is immutable call input that can avoid memory copies. Choosing the wrong location is a root of both bugs and gas waste.

topics.title: What a blockchain is
topics.description: A blockchain is an append-only ledger of blocks, each committing to its parent by hash, replicated across many nodes that agree on one history via consensus. Tampering with an old block changes its hash and breaks every child, so the chain is immutable in practice. Trust comes from cryptography and replication, not an operator.

Done when: you can explain why editing block N invalidates descendant commitments and requires overcoming honest consensus and finality.

topics.title: Hashing & Merkle trees
topics.description: keccak256 is Ethereum's workhorse hash: deterministic, one-way, collision-resistant, fixed 32-byte output. Merkle trees hash data in pairs up to a single root, so one 32-byte root commits to a whole set and any member is provable with a log-sized branch. Block headers and state use this to make tampering detectable.
topics.aiContext: Build: in scripts/phase01/merkle.ts, hash four fixed leaves with Ethereum Keccak-256, define and document pair ordering, compute the root, generate a proof for every leaf, and implement verification; compare one hash with `cast keccak`. Add negative checks for a mutated leaf, wrong sibling order, odd leaf count policy, SHA3-256 substitution, and ambiguous packed concatenation. Done when: deterministic assertions verify every membership proof, reject every mutation, and show proof length grows as ceil(log2(n)) under the documented duplication rule.

topics.title: Mnemonics & HD wallets
topics.description: A BIP-39 mnemonic encodes entropy plus a checksum and is converted into a seed; BIP-32 derives a tree of keypairs from it, BIP-44 defines the path hierarchy, and SLIP-44 assigns coin type 60 to Ethereum (e.g. m/44'/60'/0'/0/0). One phrase therefore backs up an unlimited set of addresses, and anyone holding it controls every derived key.

topics.title: Mnemonic-to-seed & child-key derivation
topics.description: BIP-39 maps entropy plus checksum bits to word indices, then uses PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 with NFKD-normalized mnemonic and salt `mnemonic` plus passphrase to produce a 64-byte seed. BIP-32 uses HMAC-SHA512 chain codes and scalar arithmetic for child keys; hardened derivation includes the private key and cannot be reproduced from an extended public key. A passphrase creates a valid but different wallet, and path, normalization, endian, or hardened-index mistakes silently produce different accounts.
topics.aiContext: Build: in scripts/phase01/hd-derivation.ts, reproduce one official BIP-39 vector from entropy through checksum/word indices and PBKDF2 seed, then derive Ethereum paths m/44'/60'/0'/0/0 and /1 with a maintained BIP-32 primitive. Assert the seed and both addresses against vectors and `cast wallet derive-private-key`; add a passphrase and show that it deterministically changes the root. Done when: tests catch a bad checksum, wrong NFKD/salt, wrong endian index, omitted hardened bit, and changed final address index.

topics.description: An Ethereum node runs an execution client (geth, reth) plus a consensus client (Lighthouse, Prysm) and exposes a JSON-RPC API — eth_call, eth_getBalance, eth_sendRawTransaction, and more. Independent clients speaking one spec is what keeps the network resilient; your tools (cast, viem) are just RPC callers.

topics.title: Raw Ethereum JSON-RPC
topics.description: Ethereum JSON-RPC is a transport-neutral request/response boundary: a client sends jsonrpc 2.0, an id, method, and positional parameters, then receives exactly one result or error. Quantities use minimal 0x-prefixed hex while byte data preserves even-length bytes; block tags change the state snapshot being queried. HTTP success does not imply RPC success, eth_call simulates without committing, and eth_sendRawTransaction accepts already-signed bytes rather than custody of a private key.
topics.aiContext: Build: in scripts/phase01/raw-rpc.ts, use Node's built-in fetch to call a local Anvil node directly—no viem/ethers wrapper—for eth_chainId, eth_getBalance, eth_getBlockByNumber, eth_call, and a deliberately invalid method. Validate id correlation and result-versus-error, parse hex quantities as bigint, keep DATA as bytes, and abort on timeout. Done when: one command starts from a configurable RPC URL and assertions cover success, RPC error under HTTP 200, malformed response, timeout, latest versus fixed block tags, and no floating-point balance conversion.

topics.title: EOAs vs contract accounts
topics.description: Ethereum has two account types sharing one 20-byte address space: EOAs, controlled by signing authority, and contract accounts, controlled by code with no private key. topics.title: Nonce & replay protection
topics.description: An EOA has a monotonically increasing account nonce used as a sequence counter. A normal sender transaction is valid only at the account's exact next nonce, which forces ordering and blocks replay after inclusion. EIP-155 folds chainId into legacy transaction signatures so a mainnet transaction cannot be replayed unchanged on another chain.

topics.title: The EVM as a state machine
topics.description: The EVM is a deterministic state machine: a transaction maps the pre-state (world state = mapping of address → account state, each with balance/nonce/code/storage) to a post-state, gas-metered every step. All nodes re-running the same transaction with the same state and block context reach the same result.

Execute fixed bytecode step by step and emit a trace; assert identical input yields identical post-state and REVERT discards state writes. Done when: tests catch stack underflow, invalid opcode, out-of-gas, 2^256 overflow, memory expansion, and reverted storage while a successful run matches `cast run --trace` or evm.codes.

topics.title: Opcodes & the interpreter loop
topics.description: EVM bytecode is a sequence of 1-byte opcodes run in a fetch-decode-execute loop over a program counter, a 1024-slot stack, and gas. Each opcode (ADD, SLOAD, CALL, …) has a specified stack effect and gas rule, with many costs depending on memory growth or execution context; the loop halts on STOP/RETURN/REVERT or exceptional failure. evm.codes is the interactive playground used in the Build.

topics.title: Reading storage slots
topics.description: Contract storage is a 2^256 mapping of 32-byte slots. Any slot is publicly readable, bypassing getters and `private`.

topics.title: World state & Merkle Patricia tries
topics.description: Ethereum's world state lives in a Merkle Patricia Trie keyed by account address; each account's storage is itself a trie. To verify a storage slot from stateRoot, first verify the account proof to obtain that account's storageRoot, then verify the storage-trie proof along the key's hashed-nibble path — the basis for verifying data a client did not compute.

topics.title: Proof-of-Stake basics
topics.description: Post-Merge Ethereum secures itself with validators whose activation minimum is 32 ETH. One proposer is pseudo-randomly selected for each 12-second slot, while committees attest and every active validator attests once per 32-slot epoch. Honest participation earns rewards; equivocation can be slashed and downtime is penalized. Economic stake, not hashpower, backs finality.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase01/pos-basics.md, explain validators, attestations, and finality in your own words with the 32-ETH activation minimum and slot/epoch timing. Done when: you can describe how a block gets attested and roughly when it finalizes.

topics.title: Slashing & the beacon chain
topics.description: Ethereum's consensus layer coordinates validators. Slashing punishes provable equivocation — a double proposal, double vote, or surround vote — by burning stake and ejecting the validator. Ordinary downtime loses rewards and incurs offline penalties; the stronger inactivity leak activates when the chain has failed to finalize. This makes attacks financially self-punishing.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase01/slashing.md, list the three slashable conditions and contrast ordinary offline penalties with the inactivity leak. Done when: you can explain why running one validator key on two machines risks slashing.

requirements.purpose: Distinguish missed-duty penalties, the non-finality inactivity leak, and slashing consequences.

topics.title: Finality & fork choice (Gasper)
topics.description: Gasper combines Casper FFG (finality) with LMD-GHOST (fork choice). Fork choice picks the head by heaviest attestation weight each slot; FFG then justifies and finalizes checkpoints every epoch. Once finalized, reverting a block would require slashing at least one-third of all staked ETH.

topics.title: Rollups: optimistic vs ZK
topics.description: Rollups execute transactions off-L1 and post data plus a state commitment back to Ethereum for security. Optimistic rollups assume validity and allow a fraud-proof challenge window, which commonly delays canonical-bridge withdrawals for days. ZK rollups post a validity proof verified on L1, avoiding that fraud-challenge window while still waiting for proof submission and L1 finality.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase01/rollups.md, make a table comparing optimistic vs ZK rollups on proof type, withdrawal latency, and trust assumptions. Done when: you can explain why an optimistic-rollup withdrawal takes ~7 days but a ZK one need not.

topics.description: EIP-4844 (proto-danksharding) added blob-carrying transactions: ~128 KiB data chunks committed to by a transaction, kept by Ethereum's consensus data-availability layer for a limited retention window, and priced in a separate blob-gas market. Rollups post data as blobs instead of permanent calldata, substantially reducing data-posting costs without bloating execution state forever.

topics.title: Sequencers & batchers
topics.description: Most rollups run a single sequencer that orders L2 transactions and gives fast soft-confirmations; a batcher then posts compressed transaction data to L1. A sequencer alone cannot authorize invalid state when the proof system and L1 contracts work, but it can censor or reorder, which is why L1 forced-inclusion escape hatches and sequencer decentralization matter.

topics.title: Account abstraction (ERC-4337)
topics.description: ERC-4337 brings smart-contract wallets without a consensus change: users sign UserOperations that bundlers collect, apply view/trace simulation to, and submit through handleOps(PackedUserOperation[]) to a supported versioned EntryPoint singleton. The EntryPoint validates and executes each operation against the user's wallet; an optional paymaster can sponsor gas. This unlocks social recovery, batching, and gasless UX.

topics.title: Bundler economics
topics.description: A bundler is the ERC-4337 actor that pays transaction gas to submit a bundle of UserOperations and is reimbursed from each operation's prefund through the EntryPoint, including its fee. To avoid loss, bundlers simulate validation and reject operations that would revert or grief them, which is why the 4337 mempool enforces ERC-7562 validation and storage-access rules.

topics.description: Value types (bool, uint/int of 8–256 bits, address, bytes1–32, enum) are copied on assignment and every variable starts at a zero value — 0, false, address(0), 0x00…. Since 0.8 arithmetic reverts on overflow/underflow unless wrapped in unchecked.

topics.title: Reference types & data location
topics.description: Arrays, structs and mappings are reference types; bytes and string are special arrays. State variables live in storage, while reference-typed parameters and locals use storage (persistent and a reference when local), memory (a mutable per-call copy), or calldata (read-only input that avoids a memory copy). Assigning a storage local from a storage state var aliases it — writes go to the original, not a copy — which is a classic source of accidental state mutation.

topics.title: Arrays in Solidity
topics.description: Arrays are fixed-size (uint[3]) or dynamic (uint[]); only dynamic storage arrays support .push/.pop, and memory arrays cannot be resized. delete on an element sets it to zero without shortening the array, leaving a gap. Iterating an unbounded, user-growable array is a DoS footgun: gas grows with length until the transaction can never fit in a block.

topics.title: Mappings
topics.description: A mapping(K => V) is a hash-table-like store where every possible key already maps to V's default; it lives only in storage and has no length, keys, or iteration. You cannot enumerate a mapping — you must track keys yourself (e.g. a parallel array) if you need to list them. Nested mappings and mappings inside structs work, but deleting the struct does not clear the nested mapping.

topics.title: Structs
topics.description: Structs group named fields into a custom type you can store, pass in memory, or return. You can construct them positionally or with named fields, but a struct that contains a mapping can only exist in storage — you cannot build such a struct in memory. Copying a storage struct to a memory struct duplicates all value fields.

topics.title: Enums
topics.description: An enum is a set of named constants represented in the ABI as uint8, defaulting to its first member (index 0) and capped at 256 members. It documents state machines (e.g. Status.Pending/Shipped/Delivered) far more safely than raw integers. Casting an out-of-range integer into an enum reverts with a Panic since 0.8, so enums also validate their own domain.

topics.description: The EVM counts value in wei; 1 ether = 1e18 wei and 1 gwei = 1e9 wei, with wei/gwei/ether literal suffixes and seconds/minutes/days time suffixes. msg.value and address.balance are always in wei, so forgetting the 18-decimal scale is a pervasive off-by-1e18 bug.

topics.title: Functions & return values
topics.description: Functions can return multiple values as a tuple, using either unnamed returns with an explicit return statement or named returns that are pre-declared and can be assigned then implicitly returned. Callers destructure tuples with (a, , c) syntax, skipping fields. An explicit return supplies its expressions directly instead of returning the current named return-variable values, so mixing the two styles is easy to misread.

topics.title: View & pure functions
topics.description: view promises to read but not modify state; pure promises to neither read nor modify it, and the compiler enforces both. External view calls use STATICCALL, so an on-chain caller cannot smuggle a state change through a normal view call. They cost gas when invoked inside a transaction — a pure/view call simulated off-chain via eth_call consumes no on-chain gas.

topics.title: Visibility specifiers
topics.description: Functions use public (internal or external calls), external (message calls, including this.f()), internal (this contract and derived contracts), or private (only the declaring contract) visibility. State variables use public, internal, or private, and public state variables receive generated getters. Crucially, private/internal restrict Solidity access only — the data is still readable on-chain, so private is not confidentiality.

topics.title: Function modifiers
topics.description: A modifier wraps a function body, splicing it in at the _ placeholder to run code before and/or after — the standard tool for access control (onlyOwner), pausing, and reentrancy guards. topics.title: Control flow: conditionals & loops
topics.description: Solidity has if/else, for, while, do-while, break and continue, but no switch (switch exists only in Yul). Because every step is gas-metered, an unbounded loop over a growable array is a denial-of-service risk once the iteration cost exceeds the block gas limit. Prefer pull-over-push and bounded loops with an explicit cap.

topics.title: Reading & writing state variables
topics.description: Persistent state variables live in contract storage; a simple value read compiles to SLOAD and a write to SSTORE, both far pricier than memory. Under the current access-list schedule, the first SLOAD of a slot in a transaction costs 2100 gas and a warm SLOAD costs 100. SSTORE metering depends on the original, current, and new values; setting a warm zero slot to non-zero has a 20000-gas base cost, a first cold touch adds 2100, and eligible clearing can earn a capped refund. Minimizing repeated storage touches is a major gas-optimization lever.

topics.title: Storage slots & variable packing
topics.description: State variables are assigned to 32-byte slots sequentially from slot 0, and the compiler packs multiple adjacent small variables (e.g. three uint64 + a bool) when they fit in one slot. Reordering declarations can reduce the number of occupied slots and can combine work when packed fields are read or written together. An isolated write to one packed field still needs a full-slot read-modify-write, so packing can have the opposite gas effect when neighboring fields are usually accessed separately.

topics.title: constant vs immutable
topics.description: constant values are fixed at compile time and substituted at every use — they occupy no storage slot and must be known before deployment. immutable values can be assigned during construction and are substituted into the deployed runtime code, also using no storage slot, but they can depend on constructor arguments. Both are much cheaper to read than a storage variable, though a constant can sometimes be cheaper than an immutable.

topics.title: Inheritance & function overriding
topics.description: A contract inherits with is, and a base function can be overridden only if it is marked virtual and the child marks override. With multiple inheritance, an explicit override list names the relevant bases unless a documented common-base exception applies. Solidity uses C3 linearization: direct bases are listed from most base-like to most derived, while function lookup searches the listed bases right-to-left. Getting virtual/override wrong is a compile error, but reordering bases can change which implementation runs.

topics.title: Calling parent contracts (super)
topics.description: You can invoke an overridden parent function directly by name (Base.foo()) or via super.foo(), which follows the C3-linearized chain rather than a single literal parent. In a diamond, super calls the next contract in the final inheritance order, not necessarily a base named directly in the current contract's is list; this is how cooperative hook chains can reach every mixin once.

topics.title: Shadowing inherited state variables
topics.description: Since 0.6 a child cannot redeclare a visible inherited state variable; it must assign the inherited variable instead, and a redeclaration is a compile error. A private base variable is not visible to the child, so the current rule permits the child to use the same name for a distinct variable. Local variables may still shadow state variables, which compiles with a warning and is a readability and audit hazard.

topics.title: Abstract contracts & virtual functions
topics.description: A contract must be abstract if it has an unimplemented function or does not supply every required base-constructor argument, and a fully implemented contract may also be declared abstract intentionally. Abstract contracts cannot be deployed directly. They can hold state, constructors, and implemented functions — unlike interfaces, which cannot declare state variables or constructors and cannot implement functions. Abstract contracts are the base-class tool for shared logic with pluggable pieces.

topics.title: Events & indexed topics
topics.description: emit writes an event to the transaction log — the standard way to surface state changes to off-chain indexers and UIs. A non-anonymous event may index up to three parameters, making them filterable topics, while the rest are ABI-encoded into the log's data. Indexing a dynamic or otherwise complex type stores a Keccak-256 hash of its special in-place encoding, so the original value cannot be decoded from the topic alone.

topics.title: Log anatomy: topics vs data
topics.description: A log entry has up to four 32-byte topics plus a data byte array. For a normal event, topic0 is keccak256 of the canonical event signature and the remaining topics represent indexed arguments; non-indexed arguments are ABI-encoded into data. An anonymous event omits topic0, freeing a fourth indexed slot but preventing filtering by an event-signature topic. Contracts cannot read logs directly — logs are output for off-chain consumers.

topics.title: require, revert & assert

topics.title: Sending ETH: transfer, send, call
topics.description: Three ways to send ETH differ in gas and error handling: transfer forwards a fixed 2300-gas stipend and reverts on failure; send does the same but returns a bool you must check; call{value: x}("") forwards the available gas by default and returns (bool, bytes). Current Solidity documentation deprecates transfer and send because fixed-stipend assumptions break as opcode costs change; use call with explicit failure handling, checks-effects-interactions, or a reentrancy guard.

Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts a failed call reverts through explicit failure handling rather than silently continuing.

requirements.purpose: Compare transfer, send, and call by gas forwarding, return value, failure behavior, and current deprecation status.

topics.title: receive & fallback
topics.description: receive() external payable runs when the contract is sent plain ETH with empty calldata; fallback() external [payable] runs when no function selector matches (or when ETH arrives with data and there is no receive). The dispatch rule: empty calldata + a receive present → receive, otherwise → fallback. A contract with neither cannot accept plain transfers, though protocol balance credits or selfdestruct can force ETH without a message call.

Done when: forge test passes and the test proves empty calldata hits receive and unknown-selector calldata hits fallback.

requirements.purpose: Apply Solidity's exact empty-calldata, unknown-selector, and payable dispatch rules.

topics.title: Low-level call
topics.description: addr.call{value, gas}(abi.encodeWithSelector(...)) is the type-unsafe primitive that forwards a raw payload and returns (bool success, bytes returndata) WITHOUT reverting on failure — you must check success yourself. It also does not verify the target has code: calling an EOA or empty address returns success = true with empty data. This is the escape hatch when you don't have the callee's ABI, at the cost of every compiler guarantee.

Done when: forge test passes and the test proves an unchecked call to a reverting target would silently continue unless success is checked.

requirements.purpose: Learn raw call payload construction, gas/value options, and the success/returndata result tuple.

topics.title: delegatecall & storage context
topics.description: delegatecall runs the target's code in the CALLER's context: the caller's storage is read and written, and msg.sender/msg.value are preserved from the original call. This is the mechanism behind every proxy, but it demands that the proxy's and implementation's storage layouts match slot-for-slot — a mismatch makes the implementation write to the wrong slots and corrupt state. address(this) is the caller, not the code's contract.

Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts the logic wrote into the caller's slots and msg.sender inside the logic equals the original caller.

requirements.purpose: Understand which code, address, balance, storage, msg.sender, and msg.value delegatecall uses.

topics.title: staticcall & read-only enforcement
topics.description: staticcall is like call but the EVM reverts the sub-call if it attempts any state change — SSTORE, log emission, contract creation, selfdestruct, or a value-bearing call. It is how external view functions are invoked, guaranteeing a call cannot mutate state behind your back. If you invoke a 'view' function through a raw call instead of staticcall, that guarantee is gone.

Done when: forge test passes and the test proves the read succeeds and the state-writing staticcall reverts.

requirements.purpose: Connect Solidity external view calls to EVM-level STATICCALL enforcement and its limits.

topics.title: try/catch for external calls
topics.description: try/catch handles reverts from an external call or a new-contract creation only — not internal/private calls. You can branch on catch Error(string reason) (a revert/require string), catch Panic(uint code) (an assert/arithmetic panic), catch (bytes lowLevelData) (custom errors and everything else), or a bare catch. It lets a caller recover instead of bubbling the callee's failure.

topics.title: abi.encode vs encodePacked
topics.description: abi.encode uses standard ABI head/tail encoding with 32-byte words, producing canonical bytes that can be decoded with a known schema; abi.encodePacked concatenates a compact representation without dynamic lengths, which is ambiguous for adjacent dynamic types. Because encodePacked(("a"),("bc")) equals encodePacked(("ab"),("c")), hashing packed user-controlled dynamic arguments can collide — a real authorization-bypass vector. Use encode when the bytes feed a security-relevant hash.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/AbiEncode.sol with both encoders and a function hashing two strings each way, with a test in test/phase02/AbiEncode.t.sol demonstrating the packed collision. Done when: forge test passes and the test proves two different string pairs produce the SAME encodePacked hash but DIFFERENT encode hashes.

requirements.purpose: Compare standard ABI encoding with packed layout and reproduce ambiguity between adjacent dynamic values.

topics.title: abi.decode & function selectors
topics.description: abi.decode(data, (uint, address)) reverses abi.encode back into typed values. A function selector is the first 4 bytes of keccak256 of the canonical signature ("transfer(address,uint256)"); calldata is selector ++ abi.encode(args). Prefer abi.encodeCall(IERC20.transfer, (to, amt)) — it is type-checked at compile time — over abi.encodeWithSignature, whose string signature typos slip through silently.

Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts the round-trip decode equals the input and the selector equals bytes4(keccak256(sig)).

topics.title: keccak256 hashing
topics.description: keccak256(bytes) is Ethereum's workhorse 256-bit hash (the pre-standard Keccak, not NIST SHA3-256) — deterministic, one-way, collision-resistant — and underlies mapping slots, merkle proofs, function selectors, commit-reveal, and signatures. You hash by first ABI-encoding the inputs, and the choice of encode vs encodePacked changes the digest and the collision risk.

topics.title: ECDSA signatures & ecrecover
topics.description: ecrecover(hash, v, r, s) returns the address that signed hash, or address(0) on failure — so you MUST reject a zero return, otherwise a bad signature 'authorizes' address(0). Signatures are malleable: for any valid (r, s) there is a second valid (r, n−s), so enforce low-s and add a nonce/deadline to stop replay. Off-chain signers hash the EIP-191 prefixed message ("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n32"); use OpenZeppelin's ECDSA and MessageHashUtils libraries to get these checks right.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/VerifySig.sol recovering a signer with the EIP-191 prefix and rejecting address(0), with a test in test/phase02/VerifySig.t.sol using vm.sign. Done when: forge test passes and the test proves a valid signature recovers the expected signer and a tampered message does not.

requirements.purpose: Verify ecrecover's parameters, zero-address failure result, and unchanged high-s malleability behavior.

topics.title: EIP-712 typed structured data
topics.description: EIP-712 makes signed structured data inspectable and domain-separated by hashing a typed struct with a domain such as name, version, chainId, and verifyingContract. The digest is keccak256("\x19\x01" ++ domainSeparator ++ hashStruct(message)). Domain fields prevent cross-chain or cross-contract reuse when included, but EIP-712 does not itself stop replay of the same message within one domain; applications still need a nonce, deadline, or idempotent action.

Done when: forge test passes and the test proves a signature valid for this contract's domain fails verification when the chainId in the domain is changed.

requirements.purpose: Derive hashStruct, the domain separator, and the 0x1901 digest while separating domain reuse from same-domain replay.

topics.title: Libraries & using-for
topics.description: A library is reusable code without its own declared state; it cannot receive ETH normally or be destroyed. internal library functions are compiled into the caller's bytecode, while public/external ones use a deployed library through DELEGATECALL, running in the caller's context. using Lib for Type attaches compatible library functions as methods on that type.

topics.title: Interfaces
topics.description: An interface declares external function signatures and can include ABI-visible types, events, and errors, but no function bodies, state variables, constructor, or modifiers; its functions are implicitly virtual. You wrap an address as IToken(addr) for type-checked high-level calls, and type(IToken).interfaceId gives the ERC-165 selector XOR. The interface is a compile-time promise, not runtime proof that the target conforms.

topics.title: Calling other contracts
topics.description: The high-level way to call another contract is Contract(addr).f(args) or Interface(addr).f(args): the compiler ABI-encodes the arguments, performs a CALL, checks the callee has code (or relies on return-data decoding), and bubbles up failures automatically. This is safer than raw call but still trusts the target's declared ABI — a wrong interface encodes and interprets data according to the wrong schema.

topics.title: Inline assembly & Yul basics
topics.description: An assembly { } block drops into Yul, giving direct access to memory, storage, calldata, and wrapping arithmetic without Solidity's usual type and overflow checks. It is used for low-level operations or measured optimizations. You must respect scratch space 0x00–0x3f, the free-memory pointer stored at 0x40–0x5f, and the zero slot at 0x60–0x7f or risk corrupting surrounding Solidity allocations.

topics.title: Storage & memory access in assembly
topics.description: In Yul, sload(slot)/sstore(slot,val) read and write storage directly, while mload/mstore/mstore8 operate on memory and keccak256(ptr, len) hashes a memory region. For a value-type mapping key, the entry slot is keccak256 over the 32-byte-padded key followed by the 32-byte base slot, equivalent to keccak256(abi.encode(key, baseSlot)). A wrong slot or damaged memory pointer can silently corrupt unrelated state or allocations.

Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts the assembly-read value equals the Solidity getter and the computed mapping slot holds the stored value.

topics.title: Transient storage (EIP-1153)
topics.description: EIP-1153 adds TSTORE/TLOAD — contract-private state that persists for one transaction and is discarded at its end. Each opcode currently costs 100 gas, avoiding persistent storage's disk access and refund accounting. Values survive across nested frames owned by the same contract, making transient storage useful for reentrancy locks and transaction-scoped accumulators. Solidity supports value-type transient state variables from 0.8.28 and tstore/tload in assembly; a composable lock must still reset before returning because clearing happens at end-of-transaction, not end-of-call.

Done when: forge test passes and the test proves a reentrant call reverts and a second independent transaction succeeds (the lock cleared).

requirements.purpose: Verify TLOAD/TSTORE lifetime, ownership, revert behavior, gas cost, and static-call restriction at protocol level.

topics.title: Defining a UDVT with wrap/unwrap
topics.description: type Duration is uint256 defines a user-defined value type — a new, distinct type over an elementary one, converted only via Duration.wrap(x) and Duration.unwrap(d). It costs nothing at runtime (the ABI uses the underlying value) but stops you from accidentally mixing, say, a Price and a Quantity that are both uint256. A UDVT has no operators or implicit conversions by default; operators can be defined through a global using-for directive, but this adds compile-time distinctness only, never runtime checks.

topics.title: Token Standards
topics.description: The ERC token interfaces every dApp speaks: ERC-20 (fungible), ERC-721 (non-fungible), ERC-1155 (multi-token), ERC-4626 (tokenized vaults), and ERC-165 interface detection. Standardization is what lets wallets, DEXes, and marketplaces integrate a token they've never seen.

topics.title: Proxies & Upgradeability
topics.description: How to ship a fixable contract on an immutable chain: a proxy holds state and delegatecalls logic, so the logic address can be swapped. Covers Transparent, UUPS, Beacon and Diamond patterns, ERC-1967 slots, the initializer discipline, and the storage-collision minefield they all share.

topics.title: Access Control Patterns
topics.description: Who is allowed to call privileged functions: single-owner (Ownable), role-based (AccessControl), and two-step ownership handoff. Getting this wrong — a missing modifier or an owner set to the wrong address — is the most common critical finding in real audits.

topics.title: ERC-20 fungible token standard
topics.description: ERC-20 defines fungible tokens through six required methods — totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, transferFrom, approve, allowance — plus Transfer/Approval events and three optional metadata methods. Every DEX, lending market, and wallet integrates against this shape. The standard specifies bool returns for transfer operations, but some deployed tokens return no value, so a typed IERC20 call can fail while SafeERC20 handles a non-reverting empty return.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Token.sol extending OpenZeppelin ERC20 with an initial mint, plus test/phase04/Token.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves transfer moves balances, emits Transfer, and reverts on insufficient balance. Threat: fee-on-transfer / rebasing tokens (amount received != amount sent), missing-return non-compliant tokens, and the approval race — never assume a token is well-behaved.

requirements.purpose: Implement and test the required fungible-token transfer and allowance interface

options.title: ERC-20: Token Standard
options.scope: Sections Token Methods and Events
options.why: The canonical final ERC distinguishes six required methods, optional metadata, boolean transfer returns, zero-value transfers, and event requirements used by the build.

topics.title: ERC-20 approvals & SafeERC20
topics.description: approve + transferFrom lets a contract pull your tokens, but changing a non-zero allowance is racy: a spender watching the mempool can spend the old allowance then the new one. ERC-20 advises clients to set an allowance to zero before another non-zero value. SafeERC20 wraps transfer calls that return false or no value, and forceApprove supports tokens that require the zero-first approval sequence.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/SafeApprove.sol that pulls a token via SafeERC20 and uses forceApprove with a token that requires zero-first approval, with test/phase04/SafeApprove.t.sol using non-returning transfer and zero-first approval mocks. Done when: forge test proves typed transfer fails on the empty return while SafeERC20 succeeds, and forceApprove sets the zero-first token's allowance. Threat: forceApprove solves token-call compatibility, not the spender race when replacing a live allowance; prefer allowance deltas or revoke and account for already-spent value.

requirements.purpose: Explain the zero-first mitigation when replacing an existing ERC-20 allowance

topics.title: ERC-165 interface detection
topics.description: ERC-165 lets a contract advertise which interfaces it implements via supportsInterface(bytes4), where the id is the XOR of the interface's function selectors. ERC-721 and ERC-1155 require ERC-165 support, so declaring it correctly lets integrations discover their interface shape. It is only a self-declaration, though — a contract can claim support it does not honor.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Introspectable.sol overriding supportsInterface for a custom interface, with test/phase04/Introspectable.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves supportsInterface returns true for the declared interface id and the ERC-165 id (0x01ffc9a7) and false for 0xffffffff. Threat: interface-detection spoofing — supportsInterface is a claim, not a proof; still guard the actual calls.

topics.title: ERC-721 non-fungible tokens
topics.description: ERC-721 gives each token a unique id with ownerOf/balanceOf, approve/setApprovalForAll, and safeTransferFrom, which calls onERC721Received on contract recipients and reverts on an invalid response. tokenURI is an optional metadata extension. The receiver callback is also an attack surface: minting via _safeMint hands control to the recipient mid-transaction.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/NFT.sol extending OZ ERC721 with a mint counter and tokenURI, plus test/phase04/NFT.t.sol including a malicious onERC721Received that re-enters mint. Done when: forge test proves ownerOf tracks transfers and the reentrant mint is stopped by CEI or a guard. Threat: onERC721Received reentrancy during _safeMint, and setApprovalForAll phishing that drains a whole collection.

topics.title: ERC-1155 multi-token standard
topics.description: ERC-1155 holds many token types — fungible and non-fungible — in one contract, with balanceOf(account,id), balanceOfBatch, and safeBatchTransferFrom for gas-efficient multi-transfers. Its optional metadata extension substitutes each token id into a shared {id} URI template, and contract recipients must return the required onERC1155Received or batch acceptance value.

Done when: forge test proves balanceOfBatch returns the minted amounts and a batch transfer updates every id atomically. Threat: receiver-callback reentrancy via onERC1155Received/Batch — apply CEI and nonReentrant on state-changing paths.

topics.title: ERC-4626 tokenized vaults
topics.description: ERC-4626 standardizes a vault as an ERC-20 share token over one underlying asset: deposit/mint add assets for shares, withdraw/redeem do the reverse, while convert, preview, max, and totalAssets expose distinct integration views. Conversion formulas are implementation-defined, but the standard mandates method-specific rounding: outputs to users round down, required inputs round up, and both convert methods round down.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Vault.sol extending OZ ERC4626 over a mock asset, plus test/phase04/Vault.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves deposit mints shares, redeem returns assets, and convertToShares rounds down (assets→shares) so a user can never round up free value. Threat: first-depositor inflation via a direct donation to totalAssets — see the dedicated inflation-attack leaf.

requirements.purpose: Distinguish vault convert, preview, max, and state-changing methods and apply their required rounding directions

topics.title: ERC-4626 inflation attack & virtual shares
topics.description: A naive empty ERC-4626 vault can be manipulated when an attacker deposits a tiny amount, then donates assets directly: the exchange rate rises and a later depositor can round to zero shares. OpenZeppelin's implementation includes virtual assets and shares in the conversion and lets _decimalsOffset() raise share precision; the virtual terms capture part of the donation, making the attack unprofitable even at offset zero and increasingly wasteful at larger offsets.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase04/InflationAttack.sol reproduce the donate-and-round exploit against a naive vault, then defend with OZ's virtual assets and shares at offset zero and a positive _decimalsOffset, with test/phase04/InflationAttack.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the naive attack is profitable, while forcing the defended vault's victim to zero shares costs the attacker at least the victim deposit at offset zero and orders of magnitude more with a positive offset. Threat: the defense makes theft unprofitable but cannot prevent a sufficiently funded attacker from griefing a depositor.

requirements.purpose: Reproduce donation-driven share inflation and quantify the virtual-offset defense

options.scope: Sections Security concern: Inflation attack and Defending with a virtual offset
options.why: The official current guide derives the donation attack and shows how virtual assets, virtual shares, and decimals offset change attacker loss.

topics.title: delegatecall & the proxy pattern
topics.description: A proxy stores state and forwards calls via delegatecall to an implementation, so the implementation's code runs with the proxy's address, storage, balance, msg.sender, and msg.value. Changing the implementation can upgrade logic without moving proxy state. Because delegated code reads and writes the proxy's slots, successive implementations must preserve the established storage layout.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/MinimalProxy.sol — a fallback that delegatecalls a stored implementation — plus a LogicV1/LogicV2 pair and test/phase04/MinimalProxy.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves state set through the proxy survives an implementation swap and the swapped logic runs against the same storage. Threat: storage collision between proxy and logic, and delegatecall to an untrusted implementation that can overwrite or drain proxy state.

requirements.purpose: Trace delegated calldata, return data, caller/value, and proxy storage context

topics.title: ERC-1967 proxy storage slots
topics.description: ERC-1967 standardizes compiler-unallocated slots for a proxy's implementation, optional admin, and beacon. The implementation slot is bytes32(uint256(keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation')) - 1). Standard slots avoid accidental clashes with ordinary Solidity layout and let clients such as block explorers discover proxy metadata.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase04/Erc1967Slots.sol write to the implementation slot with sstore in assembly and read it back, plus test/phase04/Erc1967Slots.t.sol using vm.load. Done when: forge test proves the value read at keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation')-1 matches what you stored. Threat: slot collision — a proxy that parks its implementation pointer at slot 0 lets logic variables overwrite it.

requirements.purpose: Derive and inspect standardized implementation, beacon, and admin slots

topics.title: Transparent proxy pattern
topics.description: The Transparent proxy handles selector clashes by routing on the caller: non-admin callers are delegated even when calldata matches the upgrade selector, while the admin can upgrade but cannot fall back to implementation functions. In OpenZeppelin v5 each proxy deploys an associated ProxyAdmin whose address is immutable in the proxy; ProxyAdmin ownership controls upgrades.
topics.aiContext: Build: deploy contracts/phase04 logic behind OZ's TransparentUpgradeableProxy + ProxyAdmin in a forge script/test test/phase04/Transparent.t.sol, then upgrade it. Done when: forge test proves a non-admin call reaches the logic, an admin-initiated upgrade swaps the implementation, and state persists across the upgrade. Threat: admin-key compromise (full upgrade power) and function-selector clash if you bypass the transparent routing.

topics.title: UUPS proxy pattern
topics.description: UUPS puts the upgrade mechanism in the implementation behind an ERC1967Proxy. OpenZeppelin's UUPSUpgradeable exposes upgradeToAndCall, requires an access-restricted _authorizeUpgrade override, and checks the new implementation's ERC-1822 storage-slot compatibility. Removing upgradeability still requires an intentional or custom bypass of that safety check.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/CounterUUPS.sol (UUPSUpgradeable + onlyOwner _authorizeUpgrade) behind an ERC1967Proxy, plus test/phase04/UUPS.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves an unauthorized upgradeToAndCall reverts, an owner upgrade succeeds, state persists, and the current OZ compatibility check rejects a non-UUPS implementation. Threat: unprotected _authorizeUpgrade lets anyone upgrade; deliberately bypassing the ERC-1822 check can remove future upgradeability.

options.why: The official current API defines execution-context guards, mandatory authorization, and the ERC-1822 compatibility check that prevents accidental loss of upgradeability.

topics.title: Beacon proxy pattern
topics.description: A BeaconProxy gets its implementation from a shared UpgradeableBeacon, so one beacon upgrade changes the implementation used by every attached proxy while each proxy keeps independent state. In OpenZeppelin v5 the beacon address is immutable in each proxy, and the beacon's owner controls the fleet-wide implementation pointer.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/BeaconFactory.sol deploying multiple BeaconProxy instances against one UpgradeableBeacon, plus test/phase04/Beacon.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves upgrading the beacon changes the logic seen by all deployed proxies at once while their individual state is untouched. Threat: single-beacon compromise upgrades the entire fleet — guard beacon ownership as tightly as the funds.

topics.title: Diamond pattern (EIP-2535)
topics.description: ERC-2535 defines a multi-facet proxy: a diamond maps function selectors to facet contracts and changes that mapping through diamondCut. Facet code executes by delegatecall against shared diamond storage. The standard describes Diamond Storage as one collision-avoidance approach, using a struct at a chosen namespaced slot; careful selector and storage discipline is essential.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/diamond/ with a Diamond, DiamondCutFacet, and two feature facets using Diamond Storage, plus test/phase04/Diamond.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a diamondCut adds a facet, calls route to the right facet by selector, and two facets read/write independent namespaced storage. Threat: selector clash between facets and storage-namespace collision corrupting unrelated facet state.

requirements.purpose: Add selector-routed facets and isolate their state in shared diamond storage

topics.title: Storage layout for upgrades
topics.description: Because a new implementation reads the proxy's existing storage, an upgrade must not reorder, remove, insert before, or change the type of established variables; safe additions go at the end. Storage gaps can reserve slots in upgradeable base contracts, while OpenZeppelin Contracts Upgradeable v5 uses ERC-7201 namespaced storage. Unsafe layout changes make the new code reinterpret existing bytes.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase04/LayoutV1.sol / LayoutV2.sol demonstrate a safe append and a deliberately-broken reorder, with test/phase04/Layout.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the appended-variable V2 preserves V1 state while the reordered V2 mis-reads it (values collide). Threat: storage collision on reorder/insert, or evolving a base without reserved gaps or an ERC-7201 namespace.

requirements.purpose: Classify safe and unsafe storage-layout changes, including base-contract evolution

options.title: OpenZeppelin Writing Upgradeable Contracts
options.scope: Sections Modifying Your Contracts, Storage Gaps, and Namespaced Storage Layout
options.why: The official upgrades guide gives invalid reorder/type/insert/remove cases and distinguishes storage gaps from ERC-7201 namespaced storage used in v5.

topics.title: Initializers & _disableInitializers
topics.description: Proxy instances do not receive state written by an implementation constructor, so upgradeable setup goes in an initializer and explicitly invokes parent initializers. Initializable supplies initializer and versioned reinitializer guards. The implementation's own constructor should call _disableInitializers() so an attacker cannot initialize and take over the otherwise unused implementation instance.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/InitializableLogic.sol with an initializer, _disableInitializers() in the constructor, and a reinitializer(2), plus test/phase04/Initializer.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves initialize runs once (a second call reverts), the implementation itself cannot be initialized, and reinitializer(2) runs exactly once. Threat: an unprotected proxy initializer or an unlocked implementation can be taken over by the first caller.

requirements.purpose: Initialize proxy storage once, compose parent initializers, and lock the implementation instance

options.why: The official upgrades guide defines initializer guards, explicit parent initialization, reinitializer validation limits, and the _disableInitializers constructor pattern.

topics.title: Ownable (OZ v5)
topics.description: Ownable gives a contract one privileged owner and an onlyOwner modifier, with transferOwnership and renounceOwnership. In OpenZeppelin v5 its constructor takes an explicit initialOwner and rejects address(0). Renouncing sets the owner to the zero address and disables onlyOwner functionality, so both deployment ownership and renunciation require care.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Owned5.sol extending OZ v5 Ownable with an onlyOwner setter, plus test/phase04/Owned5.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the constructor sets initialOwner, a non-owner call reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount, and renounceOwnership leaves owner == address(0). Threat: single-key compromise = full control, and renouncing to address(0) permanently disables every admin path.

topics.title: Role-based access control
topics.description: OpenZeppelin AccessControl uses bytes32 roles, onlyRole checks, and per-role admin relationships. DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is initially its own admin and administers other roles, making it especially sensitive. AccessControlDefaultAdminRules constrains that role to one account and adds a delayed two-step transfer.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Roled.sol with an explicit DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE holder plus separate MINTER_ROLE and PAUSER_ROLE accounts, with test/phase04/Roled.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a minter can mint but not pause, the role admin can revoke MINTER_ROLE, and an unauthorized call reverts with AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount. Threat: a missing onlyRole modifier or an over-broad DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE collapses least-privilege back to one god key.

topics.title: Two-step ownership transfer
topics.description: Single-step transferOwnership immediately sends control to the supplied address. Ownable2Step instead records a pendingOwner, and ownership moves only when that address calls acceptOwnership. This prevents completing a transfer to an address that cannot perform the acceptance, though the current owner must still manage or replace a mistaken pending transfer.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Owned2Step.sol extending Ownable2Step with a constructor that forwards initialOwner to Ownable, plus test/phase04/Owned2Step.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves transferOwnership only sets pendingOwner (owner unchanged), acceptOwnership from the pending address completes the move, and acceptance from any other address reverts. Threat: single-step transfer to a wrong/uncontrolled address = irreversible loss of admin.

topics.title: Safety Patterns
topics.description: The defensive reflexes every contract needs: a pause switch for emergencies, reentrancy guards, and pull-over-push payments so one bad recipient can't wedge the whole system. These are the patterns that turn a discovered bug into a contained incident instead of a total loss.

topics.title: Signatures & Meta-Transactions
topics.description: Using off-chain signatures on-chain: ERC-2612 permit for gasless approvals, ERC-2771 meta-transactions for gasless UX, ERC-1271 so smart-contract wallets can 'sign', and the replay defenses (nonce, deadline, domain) that keep a signature from being reused. Builds on Phase 2's ECDSA/EIP-712 primitives.

topics.title: Distribution & Factory Patterns
topics.description: Getting tokens out and contracts deployed at scale: Merkle and signature airdrops that claim without storing every balance, multisig custody, and factory deployment via CREATE2 and EIP-1167 minimal-proxy clones. The common thread is doing per-user work cheaply and deterministically.

topics.title: DAOs & Governance
topics.description: On-chain governance: ERC-20Votes tokens with delegated, checkpointed voting power; the Governor framework's propose/vote/queue/execute lifecycle; and a Timelock that delays execution so users can exit before a malicious proposal lands.

topics.title: Pausable circuit breaker
topics.description: Pausable adds a boolean switch with whenNotPaused/whenPaused modifiers and _pause/_unpause, so a privileged account can freeze selected functions the moment a bug is spotted — a circuit breaker that buys time to respond. Add explicit access control to the internal pause functions, and think hard about which functions to gate: freezing deposits may contain damage, but freezing withdrawals can trap user funds.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Breaker.sol with a PAUSER_ROLE, whenNotPaused on deposit but an always-open emergencyWithdraw, plus test/phase04/Breaker.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a paused deposit reverts with EnforcedPause, unpause restores it, and users can still exit while paused. Threat: centralization — a pauser can freeze funds; and gating withdrawals can trap users, so keep an exit open.

topics.title: Reentrancy guard & checks-effects-interactions
topics.description: The primary defense against reentrancy is ordering — checks, then effects (update state), then interactions (external calls) — so a re-entrant call sees already-updated state. ReentrancyGuard's nonReentrant modifier adds one contract-wide guard around protected entry points; ReentrancyGuardTransient offers the same pattern on chains with EIP-1153 transient storage. Unguarded cross-function paths and read-only callbacks can still expose inconsistent state.

Done when: forge test proves the attacker drains the vulnerable contract and the reentrant call reverts (ReentrancyGuardReentrantCall) or nets zero against the fixed one. Threat: single-function, cross-function, and read-only reentrancy — CEI first, guard second. (cf. Ethernaut Reentrancy)

topics.title: Pull-over-push payments
topics.description: Pushing funds — looping to send ETH to a list of recipients — fails when one recipient reverts (a contract with no receive, or a deliberate griefer), bricking the whole batch, and each external send is a reentrancy opening. Pull payments invert it: record what each account is owed in a mapping and let them withdraw individually, isolating failures and moving the external call to a single, guarded path. This is the standard fix for auction refunds and reward distribution.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Auction.sol where outbid refunds are credited to a pendingReturns mapping and withdrawn via a pull function, plus test/phase04/PullPayment.t.sol with a griefing bidder that reverts on receive. Done when: forge test proves the griefer cannot block other bidders, its failed withdrawal does not erase its credit, and another recipient can withdraw. Threat: push-payment DoS via a reverting recipient, and reentrancy on the send.

requirements.purpose: Replace recipient-driven push failure with isolated withdrawal credits

topics.title: ERC-2612 permit (gasless approvals)
topics.description: ERC-2612 adds permit(owner, spender, value, deadline, v, r, s) to an ERC-20, letting a user grant an allowance with an off-chain EIP-712 signature instead of a separate on-chain approve tx — so a dApp can approve-and-act in one transaction. Each owner has a monotonic nonce that the signature includes and permit increments, so a signature can't be replayed; the deadline bounds its validity. A permit can be submitted by anyone, so integrations should tolerate it being submitted before their bundled call when the intended allowance is already set. OZ's ERC20Permit implements it.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/PermitToken.sol extending OZ ERC20Permit, plus test/phase04/Permit.t.sol using vm.sign to build a valid permit. Done when: forge test proves a valid signature sets the allowance, replaying the same signature reverts (nonce consumed), and an expired deadline reverts. Threat: signature replay (guarded by nonce+deadline) and permit front-running — an integration that requires its permit call to succeed can be griefed after the same permit is submitted first.

requirements.purpose: Construct and test ERC-2612 permits with nonce, deadline, and domain checks

topics.title: ERC-2771 meta-transactions
topics.description: ERC-2771 enables gasless UX: a user signs a request, a relayer pays gas and calls a trusted forwarder, and the target contract (using ERC2771Context) recovers the real user from the last 20 bytes the forwarder appends to calldata via _msgSender(). The security hinges entirely on trusting only a vetted forwarder — if an untrusted contract is trusted, it can append an arbitrary address and impersonate anyone. Use the Context accessors consistently in meta-transaction-aware logic.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Forwardable.sol using OZ ERC2771Context with an ERC2771Forwarder, plus test/phase04/MetaTx.t.sol relaying a signed request. Done when: forge test proves _msgSender() returns the signer (not the relayer) for a forwarded call and a direct call still reports the direct caller. Threat: trusting a malicious/unvetted forwarder → sender spoofing; and using msg.sender instead of _msgSender() breaks the abstraction.

requirements.purpose: Recover the effective sender only from calls made by a trusted forwarder

topics.title: ERC-1271 contract signatures
topics.description: ecrecover only validates EOA signatures, so smart-contract wallets (Safe, ERC-4337 accounts) need a contract validation path. ERC-1271 defines isValidSignature(hash, signature) returning the magic value 0x1626ba7e when the contract considers the signature valid, letting the wallet implement its own scheme. OZ's SignatureChecker supports EOAs and contract signatures through one interface; unlike ECDSA signatures, a contract signature's validity can change over time.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/SmartWallet.sol with isValidSignature plus a consumer using OZ SignatureChecker, and test/phase04/Erc1271.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves SignatureChecker accepts a valid EOA signature and a valid contract (ERC-1271) signature, and rejects a bad one. Threat: an isValidSignature that doesn't bind the hash to a nonce/domain enables signature replay across contexts.

topics.title: Signature replay protection
topics.description: A bare signed message is a bearer token: without extra binding it can be replayed on the same contract, across chains, or across contracts. Consume a per-signer nonce for one-time use, add a deadline when authorization should expire, and use an EIP-712 domain containing chainId and verifyingContract to separate chains and verifiers. EIP-712 supplies domain separation but explicitly does not supply replay protection by itself.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/SignedActions.sol that executes an EIP-712-signed action guarded by a mapping nonce and a deadline, plus test/phase04/Replay.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a valid signed action executes once, a replay reverts (nonce spent), an expired deadline reverts, and a signature for another chainId reverts. Threat: same-contract / cross-chain / cross-contract replay — bind nonce + deadline + domain.

topics.title: Merkle-proof airdrops
topics.description: A Merkle airdrop commits to an eligibility list with one 32-byte root; each claim supplies a leaf and logarithmic-size proof, and the contract verifies it with MerkleProof.verify. This avoids preloading every allocation, though replay tracking still grows with successful claims. Encode the recipient and amount in the leaf and pay that recipient so a caller cannot redirect a claim; use an unambiguous leaf encoding (OpenZeppelin's StandardMerkleTree double-hashes leaves) so internal nodes cannot be reinterpreted as leaves.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/MerkleAirdrop.sol verifying claims against a root with a claimed mapping, plus test/phase04/MerkleAirdrop.t.sol building a tree and a proof. Done when: forge test proves a valid proof claims the exact amount once, a second claim reverts, and a forged/altered proof reverts. Threat: second-preimage leaf collision, double-claim, and claim front-running — hash leaves safely and bind the recipient.

topics.title: Signature-based airdrops
topics.description: An alternative to Merkle trees: an off-chain signer issues an EIP-712 authorization for a specific recipient, amount, nonce, and deadline, and the contract verifies it before paying out. It needs no on-chain root and lets eligibility be computed lazily, but centralizes issuance authority in the signer's key and needs explicit replay protection. SignatureChecker lets the authorized signer be either an EOA or a contract wallet.

topics.title: Multisig wallets
topics.description: A multisig requires M-of-N owner approvals before a transaction executes: owners submit or sign, and execution proceeds once the threshold is met. A threshold above one removes any single owner key as sufficient authority; 1-of-N does not. Safe is a widely used implementation with modules and guards for extensibility. Enabled modules can bypass normal signature verification and execute arbitrary transactions, so module trust is part of the wallet's security boundary.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/MultiSig.sol with submit/confirm/execute over N owners and an M threshold, plus test/phase04/MultiSig.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a tx executes only after M confirmations, a non-owner cannot confirm, and a re-execution of an already-executed tx reverts. Threat: threshold misconfiguration (1-of-N) and owner-key compromise; and delegatecall modules can bypass the threshold if unvetted.

topics.title: CREATE2 deterministic deployment
topics.description: CREATE2 derives a contract's address from keccak256(0xff ‖ deployer ‖ salt ‖ keccak256(init_code))[12:], so the address depends on the deployer, salt, and init code rather than the deployer's nonce. This enables counterfactual addresses and the same address across chains only when those inputs match. EIP-6780 means SELFDESTRUCT normally no longer deletes existing code, so historical metamorphic redeployment assumptions no longer hold outside creation-and-destruction in one transaction.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Create2Factory.sol that deploys via create2 and a pure predictAddress helper, plus test/phase04/Create2.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves predictAddress equals the actual deployed address and redeploying with the same salt+init_code reverts (address taken). Threat: treating a counterfactual address as if code already exists or assuming cross-chain equality when the deployer or init code differs.

topics.title: Minimal-proxy clones (EIP-1167)
topics.description: ERC-1167 standardizes a 45-byte runtime proxy that delegates every call to a fixed implementation and bubbles return or revert data. OZ's Clones library deploys ordinary or deterministic clones and predicts deterministic addresses. Because construction initializes the implementation rather than each clone's storage, each clone needs its own initialization, ideally atomically in the factory.

Threat: an uninitialized clone (anyone can initialize it) — always initialize atomically in the factory.

topics.description: ERC20Votes extends ERC-20 with delegation and checkpointed voting weight: getPastVotes(account, timepoint) reads an immutable past value so tokens transferred after a proposal snapshot cannot vote again from a new account. topics.title: Governor framework
topics.description: OZ Governor is a modular on-chain governance engine: propose() registers actions, voting starts after votingDelay, holders cast votes during votingPeriod using snapshot weight, and a successful proposal can be executed or queued first when a timelock module requires it. Modules supply vote counting, voting-power source, quorum, and execution policy. A proposalThreshold can limit who may propose.

topics.title: Timelock controller
topics.description: TimelockController enforces a minimum delay between scheduling and executing an operation, giving users a reaction window after governance decisions. PROPOSER_ROLE schedules, EXECUTOR_ROLE executes ready operations, and CANCELLER_ROLE cancels pending ones; granting EXECUTOR_ROLE to address(0) lets anyone execute a ready operation. In a Governor integration, governed assets and permissions belong to the timelock because it performs the eventual calls.

Done when: forge test proves a scheduled operation reverts if executed before minDelay, succeeds after warping past it, and only the CANCELLER can cancel a pending op. Threat: a zero minDelay or mis-set PROPOSER/EXECUTOR roles removes the exit window entirely.

topics.title: Storage gas
topics.description: Persistent storage access is among the EVM's most expensive work, so many gas wins come from touching fewer slots, avoiding redundant loads and stores, and choosing layouts that match access patterns.

topics.title: Calldata & memory gas
topics.description: Calldata is read-only input supplied by the caller, while memory is mutable per-call scratch space. Calldata bytes affect intrinsic transaction gas and expanding memory charges execution gas according to the highest word accessed.

topics.title: Control-flow gas
topics.description: Loops and conditionals can magnify repeated work. Optimize measured compiler output: short-circuit expensive branches, remove only proven redundancy, cache stable values when the compiler does not, and return once the result is known.

topics.title: Packing variables into slots
topics.description: The compiler places state variables contiguously and packs adjacent value types smaller than 32 bytes when they fit. Packing can reduce the number of slots touched when fields are read or written together, but updating one packed value requires a read-modify-write and can cost more than an unpacked value. Optimize the layout for actual access patterns, not slot count alone.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/SlotPacking.sol — compare two equivalent layouts, then reorder fields used together so the measured write path touches fewer slots. Done when: forge test passes, storageLayout confirms the slot mapping, and forge snapshot records the before/after gas delta under the same compiler settings.

requirements.purpose: Apply Solidity's exact packing rules and account for packed-value read-modify-write costs

options.title: Layout of State Variables in Storage and Transient Storage
options.scope: Sections Layout of State Variables in Storage and Transient Storage through the warning about sub-32-byte values, plus JSON Output
options.why: The canonical compiler documentation defines slot boundaries, lower-order alignment, packed update overhead, and the storageLayout output used by the build.

topics.title: Warm vs cold access (EIP-2929)
topics.description: EIP-2929 charges the first access to a storage key or covered account absent from the transaction-wide accessed sets at the cold rate and later accesses at the warm rate: SLOAD is 2100 cold versus 100 warm, while covered account-access opcodes charge 2600 cold versus 100 warm. The sender, destination, precompiles, and EIP-2930 access-list entries begin warm; access-list entries have their own intrinsic charges.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/WarmCold.sol — measure first and repeated accesses to one storage key and one external account, with and without an EIP-2930 access list. Done when: tests preserve behavior and the trace plus transaction gas accounting explains the cold charge, warm charge, and access-list intrinsic charge separately.

topics.title: Minimizing SLOAD and SSTORE
topics.description: SLOAD pricing depends on warm or cold access, while SSTORE metering depends on the slot's original, current, and new values plus any cold-access surcharge and refund. Accumulating in a local and committing once can remove repeated storage operations, but a no-op guard is worthwhile only when its saved store outweighs the added branch and load on real call distributions.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/StorageWrites.sol — change an accumulator loop from repeated storage updates to one final commit, and benchmark a guarded no-op write against the unguarded form. Done when: forge test passes, the trace shows one final SSTORE, and snapshots document both changed-value and same-value paths.

topics.title: Caching storage in memory
topics.description: Copying a stable storage value into a local can let later uses avoid repeated SLOADs. The local may live on the stack or in memory depending on compiler output, and caching is unsafe across code that can change the underlying state, including relevant external-call reentrancy.

Done when: behavior tests pass, compiler output shows the actual load count, and snapshots quantify the delta without allowing a stale cache across state-changing code.

topics.title: constant vs immutable for gas
topics.description: A constant's expression is replaced where it is used, while an immutable is assigned during construction and its value is copied into reserved locations in runtime code. Neither occupies a normal storage slot, so reads avoid SLOAD; constants suit compile-time expressions and immutables suit deploy-time values.

Done when: tests pass, storageLayout and opcode output show no normal storage slot or SLOAD, and snapshots include deployment size and read-path deltas.

topics.title: SSTORE refunds (EIP-3529)
topics.description: EIP-3529 set the storage-clear refund schedule to 4800 gas, removed the SELFDESTRUCT refund, and limits applied refunds to one fifth of gas used. Whether deleting a slot realizes all 4800 depends on the transaction's refund counter and cap; clearing state still consumes gas before the refund is applied.

topics.title: Transient storage for gas (EIP-1153)
topics.description: EIP-1153 defines TSTORE and TLOAD at 100 gas each for transaction-scoped state discarded after the transaction. Transient state is shared across a contract's frames under the same ownership rules as persistent storage, so a lock must still be explicitly cleared before returning if later calls in the same transaction should proceed.

topics.title: Packing structs and enums
topics.description: Struct members start a new slot and then follow the same contiguous packing rules as state variables; items after a struct also begin a new slot. Current Solidity enums have at most 256 members and occupy one byte in storage. Reordering members can reduce slots, but packed partial updates add read-modify-write work.

topics.description: Calldata is non-modifiable call input. For read-only reference-type parameters, keeping data in calldata can avoid a memory copy, but the exact generated operations and savings depend on ABI decoding, access patterns, compiler version, optimizer settings, and whether downstream code requires memory.

topics.title: Custom errors over require strings
topics.description: Custom errors ABI-encode a four-byte selector plus typed arguments and are usually cheaper than string descriptions. They can reduce deployed bytecode and revert-data work, but exact savings depend on the string, arguments, compiler, and optimizer. Solidity supports custom errors with revert and, in current versions, require.
