topics.title: Shrinking calldata
topics.description: EIP-2028's standard calldata accounting assigns 16 gas per nonzero byte and 4 per zero byte, while EIP-7623 applies a 10-gas-per-token floor that can make data-heavy transactions effectively pay 40 and 10 respectively. Standard ABI arguments still occupy 32-byte words even when their Solidity integer types are narrow, so meaningful shrinking requires fewer arguments or an explicitly compact, unambiguous encoding whose on-chain decode cost and calldata floor are included in the comparison.

Done when: round-trip tests pass and receipt accounting separates the 21000 base, EIP-2028 standard calldata charge, execution/decode gas, and EIP-7623 total-cost floor to identify the break-even point.

topics.title: Avoiding memory expansion
topics.description: EVM memory cost for a high-water mark of a 32-byte words is Cmem(a) = 3a + floor(a² / 512); expansion charges only the difference from the previous high-water mark. Reaching the same final size incrementally does not repeatedly repay prior expansion, so optimization means reducing the highest word touched or avoiding repeated allocation and copying—not merely preallocating the same final range.

Done when: tests pass and measured expansion deltas match Cmem(new) - Cmem(old), separating expansion from copy and allocation work.

topics.title: abi.encodePacked encoding cost
topics.description: abi.encodePacked concatenates direct arguments without standard ABI padding and omits lengths for dynamic values. It can reduce encoded size, but exact gas is compiler- and workload-dependent; with two dynamic arguments the encoding is ambiguous and can create hash collisions. Prefer abi.encode unless a bounded fixed layout makes packed encoding unambiguous and measured savings matter.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/EncodePacked.sol — compare abi.encode and abi.encodePacked for fixed-width fields, then demonstrate the documented collision with two dynamic strings. Done when: tests prove the fixed layout is unambiguous, reproduce the dynamic collision, and snapshots record encoded lengths and gas under pinned compiler settings.

requirements.purpose: Use non-standard packed encoding only with an unambiguous bounded layout

topics.title: Short-circuit ordering
topics.description: Logical && and || short-circuit, so putting a cheap, selective condition first can skip later work. Reordering is semantics-preserving only when evaluation order is not observable: operands must not rely on side effects, reverts, or state changes from the original order.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/ShortCircuit.sol — reorder a compound guard so a cheap side-effect-free condition can skip an expensive storage read, and add a counterexample whose operands cannot be reordered. Done when: behavior tests pass and traces plus snapshots show which paths evaluate the SLOAD.

requirements.purpose: Preserve observable evaluation order while using logical short-circuiting

options.scope: Section Order of Evaluation of Expressions and the short-circuiting note for && and ||
options.why: The canonical language reference establishes short-circuit behavior while warning that expression evaluation order otherwise is not specified.

topics.title: Unchecked increments
topics.description: Solidity arithmetic reverts on overflow by default; an unchecked block restores wrapping arithmetic. A loop increment can be unchecked only when its bound and control flow prove that increment cannot wrap. Any gas delta is compiler- and optimizer-dependent and must be measured rather than assumed.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/UncheckedLoop.sol — compare checked and unchecked increments in a bounded loop and document the proof that wrapping is unreachable. Done when: boundary tests cover zero and maximum permitted lengths, compiler output shows the removed check if any, and snapshots record the measured delta.

requirements.purpose: Use wrapping arithmetic only where loop bounds prove overflow unreachable

options.why: The canonical language reference defines default panic-on-overflow behavior and the exact wrapping semantics introduced by unchecked blocks.

topics.title: ++i over i++
topics.description: Postfix i++ evaluates to the old value and prefix ++i to the new value, but when that result is unused a current optimizer can produce equivalent code. Do not claim a gas win from syntax alone: inspect optimized output and benchmark the pinned compiler; choose the clearer form when they are identical.

requirements.purpose: Separate prefix/postfix language semantics from optimizer-dependent generated gas

topics.title: Caching array length
topics.description: A loop condition that reads a storage array's length may cause repeated warm SLOADs; caching a length that cannot change during the loop can remove them. It is incorrect when the body can change the length, and current compiler optimization must be inspected because it may already hoist some invariant reads.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/CacheLength.sol — compare cached and uncached loops over a storage array under pinned optimizer settings, then add a mutation case showing why caching is not always valid. Done when: tests cover both stable and changing lengths and traces plus snapshots show whether repeated length loads remain.

topics.title: Removing redundant checks
topics.description: A check is removable only when the same invariant is enforced on every path by the language, an earlier dominating condition, or a trusted boundary. Solidity address types do not imply nonzero, and external calls can invalidate earlier state assumptions; preserve load-bearing checks and prove redundancy with negative tests.

Done when: positive, overflow, and authorization tests pass and compiler output plus snapshots show whether the redundant branch remains.

topics.title: Early return
topics.description: Returning once a result is known can skip later reads and computation on that path. The optimization depends on path frequency and compiler output, and an early return must not bypass required state changes, cleanup, authorization, or invariant checks.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/EarlyReturn.sol — return on a trivial case before expensive storage work without bypassing authorization or required effects. Done when: tests cover every path and traces plus snapshots confirm the trivial path skips the intended work under pinned compiler settings.

requirements.purpose: Restructure early exits while preserving every required state effect and validation

options.title: Return Variables
options.scope: Section Return Variables, including explicit return and implicit named-variable return

topics.title: Types & layout gas
topics.description: The EVM is a 256-bit machine, so type and data-structure choices have non-obvious gas effects: smaller types can cost more when they do not reduce storage slots, bitmaps compact indexed flags, and mappings suit keyed access.

topics.title: Assembly & Yul gas
topics.description: Inline assembly exposes EVM operations and memory or storage locations directly. It can remove work on measured hot paths, but the author must preserve Solidity's memory, type-cleaning, call-failure, and storage-layout invariants.

topics.title: Architecture-level gas
topics.description: The biggest wins can be structural: deploy clones instead of full contracts, share a singleton where its coupling is acceptable, batch calls, verify compact off-chain commitments, and use withdrawal-based payments to isolate recipients.

topics.title: Word-size choices
topics.description: The EVM operates on 256-bit words. A narrow integer only saves storage gas when layout packing reduces the number of slots; otherwise Solidity may need extra operations to clean or mask it. Treat `uint256` as the baseline for standalone arithmetic and loop counters, use narrow storage fields deliberately for packing, and compare optimized bytecode or gas measurements instead of assuming the type name determines cost.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/WordSize.sol — compare optimized `uint8` and `uint256` standalone counters, then pack two narrow storage fields and explain the different result. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot records both comparisons without assuming a compiler-independent numeric threshold.

requirements.purpose: Relate integer width to actual storage-slot packing and read-modify-write cost

options.why: The compiler's canonical layout documentation states when narrow values share a slot and why sub-word operations can cost more.

requirements.purpose: Understand when the compiler cleans narrow values before using them

options.scope: Section Cleaning Up Variables, cleanup-timing paragraphs through the cleanup-rules table and integer examples

topics.title: bytes32 over string
topics.description: A `bytes32` value is a fixed-size value type with direct equality and no runtime length. Solidity packs a `string` or `bytes` value of at most 31 bytes together with its encoded length in one storage slot, while longer values use a length marker plus data starting at a hashed location. Use `bytes32` for truly fixed, byte-oriented identifiers; use `string` for variable-length UTF-8 text. The short forms may occupy the same number of storage slots, so measure the operations that matter.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Bytes32Label.sol — compare store, read, and equality paths for the same short label as `bytes32` and `string`. Done when: forge test passes, snapshot results are recorded, and the explanation notes that both short values can occupy one storage slot while their operations differ.

requirements.purpose: Choose fixed-size bytes versus variable raw bytes or UTF-8 strings by semantics

topics.title: Bitmaps for boolean flags
topics.description: A bitmap addresses 256 indexed flags inside each `uint256` storage word. It is especially compact compared with `mapping(uint256 => bool)`, whose independently hashed entries occupy distinct slots; contiguous declared `bool` fields and array elements may already be packed by Solidity. Bitmap updates still perform a read-modify-write on the containing word, so the saving depends on flag density and access patterns.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Bitmap.sol — replace a `mapping(uint256 => bool)` claim tracker with word-index and bit-mask addressing. Done when: forge test passes for unset, set, duplicate, and word-boundary indices, and forge snapshot compares first and subsequent writes without claiming that one SSTORE sets 256 flags at once.

topics.title: Mappings vs arrays
topics.description: Mappings provide direct keyed access but have no length, key set, or enumeration order. Dynamic arrays provide indexed access, length, ordering, and iteration; `push` updates their length, while indexed reads are also constant-time rather than linear scans. Choose by required semantics: use a mapping for a known key, an array for ordered enumeration, or both only when the product needs both capabilities.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/MappingVsArray.sol — replace an application-level linear search by record id with a mapping, while retaining an array only if enumeration is required. Done when: forge test preserves the required lookup and enumeration behavior and forge snapshot compares mapping lookup, direct array indexing, and linear search honestly.

options.scope: Section Mappings and Dynamic Arrays

topics.title: Cheap hashing in assembly
topics.description: For two full-word values, inline assembly can write at `0x00` and `0x20` and hash the 64-byte scratch region with `keccak256(0x00, 0x40)`, avoiding a separate ABI-encoded dynamic object. Solidity reserves `0x00`–`0x3f` as scratch space between statements and stores the free-memory pointer at `0x40`; code must not overwrite memory outside the promised region or rely on scratch contents surviving another statement.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/AsmHash.sol — compute `keccak256(abi.encode(a, b))` equivalently from the 64-byte scratch region. Done when: forge test compares hashes across fuzzed words, a memory-safety test preserves the free-memory pointer, and forge snapshot records rather than presupposes the compiler-dependent delta.

requirements.purpose: Use only Solidity's documented scratch region without corrupting the free-memory pointer

options.why: The compiler's memory contract precisely identifies scratch space, the free-memory pointer, and the zero slot.

topics.title: Direct storage slots in assembly
topics.description: Inline assembly can read and write an explicitly chosen storage slot with `sload` and `sstore`, outside Solidity's declared-variable layout. ERC-7201 standardizes NatSpec annotations and the formula `keccak256(keccak256(id) - 1) & ~0xff` for aligned namespaced roots. A wrong or overlapping slot silently corrupts unrelated state, so use a specified layout formula, inspect compiler storage layout, and test collision boundaries.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/AsmSlot.sol — store a guard flag at an ERC-7201-formula namespace root via `sstore`/`sload`. Done when: forge test proves the guard works and declared state remains unchanged, and the namespace annotation and computed root agree with ERC-7201; record gas without an impossible cold zero-to-nonzero threshold.

topics.title: Low-level calls in Yul
topics.description: Yul exposes `call`, `staticcall`, and `delegatecall` directly, including input/output memory regions, forwarded gas, value, and the success flag. This control can avoid unused return-data handling on a measured path, but it also removes Solidity's typed return decoding and automatic failure behavior. Correct code checks success, copies and bubbles revert data when required, validates any expected return shape, and treats calls to addresses without code according to the application's contract.

Done when: forge tests cover success, empty return, malformed return, bubbled revert, and no-code target behavior, and forge snapshot compares the complete safe wrapper with the high-level path without a fixed 200-gas promise.

topics.title: Bit masking
topics.description: Shift a packed field down and apply a width-accurate mask to extract it; clear that field's mask and OR a bounded replacement to update it without changing neighbors. Solidity does not guarantee that high bits outside a narrow type are clean in every assembly-visible context, so mask narrow values before depending on them. The same operations are available in Solidity itself; assembly is warranted only when measurement and layout control justify it.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Masking.sol — read and update one packed field with shift, clear-mask, bounded replacement, and OR. Done when: boundary and fuzz tests prove neighboring fields are unchanged and oversized input cannot leak into them; forge snapshot compares Solidity and assembly implementations without a fixed threshold.

requirements.purpose: Construct width-correct masks and shifts using Solidity's integer semantics

topics.title: Function selector optimization
topics.description: An external function selector is the first four bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of its canonical signature, and compiler-generated dispatch code routes calldata by that selector. Selector value alone does not create a portable source-level gas guarantee: dispatch structure can change with compiler version, optimizer pipeline, and interface size. Mine or rename selectors only after inspecting the exact compiled bytecode and benchmarking a genuinely hot entrypoint, while preserving ABI and readability costs.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Selector.sol — compile the same interface under the project's exact compiler and optimizer settings, inspect its dispatcher, and test whether a mined hot-function name changes measured call gas. Done when: ABI changes are explicit, behavior tests pass, bytecode evidence explains the result, and no compiler-independent 50-gas claim is made.

topics.title: Minimal-proxy clones for gas (EIP-1167)
topics.description: ERC-1167 standardizes a minimal 45-byte runtime proxy that delegates calls to one fixed implementation and returns or reverts with its returndata. Clones avoid redeploying the implementation bytecode for every instance, but each call pays delegation overhead and executes against the clone's storage. Per-instance state therefore needs a protected initializer or immutable-arguments design rather than the implementation's constructor.
topics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Clones.sol — deploy initialized instances with OpenZeppelin `Clones` and compare them with full `new` deployments. Done when: forge tests cover initialization exactly once, isolated clone storage, delegation, and implementation behavior, and forge snapshot records both deployment and steady-state call costs.

topics.title: Singleton contracts
topics.description: A singleton can hold many logical instances behind one deployed contract, keyed by an identifier rather than one address per instance. Uniswap v4's PoolManager uses this architecture for pools and supports flash accounting across actions. It removes repeated deployments and can share warmed state, but concentrates trust, upgrade, accounting, and access-control boundaries; choose it for cross-instance benefits, not as a universal replacement for isolated contracts.

Done when: tests prove state and authorization are isolated by id, invalid cross-instance actions fail, and snapshots include registration plus steady-state calls rather than promising a sub-5000-gas storage write.

topics.title: Batching and multicall
topics.description: A batch entrypoint or multicall amortizes per-transaction intrinsic gas across several operations. Within one transaction, later accesses to the same account or storage key use the warm-access schedule introduced by EIP-2929. The batch still pays loop, calldata, and dispatch costs, and its atomicity must be explicit: either bubble a failure and revert the whole batch or deliberately represent per-item results.

Done when: tests establish chosen failure atomicity and caller/value semantics, and snapshots separate intrinsic-gas amortization from warm-access savings without a universal 84000-gas cap.

topics.title: Pull over push payments
topics.description: A push loop invokes every recipient during distribution, grows with recipient count, and can let one reverting recipient block an atomic batch. The withdrawal pattern records each recipient's credit and lets recipients claim separately, isolating external calls and moving withdrawal gas to each claimer. Crediting N recipients still requires N accounting updates unless a compact commitment is used, and withdrawal must zero credit before the external call to prevent reentrancy.

Done when: tests prove one reverting recipient cannot block others, credit is cleared before interaction, reentrancy cannot double-withdraw, and snapshot compares distribution and per-recipient withdrawal without an impossible 30000-gas cap for five fresh credits.

topics.title: Off-chain compute, on-chain verify
topics.description: A contract can verify an off-chain commitment instead of storing or recomputing the full dataset. A Merkle root commits to leaves and an inclusion proof supplies a logarithmic hash path; EIP-712 signs typed structured data bound to a domain. These tools reduce some on-chain state or computation but introduce proof construction, replay protection, leaf-encoding, trusted-input, and data-availability responsibilities; they do not make every verification cheaper than a direct lookup.

topics.title: Audit Process & Methodology
topics.description: How a smart-contract security review actually runs, end to end: scoping the codebase, building a mental model before hunting bugs, and balancing manual review against tooling. This is the operating discipline the rest of Phase 6 (classification, tooling, fuzzing, reporting) assumes.

topics.title: Severity & Vulnerability Classification
topics.description: The frameworks that turn 'this looks bad' into defensible analysis: the OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026) for risk categories, Immunefi's impact-led scale with likelihood downgrade factors for bounty severity, and the EEA EthTrust levels for certification — plus why the unmaintained SWC registry needs current supporting guidance.

topics.title: Static Analysis Tooling
topics.description: Static analyzers inspect source and compiler representations without executing generated transaction sequences. Slither provides detectors and code-comprehension printers; Aderyn produces Markdown, JSON, and SARIF reports and supports editor integration. Their output is evidence to triage, not a substitute for manual protocol reasoning.

topics.title: Fuzzing & Invariants for Security
topics.description: Where static analysis stops, dynamic testing over random/guided call sequences picks up: Foundry's built-in invariant testing, Echidna, and Medusa all hammer a contract with call sequences looking for a property that should always hold to break. The hard part isn't running the fuzzer — it's writing invariants specific enough to catch a real bug.

topics.title: Security Report Writing
topics.description: Turning findings into a report a client, a bounty payout, or a public disclosure can act on: justifying the severity you assigned against a named framework, keeping the proof of concept as small as possible while still convincing, and writing recommendations specific enough to implement without another meeting.

topics.title: Reading an unfamiliar codebase
topics.description: Auditing starts by orienting, not reading top-to-bottom: find every external/public entry point, trace which ones move value or change privileged state, and sketch a call graph of who calls whom before hunting for bugs. A codebase read in file order hides the actual attack surface, which is defined by reachability from an attacker-controlled call, not by file layout.
topics.aiContext: Build: pick any contract in security/samples/, and in security/notes/<contract>-entrypoints.md list every external/public function, mark which ones move value or change access-control state, and draw a one-page call graph. Done when: the notes file names at least one function you would NOT have flagged as security-relevant on a top-to-bottom read.

requirements.purpose: Map attacker-reachable state-changing entry points, authorization, and call relationships before review

topics.title: Audit scoping & the audit lifecycle
topics.description: A scope pins down exactly what's being reviewed before work starts: a commit hash (not a moving branch), a list of in-scope files/contracts, known issues excluded up front, and a fixed time window. The lifecycle then runs scoping → initial review → findings drafted → fix review (re-checking patches against the same commit range) → final report — skipping fix review is how 'fixed' bugs ship half-fixed.

Done when: the template has a named commit-hash field and a distinct 'fix review' stage separate from the initial review.

topics.title: Note-taking and building a mental model
topics.description: Good audit notes aren't a transcript of the code — they're an evolving model of invariants ('X should never exceed Y') and open questions ('what happens if this reverts mid-loop?') tagged to specific lines, so a two-line hunch survives to become a real finding a week later. Auditors who don't write down assumptions re-derive (or forget) them every time they revisit a file.

topics.title: Manual review vs. automated tooling
topics.description: Static analyzers quickly match structural bug patterns, while fuzzers execute generated call sequences against explicit properties; neither can decide whether an unstated business rule is correct. A competent review runs tools early for the checks they can express, then spends human time defining protocol intent and reasoning about business logic and cross-contract behavior.

topics.title: Immunefi severity classification
topics.description: Immunefi's classification system grades a bug largely by the consequence of a successful exploit. Smart-contract examples include Critical for direct theft or permanent freezing of funds, High for theft of unclaimed yield or temporary freezing, Medium for griefing with no profit motive, and Low when a contract fails to deliver promised returns without losing value. Elevated privileges or uncommon user interaction may downgrade or disqualify a report.

topics.title: What static analysis catches vs misses
topics.description: Static tools can flag detector-defined syntactic and structural patterns without generated execution, but their approximations can produce false alarms and miss bugs outside the encoded checks. Protocol-specific intent must still be supplied through manual reasoning or explicit properties for dynamic analysis. Treat tool output as a prioritized list to investigate, not a verdict.

topics.title: Foundry invariant testing
topics.description: Foundry invariant tests run generated sequences of calls against targeted contracts and re-check `invariant_` properties as the sequence advances. A handler is an intentional layer for constraining actions and tracking ghost state, not a requirement of every campaign. A failing run reports the call sequence that broke the property.

topics.description: Medusa is a Go, go-ethereum-based smart-contract fuzzer inspired by Echidna. It runs property and assertion campaigns across parallel workers, retains coverage-increasing call sequences in a corpus, and mutates that corpus to guide exploration. Its concurrency makes worker count and tool-specific metrics important context for any benchmark.

topics.title: Writing good invariants
topics.description: A good invariant states something that must be true after ANY sequence of allowed calls, in terms an attacker can't route around — 'totalSupply equals the sum of balances', 'a user can never withdraw more than they deposited', 'share price is monotonically non-decreasing except on explicit loss events'. A weak invariant either restates something trivially true regardless of bugs, or is so narrow it only covers the one path you already checked by hand — the fuzzer can only find what your invariant is capable of catching.
topics.aiContext: Build: for a sample contract in security/samples/, write 2 invariants in test/security/invariant/ — one about conservation of value (e.g. sum-of-parts equals total) and one about an access-control property (e.g. only role X ever changes Y) — and run both with explicit campaign settings. Done when: you can explain, for each, a bug that WOULD violate it and one that WOULD NOT (its blind spot).

topics.title: Stateful vs stateless fuzzing
topics.description: Stateless fuzzing resets state between generated transactions, which suits properties that can be checked from one call against the initial state. Stateful fuzzing preserves state across a sequence, so it can reach and test properties that depend on accumulated state or several transactions in a specific order.

Done when: you can name the exact 2nd/3rd call your stateless test would be missing.

topics.title: Writing a minimal PoC
topics.description: A minimal proof of concept is the smallest Foundry test that reproduces the bug end to end — one setup, the exact call sequence that triggers it, and an assertion showing the bad outcome (funds moved, invariant broken) — with every unrelated setup step, mock, or helper stripped out. Padding a PoC with the whole protocol's deployment script obscures the one thing that matters: what a reviewer must change to make the assertion fail again.

topics.title: Reentrancy attacks
topics.description: The archetypal external-call bug family: a contract calls out to an address that re-enters it before its own state is updated, so a stale balance or flag is trusted twice. Spans single-function, cross-function, cross-contract, read-only, and callback-hook variants; defenses include restoring invariants before external calls and applying a shared reentrancy guard where needed.

topics.title: Access control & authorization attacks
topics.description: OWASP SC01 in the current Smart Contract Top 10: functions that fail to check who is calling, or check it wrongly. Missing modifiers, tx.origin authorization, unprotected initializers or privileged opcodes, and weak signature checks can all let an attacker invoke privileged logic.

topics.title: Arithmetic & precision attacks
topics.description: Bugs where the math is the vulnerability: overflow or underflow (pre-0.8 or inside unchecked arithmetic, casts, or assembly), premature integer division, wrong rounding direction, and share-price manipulation in vaults. Small rounding edges can compound into drainable value.

topics.title: Price oracle & flash-loan attacks
topics.description: OWASP SC03/SC04: an attacker distorts the price or voting power a protocol reads — a spot AMM reserve, a weak TWAP, or a current-balance governance vote — often funding the distortion with a single-transaction flash loan. Root cause is trusting state that temporary borrowed liquidity can rewrite.

topics.title: Single-function reentrancy
topics.description: A withdraw() that sends ETH via a low-level call before zeroing the caller's recorded balance lets the recipient's receive()/fallback re-enter withdraw() and drain the contract, because the balance check still passes on each re-entry. The 2016 DAO attack recursively called its split path and drained more than 3.6 million ETH, prompting the DAO fork. Fix the stale-state window with Checks-Effects-Interactions and, where appropriate, a reentrancy guard.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/reentrancy-single/ write a vulnerable Vault (balance decremented AFTER the call), an Attacker that re-enters withdraw() from receive() to drain it, and a Foundry test that proves the drain; then apply CEI + OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard. Done when: the exploit test empties the vault on the vulnerable contract and reverts after the fix.

requirements.purpose: Trace the inconsistent-state window and apply Checks-Effects-Interactions without relying on a gas stipend

topics.title: Cross-function & cross-contract reentrancy
topics.description: Guarding only one entry point is not enough when another function or contract can observe the same inconsistent state: the attacker re-enters an unguarded function that reads the not-yet-updated balance, or bounces through a second contract outside the lock. The shared invariant, not one named function, must hold before control leaves the system.

Done when: the test double-spends on the vulnerable version and fails once CEI is applied across BOTH functions.

topics.title: Read-only reentrancy
topics.description: A view function writes no state, yet an attacker can call it mid-manipulation: during a callback such as Curve's ETH-paying remove_liquidity path, pool balances and LP supply can be temporarily inconsistent, so get_virtual_price() reports a wrong value that an integrating contract trusts. The 2022 disclosure exposed several major integrations. Fix the read path or reject reads while the upstream pool's lock is entered.

Done when: the test over-borrows on the vulnerable consumer and reverts after the read is guarded by the pool's reentrancy lock.

topics.title: ERC-777 & callback-hook reentrancy
topics.description: Tokens with transfer hooks — ERC-777 tokensToSend/tokensReceived, ERC-1155 onERC1155Received, and ERC-721 onERC721Received — execute external code during a transfer. A caller that assumes an ERC-20-compatible transfer is inert can therefore expose stale accounting; the disclosed Uniswap V1/ERC-777 vulnerability used this compatibility edge. Restore invariants before the hook can observe them and use a guard where necessary.

Done when: repeated hook-driven sales extract excess ETH on the vulnerable exchange and fail once reserve/accounting effects precede the interaction and the entry point is guarded.

topics.title: tx.origin authentication
topics.description: Authenticating with `tx.origin == owner` instead of `msg.sender == owner` is phishable: if the owner is tricked into calling a malicious contract, that contract calls the victim, and tx.origin is still the owner, so the check passes. Authorize the immediate caller with msg.sender.

Done when: the phishing test drains the wallet pre-fix and reverts post-fix.

topics.title: Uninitialized proxy & unprotected initializer
topics.description: Proxy deployments move setup from the implementation's constructor to an initializer executed in proxy storage. If initialization is omitted or repeatable, an attacker can claim ownership of the proxy; if the implementation is left initializable, it can be taken over directly and may endanger the proxy. Use a one-shot initializer, initialize the proxy atomically, and call _disableInitializers() in the implementation constructor.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/uninit-proxy/ write an upgradeable Vault whose initialize() sets owner but lacks the initializer guard, and a test where an attacker calls initialize() to claim ownership; then add the guard + _disableInitializers(). Done when: the attacker becomes owner pre-fix and initialize() reverts as already-initialized post-fix.

topics.title: Unprotected selfdestruct
topics.description: An unguarded path to SELFDESTRUCT lets any caller force the contract's entire ETH balance to the chosen beneficiary. Since Cancun/EIP-6780, it does not delete code or storage unless executed in the same transaction as creation, but the balance transfer and execution halt remain; the opcode is deprecated and new uses are strongly discouraged. Avoid it, or strictly authorize any unavoidable legacy path.

Done when: the unauthorized balance transfer succeeds pre-fix and reverts after onlyOwner is added; separately assert the code-preservation behavior required by EIP-6780.

topics.title: Signature-based authorization gaps
topics.description: When authorization is proven by an off-chain signature instead of msg.sender, the contract must recover a nonzero signer, verify that signer has the required role, and hash the intended structured action under the correct domain. topics.title: Integer overflow & underflow
topics.description: Before Solidity 0.8 arithmetic wrapped silently; Solidity 0.8+ reverts on ordinary overflow and underflow by default. The protection does not make unchecked arithmetic, explicit narrowing conversions, or inline assembly safe: unchecked operations wrap and explicit integer conversions truncate. Keep value-bearing arithmetic checked and use range-checked casts such as SafeCast.

topics.title: Division-before-multiplication & precision loss
topics.description: Solidity integer division rounds toward zero, so `(a / b) * c` discards a remainder before the multiplication can preserve it. Moving multiplication first may overflow even when the final quotient fits, so use full-precision mulDiv where necessary and choose the rounding direction for the economic operation explicitly. Repeated favorable rounding can turn small errors into extractable value.

Done when: the test shows a non-zero cumulative edge pre-fix and no attacker-favorable residue post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Predict when integer division discards precision and choose an explicit rounding direction

topics.title: ERC-4626 first-depositor share inflation

OpenZeppelin's defense combines virtual assets and shares with a decimals offset, making the attack unprofitable while reducing rounding loss.

topics.description: The oracle-focused read-only reentrancy variant occurs when a consumer prices assets from a pool view while the pool is mid-callback and its balances and share supply are transiently inconsistent. topics.title: External-call & token-integration attacks
topics.description: OWASP SC06: bugs at the boundary where a contract calls out or integrates a token it doesn't control — unchecked return values, tokens that don't return a bool or take a fee on transfer, ETH force-fed in, and callees that grief the caller's gas. 'It's just an ERC-20' is where these hide.

topics.title: Signature & cryptography attacks
topics.description: Bugs in how contracts verify off-chain signatures and proofs: replayable signatures (no nonce, no chainId, no domain separator), ECDSA malleability and zero-address ecrecover, permit front-running, and Merkle proof forgery. The crypto is sound; the misuse around it is the vulnerability.

topics.title: Ordering, timing & MEV attacks
topics.description: Everything in the public mempool is visible and reorderable before inclusion, so an attacker (or the proposer) can front-run, back-run, or sandwich a victim's transaction, exploit weak on-chain randomness and timestamp dependence, or stuff blocks. Defense is slippage/deadline limits, commit-reveal, and off-chain ordering (private relays).

topics.title: Unchecked low-level call returns
topics.description: `address.call`, `send`, and `delegatecall` return a bool on failure rather than reverting; ignoring that bool means a failed transfer or call is treated as success, so the contract updates state as if value moved when it didn't (the 2016 King of the Ether payout bug). Fix: check every low-level return (`(bool ok,) = ...; require(ok)`), or use a wrapper that reverts.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/unchecked-call/ write a payout function that uses `to.send(amount)` (or .call) and ignores the result, and a test where a reverting recipient makes the contract mark a payment complete without paying; then require the return. Done when: the accounting desyncs pre-fix and reverts post-fix.

topics.title: Missing-return-value tokens & SafeERC20
topics.description: Some legacy ERC-20s return no value from transfer/approve, so an ABI call expecting `bool` reverts while decoding empty return data even though the token call itself returned successfully; that caller revert unwinds the whole transaction. Some tokens also require allowance to be set to zero before a new non-zero value. Fix: OpenZeppelin SafeERC20's safeTransfer treats empty return data as success only after a successful call, while forceApprove supports zero-first tokens. This does not erase ERC-20's transaction-ordering allowance race.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/missing-return/ write a mock legacy token whose transfer returns nothing and a vault that calls `require(token.transfer(...))`, showing the typed call reverts while decoding empty return data and rolls back the transaction; then swap to SafeERC20.safeTransfer. Add a second mock whose approve requires zero-first and exercise forceApprove. Done when: both non-standard behaviors work through the matching SafeERC20 wrappers, and notes keep the separate allowance-ordering race explicit.

topics.title: Gas griefing & return-bomb
topics.description: A callee can weaponize gas: consume its forwarded allotment so a relayed/sub-call fails, or expose enormous returndata so a caller that decodes or stores unbounded `bytes` pays memory-expansion and copy costs — the 'return bomb'. A gas limit on the subcall alone does not cap the caller's returndata-copy cost. Fix: bound forwarded gas for the call's work and separately cap how many returndata bytes are copied, as ExcessivelySafeCall does.

topics.title: Signature malleability & zero-address ecrecover
topics.description: ECDSA on secp256k1 is malleable: for a valid (v, r, s), flipping v and replacing s with n-s yields another valid signature for the same message, which breaks replay keys based on signature bytes. Separately, raw `ecrecover` returns address(0) on malformed input, so a zero/uninitialized trusted signer is dangerous. Fix: enforce lower-half-order s and reject failed recovery; OpenZeppelin ECDSA performs these validations.

Done when: the malleable/zero-address bypass works pre-fix and reverts once you use OZ ECDSA (low-s + non-zero) checks.

topics.title: Merkle proof forgery & second-preimage
topics.description: In a commutative keccak Merkle tree, a 64-byte raw leaf preimage can be confused with the concatenation of two 32-byte internal nodes: hashing that preimage reproduces an internal-node hash and can prove data that was never intended as a leaf. Fix by domain-separating or double-hashing leaves (OpenZeppelin's standard tree does this). Double-claim prevention is separate stateful accounting, commonly keyed by a stable leaf index or identifier.

Done when: the node-as-leaf proof succeeds pre-fix, fails post-fix, and a valid claim cannot execute twice.

topics.title: Front-running & back-running
topics.description: Transactions broadcast through a public mempool reveal their calldata before inclusion. Front-running places an action before a target; back-running places one immediately after a known state change. Searchers can bid for ordering, but builders/proposers determine the final block order. Defenses depend on the mechanism: hide information until commitment, use protected order flow, enforce user bounds, or remove the ordering profit entirely.

topics.title: Sandwich attacks & missing slippage/deadline
topics.description: A swap with no meaningful minimum-output bound can be sandwiched: the attacker trades before the victim to move the AMM price, the victim accepts the worse fill, and the attacker trades back after it. A deadline addresses a separate stale-execution risk; it does not itself prevent a sandwich. Fix: derive a user-acceptable amountOutMin from a quote and bounded slippage, and use a near-term deadline.

topics.title: Weak randomness & timestamp dependence
topics.description: Block values are public at execution time and some are proposer-influenced, so lotteries or games built from `block.timestamp`, recent `blockhash`, or same-transaction mixes are predictable or biasable. Use a verifiable randomness flow such as VRF and follow its request/fulfillment rules. Timestamps are appropriate for ordinary time gates with tolerance, but exact-boundary outcomes or randomness must not depend on a proposer-adjustable timestamp.

topics.title: Commit-reveal absence & JIT liquidity
topics.description: A value disclosed before it is irrevocably bound can be copied or ordered against, so auctions and guessing games often separate commit(hash) from a later reveal(value, salt), with explicit deadlines and non-reveal handling. JIT liquidity is a different public-ordering strategy: an LP observes a pending swap, mints concentrated liquidity immediately before it, earns fees, burns immediately after, and usually hedges inventory elsewhere. Uniswap's study found JIT rare and generally beneficial to swap execution, not risk-free theft.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/commit-reveal/ implement a sealed-bid auction as (a) a naive plaintext bid and (b) commit(hash(value, salt, bidder)) then reveal(value, salt) in a later phase; test copied plaintext bidding, early/late reveal, and non-reveal handling. Done when: the naive bid is order-exploitable, the phased version binds each bidder before disclosure, and notes contrast commit-reveal with JIT liquidity's mint-swap-burn bundle and hedging tradeoff.

topics.title: Proxy, storage & DoS attacks
topics.description: OWASP SC10 plus denial-of-service: upgradeable-contract hazards (storage-slot collisions, selector clashes, uninitialized implementations, delegatecall to untrusted code that rewrites your storage) and availability attacks (unbounded loops, push-payment reverts, block stuffing).

topics.title: Business-logic & misc attacks
topics.description: OWASP SC02 business-logic vulnerabilities arise when code runs as written but implements an unsafe rule — a broken accounting invariant, a skippable state machine, unvalidated input, a bypassable EXTCODESIZE check, CREATE2 address reuse, or an outright honeypot. Find them by understanding intent, stating invariants, and testing adversarial sequences.

topics.title: Storage-slot collision in proxies
topics.description: A delegatecall proxy and its implementation share ONE storage layout; if the proxy keeps its own variables (admin, implementation) in low slots that the logic contract also uses for different variables, a write to one silently overwrites the other. Fix: ERC-1967 puts proxy internals in keccak-derived slots that Solidity's compiler will not allocate for ordinary state variables; upgrades must also preserve the implementation's storage layout.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/storage-collision/ write a proxy that stores `admin` in slot 0 and a logic contract whose slot 0 is a different variable, and a test where calling the logic overwrites the proxy's admin; then move the admin to ERC-1967's specified admin slot. Done when: the collision hijacks control pre-fix and the ERC-1967 admin slot prevents accidental compiler-allocated overlap post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Explain why proxy state and implementation writes collide, then isolate proxy metadata from compiler-allocated slots

options.title: ERC-1967: Proxy Storage Slots
options.scope: Sections Abstract, Specification through Admin address, and Rationale
options.why: The canonical ERC defines delegatecall proxy state, the keccak-derived implementation and admin slots, and the collision rationale exercised by the build.

topics.title: Function selector clash
topics.description: A proxy forwards unknown 4-byte selectors to its implementation; if a proxy-level function shares a selector with an implementation function, the proxy's own function wins and the call never reaches the implementation. Because selectors are only 4 bytes, collisions are brute-forceable. Fix: transparent admin-versus-user routing, and reject already-mapped selectors when adding diamond facets.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/selector-clash/ construct two functions with colliding 4-byte selectors (brute-force names), put one in a proxy and one in the implementation, and a test showing a call meant for one hits the other; then apply transparent-proxy routing. Done when: the misroute is demonstrable pre-fix and blocked post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Demonstrate how a four-byte proxy selector intercepts a call intended for its implementation

options.why: The canonical ERC states that differently named functions can share a four-byte selector and that the proxy's match bypasses implementation code.

topics.title: Uninitialized implementation & delegatecall to untrusted
topics.description: delegatecall runs the CALLEE's code in the CALLER's context (its storage, msg.sender, address(this)), so delegatecalling untrusted code lets it rewrite caller storage. An implementation left initializable is also directly callable: an attacker can initialize and control it; historical pre-EIP-6780 UUPS exploits then used delegated SELFDESTRUCT to delete the implementation and brick its proxies. Fix: _disableInitializers() in the implementation constructor; never delegatecall attacker-controlled targets.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/delegatecall-untrusted/ write a wallet that delegatecalls a user-supplied library address and an attacker library that overwrites `owner`; then write an implementation left initializable and claim it directly. In a local pre-Cancun EVM only, reproduce the historical delegated-SELFDESTRUCT brick, and document why EIP-6780 prevents that deletion on current Ethereum. Done when: the storage takeover and initializer claim succeed pre-fix, fail after target restriction and _disableInitializers(), and the fork-dependent brick is accurately bounded.

requirements.purpose: Trace untrusted code executing against the caller's address, balance, storage, and original message context

topics.title: Unbounded loops & gas-limit DoS
topics.description: A function that loops over an array anyone can grow can eventually exceed the block gas limit and become uncallable, freezing whatever that path gates (distributing to all users, clearing a queue). The attacker adds entries until the transaction no longer fits. Fix: pull-over-push, pagination or bounded batches, and caps on attacker-growable collections.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/unbounded-loop/ write a rewards distributor that loops over all participants in one call, and a test where an attacker registers many addresses until distribute() exceeds the block gas limit; then refactor to a pull-based claim. Done when: distribute() is bricked pre-fix and the pull version is unaffected by list size post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Relate attacker-controlled iteration growth to the per-transaction block gas ceiling

topics.title: Push-payment reverts & revert griefing
topics.description: Pushing ETH to a recipient inside a critical flow lets a malicious recipient revert and block everyone — the King-of-the-Ether / auction-refund bug: if the previous leader is a contract whose receive() always reverts, no new bid that must refund them can succeed. Fix: record what each party is owed and let them withdraw separately, so one reverting party cannot stall the rest.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/push-pull/ write an auction that refunds the previous bidder by push inside bid(), and an attacker contract that reverts on receive() to freeze the auction; then convert refunds to a pending-withdrawals mapping. Done when: the auction is stuck pre-fix and the pull-based refunds keep it live post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Reproduce a recipient-controlled revert that freezes leader replacement, then isolate refunds behind withdrawals

topics.title: Block stuffing
topics.description: An attacker can pay to fill consecutive blocks and suppress competing transactions until a deadline passes — the historical Fomo3D winner used block stuffing to remain the last buyer. It attacks time-critical liveness when short-lived censorship has a larger payoff than its cost. Fix the incentive and failure mode: avoid winner-take-all deadlines, widen or randomize action windows where appropriate, and use redundant actors rather than a single required transaction.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/block-stuffing/ write a last-actor-wins deadline game. Use vm.warp to model an honest action being absent through the censorship window; explicitly note that Foundry does not simulate mempool ordering or real block packing. Compare the attacker's measured historical gas spend with the prize, then redesign so suppressing one actor for a short window does not decide the payout. Done when: the test demonstrates only the deadline/liveness assumption, the notes separate that model from actual block stuffing, and the mitigation removes the single-transaction deadline dependency.

requirements.purpose: Separate historical Fomo3D block inclusion suppression from a local deadline-liveness model

topics.title: Accounting & invariant violations
topics.description: The core of business-logic bugs: a protocol invariant that should always hold (sum of user balances == totalSupply; debt remains within collateral limits; shares are priced consistently) is broken by some path — a double-count, forgotten decrement, or duplicated fee. State the economic property and exercise adversarial call sequences with invariant tests; static pattern matching alone does not know the intended rule.

topics.title: State-machine & sequencing errors
topics.description: Protocols with phases (created → funded → active → settled) break when a function can be called in the wrong phase, twice, or in an unintended order — claiming before finalize, initializing after use, repeating a one-shot step, or skipping a transition. Fix: model explicit states and guard every phase-sensitive entry point; use one-shot state where a step must run exactly once.

Validate untrusted external inputs at each reachable boundary before using them, including privileged configuration inputs.

topics.title: Contract-size (EXTCODESIZE) checks
topics.description: Using `extcodesize(addr) == 0` (or address.code.length) to reject contracts is bypassable: during a contract's constructor its runtime code is not deployed, so a call from that constructor passes the 'EOA-only' check. `tx.origin == msg.sender` is not a sound replacement. Fix: do not base authorization on caller code presence; use the actual permission or protocol property you need.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/contract-size/ write a reward gated by extcodesize(msg.sender)==0, and an attacker whose constructor calls it (code size 0) to bypass the check; then replace caller-type guessing with an explicit eligibility allowlist. Done when: the constructor bypass claims the reward pre-fix, the unauthorized attacker is rejected post-fix, and an authorized claimant still succeeds.

requirements.purpose: Bypass caller-code authorization from a constructor and replace it with an explicit permission rule

topics.title: create2 address reuse & metamorphic contracts
topics.description: CREATE2 derives an address from the deployer, salt, and hash of init code. Under pre-EIP-6780 deletion semantics, a fixed piece of metamorphic init code could be reused after SELFDESTRUCT while returning different runtime bytecode, so one address served different code over time. EIP-6780 now prevents later-transaction SELFDESTRUCT from deleting code on Ethereum; counterfactual addresses funded before first deployment remain a separate trust risk.
topics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/create2-reuse/ use a local pre-Cancun EVM to deploy fixed metamorphic init code via CREATE2, make the resulting contract SELFDESTRUCT, change the runtime code returned by that same init code, and redeploy with the same deployer and salt. Then run the same lifecycle under Cancun semantics and show EIP-6780 prevents deletion and redeployment. Done when: the legacy test serves two runtime bytecodes at one address, the current-EVM test cannot replace the code, and notes explain that changing the init-code hash would change the CREATE2 address.

requirements.purpose: Hold deployer, salt, and init-code hash constant when reasoning about address reuse

topics.title: Honeypots & tx.origin phishing
topics.description: Not every victim is a protocol — some contracts are bait. A honeypot appears exploitable but hides a second mechanism that makes the attempt fail after the victim commits funds. tx.origin phishing is a separate social-engineering pattern: lure a privileged user into calling an attacker contract so the downstream victim still sees that user as tx.origin. Analyze unfamiliar exploit targets in a local sandbox and authorize with msg.sender, not tx.origin.

Separately, write a wallet authorized by tx.origin and a phishing intermediary, then change wallet authorization to msg.sender. Done when: the honeypot victim loses ETH for the documented reason, the phishing call drains the tx.origin wallet pre-fix, and the intermediary is rejected post-fix.

topics.title: Automated Market Makers (AMMs)
topics.description: How on-chain exchanges price and settle without an orderbook: a bonding curve invariant (constant-product, constant-sum, or stableswap) holds reserves in a pool, and every trade moves along the curve.

topics.title: Uniswap V2
topics.description: The canonical constant-product AMM: pair contracts holding two reserves, LP tokens for shares, a cumulative-price TWAP oracle, flash swaps, and an optional protocol fee. The reference every later AMM is measured against.

topics.title: Uniswap V3
topics.description: Concentrated liquidity: LPs supply capital only within a chosen price range, expressed via ticks and a sqrtPriceX96 fixed-point price, with per-position fee-growth accounting. Far higher capital efficiency at the cost of active management.

topics.title: Uniswap V4
topics.description: A singleton PoolManager holding all pools, flash accounting via transient storage, hooks for custom pool logic, and ERC-6909 claim balances. Same concentrated-liquidity math as V3 with a radically cheaper, more extensible architecture.

topics.title: DeFi Oracles
topics.description: How contracts learn off-chain prices safely: Chainlink push feeds, Uniswap TWAPs, and Pyth pull updates, plus the manipulation-resistance decisions that separate a safe price source from a drainable one.

topics.title: Constant-product market maker (x*y=k)
topics.description: The core AMM invariant: reserves x and y must satisfy x*y=k, so a fee-free swap of dx in yields dy = y*dx/(x+dx) out, keeping the product constant. Price is the reserve ratio y/x and moves against the trader as the pool depletes — large trades suffer growing price impact because the curve is convex. With Uniswap V2's 0.3% input fee, only 99.7% of dx is used to price output and the reserve product grows after the full input arrives.
topics.aiContext: Build: implement defi/amm/ConstantProduct.sol from scratch — swap/addLiquidity/removeLiquidity + a getAmountOut using the (amountIn*997*reserveOut)/(reserveIn*1000+amountIn*997) fee formula; Foundry test in test/defi/ConstantProduct.t.sol. Done when: an invariant/fuzz test proves k (reserve0*reserve1) never DECREASES across any sequence of swaps and that removeLiquidity rounds in the pool's favor.

topics.title: Constant-sum & hybrid AMMs
topics.description: A constant-sum curve x+y=k gives zero price impact and a fixed 1:1 price but can be fully drained of one asset, so it is unusable alone. StableSwap interpolates between constant-sum near a balanced peg and constant-product as reserves become imbalanced. Understanding both extremes is the setup for its invariant.

Done when: a test drains reserveY to 0 with a single large swap, demonstrating the failure mode.

topics.title: Stableswap invariant & amplification (Curve)
topics.description: Curve's StableSwap blends constant-sum and constant-product with an amplification coefficient A: higher A keeps prices near 1:1 across a wider balanced region. With S=Σxᵢ and P=Πxᵢ, its invariant is A*n^n*S + D = A*n^n*D + D^(n+1)/(n^n*P); implementations solve iteratively for D and the output balance. The assumption is correlated assets — a depeg lets arbitrageurs exchange the impaired asset through the flat region.
topics.aiContext: Build: in defi/amm/StableSwap.sol implement the 2-asset stableswap invariant with a fixed A, solving for D and for get_dy via Newton iteration; test/defi/StableSwap.t.sol compares its slippage to x*y=k. Done when: a test shows near-zero slippage for balanced swaps at high A and that raising A flattens the price curve near the peg.

topics.title: LP shares & impermanent loss
topics.description: Liquidity providers deposit both assets and receive fungible LP tokens representing a pro-rata claim on the reserves. Because a constant-product pool is arbitraged to the external price, an LP ends up with more of the relatively cheaper asset. Impermanent loss is the pool-versus-hold value gap before fees; for an initially balanced, fee-free position it depends on the ending price ratio, while path-dependent fees can offset it.
topics.aiContext: Build: in defi/amm/LiquidityMath.sol add a pure function computing IL as a function of the price ratio r (IL = 2*sqrt(r)/(1+r) - 1) and test it against hand-worked cases (r=2 -> ~5.7% loss, r=4 -> 20%). Done when: test/defi/LiquidityMath.t.sol matches the closed-form IL at r=1,2,4 within rounding.

topics.title: Uniswap V2 pair & reserves
topics.description: Each pair holds reserve0/reserve1 of two sorted tokens and enforces x*y=k in swap(): it optimistically sends the requested outputs, then requires the post-balances adjusted for the 0.3% fee (balance*1000 - amountIn*3) to satisfy the scaled invariant. The factory deploys one pair per sorted token pair with CREATE2, so its address is derivable from factory, salt, and init-code hash. sync() updates reserves to balances; skim() transfers only balance excess without changing reserves.

topics.title: Uniswap V2 LP mint/burn math
topics.description: The first liquidity provider mints sqrt(amount0*amount1) - MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY shares, while MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY (1000 units) is permanently locked at address(0), increasing the cost of share-value inflation. Later deposits mint min(amount0*totalSupply/reserve0, amount1*totalSupply/reserve1); integer division rounds down, and depositing an unmatched excess does not increase shares.

topics.title: Uniswap V2 TWAP oracle
topics.description: The pair accumulates price0CumulativeLast += price0*timeElapsed, with price0 encoded as the UQ112.112 ratio reserve1/reserve0. _update records the previous reserves' price before replacing them, at most once per block because timeElapsed is then zero. A consumer differences two cumulative snapshots and divides by elapsed time; if no pair write occurs at the endpoint, it must first extend the cumulative counterfactually from the current reserves. Manipulating a longer average requires sustaining distortion across time, but short windows and thin liquidity remain weak.
topics.aiContext: Build: in defi/oracle/Univ2Twap.sol compute the time-weighted average from two cumulative snapshots, extending the endpoint cumulative from the current reserves when no pair write occurred; test/defi/Univ2Twap.t.sol uses vm.warp to advance blocks. Done when: an idle endpoint still produces the manually accumulated TWAP within fixed-point rounding, and a single-block spike barely moves a long-window average.

topics.description: When feeTo is enabled, _mintFee lazily mints protocol LP shares during the next mint or burn. topics.title: Concentrated liquidity & the L parameter
topics.description: V3 lets an LP concentrate liquidity L within [pa,pb]. In range, amount0 = L*(sqrt(pb)-sqrt(P))/(sqrt(P)*sqrt(pb)) and amount1 = L*(sqrt(P)-sqrt(pa)); below the range it is all token0, and above it is all token1. Concentration provides greater depth in-range, but a position earns swap fees only while its liquidity is active.

topics.title: sqrtPriceX96 & Q64.96 fixed point

topics.title: Uniswap V3 fee growth & positions
topics.description: V3 tracks feeGrowthGlobal0/1X128 per unit of active liquidity. Tick.getFeeGrowthInside conditionally derives growth below and above each boundary from feeGrowthOutside, then subtracts both from global growth. A position snapshots inside growth and accrues liquidity*(insideNow-insideLast)/2^128 with modular-overflow semantics. Distinct ranges and snapshots make positions non-fungible at the periphery layer.

Done when: a position accrues fees only for swaps that occur while the price sits inside its range, and zero while price is outside.

topics.title: Uniswap V4 flash accounting (lock/unlock)
topics.description: State-changing V4 pool operations run after PoolManager.unlock calls the caller's unlockCallback. Operations accrue signed per-caller currency deltas in transient storage; unlock reverts unless the count of nonzero deltas returns to zero. settle pays a negative delta and take withdraws a positive one, so a route can settle net currency movement rather than transfer at every hop.

Done when: a route that leaves any non-zero delta reverts on unlock, while a correctly settled route pays and withdraws only its net currency deltas.

topics.title: Uniswap V4 hooks
topics.description: A V4 hook is a contract called at selected pool lifecycle points. Hooks.sol derives enabled callbacks from the least-significant bits of the hook address, so CREATE2 salt mining is commonly used to obtain a matching address. A beforeSwap hook can return a fee override only for a dynamic-fee pool and must set the override flag; hook code can alter or block execution, so its trust model is part of pool risk.

Done when: the override changes the swap fee, omitting the override flag does not, and PoolManager rejects a hook address whose permission bits are invalid.

topics.title: Uniswap V3 TWAP from tick cumulatives
topics.description: V3 observations store tickCumulative and secondsPerLiquidityCumulativeX128 in a ring. observe([window,0]) returns past and current cumulatives; dividing their tick-cumulative difference by window yields the arithmetic mean tick, with negative division rounded toward negative infinity before quote conversion. increaseObservationCardinalityNext expands capacity only as later observations are written. A request older than initialized history reverts with OLD.

topics.title: Oracle manipulation resistance
topics.description: Oracle safety depends on the source, liquidity, averaging window, update model, staleness policy, and value at risk. A same-transaction AMM spot read is manipulable because the attacker can trade before use and reverse afterward. TWAPs increase the cost of sustaining distortion but do not guarantee safety; external feeds introduce different liveness and configuration risks. Cross-checks need explicit divergence and failure policies rather than blind averaging.

topics.title: Lending Protocols
topics.description: Overcollateralized on-chain money markets: suppliers earn interest, borrowers post collateral and draw debt, and a health-factor plus liquidation mechanism keeps the system solvent. Aave V3 and Compound V3 are the reference designs.

topics.title: Stablecoins
topics.description: Assets engineered to hold a peg: overcollateralized CDPs (DAI/USDS), algorithmic/seigniorage designs (and why they fail), and the mechanics of minting, burning, and liquidating against a price feed.

topics.title: Staking, LSTs & Restaking
topics.description: Turning staked ETH into a liquid, composable asset: Lido's rebasing stETH and wrapped wstETH, and EigenLayer's restaking that reuses that stake to secure additional services for extra yield and extra slashing risk.

topics.title: Perpetual Futures
topics.description: Leveraged derivatives with no expiry, kept near spot by a funding rate exchanged between longs and shorts. Covers mark vs index price, funding, and the GMX pooled-liquidity and Hyperliquid orderbook models.

topics.title: Yield Vaults (ERC-4626)
topics.description: The tokenized-vault standard that turned yield strategies into composable share tokens: deposit an asset, mint shares whose price grows as yield accrues, redeem for more of the asset — with the rounding and inflation-defense rules that make it safe.

topics.title: Flash Loans
topics.description: Uncollateralized loans that are safe because they are atomic: borrow, act, and repay plus a fee within a single transaction, or the whole thing reverts. The primitive behind arbitrage, liquidations, collateral swaps — and many exploits.

Variable debt uses the same scaled-balance pattern with a variable-borrow index, and rates respond to utilization. aTokens remain transferable receipts, but integer ray math means mint, burn, and transfer paths must preserve the scaled accounting.

topics.title: Health factor & liquidation
topics.description: Aave gates solvency with the health factor: HF = sum(collateral_i * liquidationThreshold_i) / totalDebt, all in a common base currency. Borrow capacity uses max LTV, while liquidation eligibility uses the higher liquidation threshold: HF below 1 permits liquidation. A liquidator repays an allowed portion of debt and receives corresponding collateral plus a configured liquidation bonus; current V3 close-factor behavior depends on health and dust conditions.

topics.title: Algorithmic stablecoins & the UST collapse
topics.description: Terra Classic's market module implemented native stablecoin/Luna swaps by burning the offered coin and minting the requested coin at oracle exchange rates. That makes redemption capacity reflexive: absorbing stablecoin exits expands Luna supply, so falling demand and price can require still more issuance. After the May 2022 collapse, the original chain was renamed Terra Classic and market-module mint/burn swaps were disabled; the new Terra chain launched without native stablecoins or the market module.

The delegation relationship therefore adds operator and service-specific risk beyond ordinary Ethereum staking.

Positive funding makes longs pay shorts; negative funding reverses the direction.

topics.title: ERC-4626 yield vault mechanics

topics.title: Opcode gas accounting
topics.description: Opcode charges combine schedule groups with operation-specific dynamic components: account and storage access can be cold or warm (EIP-2929), memory growth charges the increase in the memory-cost function, and SSTORE depends on original, current, and new values. EIP-150 caps ordinary CALL-family forwarded gas at all but one sixty-fourth of the available gas after call costs. If a frame cannot pay a charge, it halts exceptionally: that frame's state changes are discarded and it returns no remaining gas.

topics.title: Stack, arithmetic & bitwise opcodes
topics.description: The stack holds at most 1024 256-bit words. PUSH0 pushes zero; PUSH1–PUSH32 push 1–32 immediate bytes; DUP1–DUP16 copy and SWAP1–SWAP16 reorder accessible stack items. Arithmetic includes ADD/MUL/SUB/DIV/SDIV/MOD/SMOD/EXP/ADDMOD/MULMOD; comparisons include LT/GT/SLT/SGT/EQ/ISZERO; AND/OR/XOR/NOT/BYTE/SHL/SHR/SAR operate on bits. Signed opcodes interpret the same 256 bits as two's-complement values.
topics.aiContext: Build: on evm.codes' playground assemble PUSH1 0x03 PUSH1 0x02 ADD and one signed vs unsigned case (e.g. SDIV of a negative), recording each in contracts/phase08/stack-ops.md. Done when: you can predict the stack after each opcode and explain why DIV by zero yields 0 rather than reverting.

topics.title: Memory opcodes & expansion
topics.description: Memory is a volatile, zero-initialized byte array. MLOAD reads 32 bytes, MSTORE writes 32 bytes, MSTORE8 writes one byte, and MSIZE reports the active-memory size in bytes. The active range rounds up to 32-byte words; expanding from a to b words charges Cmem(b)−Cmem(a), where Cmem(x)=3x+⌊x²/512⌋. A high offset therefore pays for the entire newly activated range.

topics.title: Storage & transient opcodes
topics.description: SLOAD costs 2100 gas for a cold slot and 100 once warm. SSTORE metering depends on the slot's original, current, and new values under EIP-2200, with a 2100 first-touch surcharge under EIP-2929 and transaction refunds capped to one fifth of gas used under EIP-3529. TLOAD and TSTORE each cost 100 gas, share contract-owned transient state across its frames, journal writes across reverts, and discard all transient state at transaction end; TSTORE is forbidden in a static context.

topics.title: The CALL family opcodes
topics.description: CALL executes target code with the target's state context, msg.sender set to the current account, and an explicit value. DELEGATECALL executes target code in the caller's state context while preserving the current frame's sender and value. STATICCALL enters a static context in which state-changing operations fail. CALLCODE is the legacy call variant that keeps the caller's state context but replaces sender/value semantics differently. EIP-150 caps requested forwarded gas after call costs; value-bearing CALL also receives the specified stipend.

topics.title: CREATE & CREATE2 opcodes
topics.description: Both instructions execute init code whose successful output becomes the account's runtime code. topics.title: Context, external-code & halting opcodes
topics.description: EXTCODESIZE/EXTCODECOPY inspect another account's code. RETURNDATASIZE/RETURNDATACOPY expose the previous subcall's output buffer. LOG0–LOG4 charge 375 base, 375 per topic, and 8 per data byte, plus memory expansion. RETURN and REVERT both return a memory range; REVERT rolls back the frame without consuming all remaining gas, while an invalid instruction halts exceptionally and leaves no gas in that frame.

topics.title: Solidity memory layout & the free memory pointer
topics.description: Solidity reserves 0x00–0x3f as scratch space, stores the free-memory pointer at 0x40 (initially 0x80), and reserves 0x60–0x7f as a zero slot that must not be written. Manual allocation reads 0x40, uses an appropriately aligned region, and advances the pointer. Some compiler temporaries larger than scratch space may use memory at the free pointer without advancing it, so unallocated memory is not guaranteed to remain zero.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/FreeMem.sol write assembly that allocates one aligned word by reading and advancing the 0x40 pointer, captures that post-allocation pointer, stores a sentinel there, then performs abi.encode; test in test/phase08/FreeMem.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the captured pointer is exactly the initial pointer plus 0x20, abi.encode does not overwrite the allocated sentinel, and the zero slot at 0x60 remains zero.

topics.title: Decoding calldata in Yul
topics.description: The EVM dialect exposes calldataload, calldatacopy, and calldatasize. For a standard external ABI function call, bytes 0–3 hold the selector and the encoded argument tuple starts at byte 4. Static values occupy 32-byte head words; a dynamic head word is an offset relative to the start of that tuple, pointing to length and data in the tail. Opcode reads beyond calldata are zero-padded, so manual decoders must enforce the ABI bounds and canonical-shape checks they rely on.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/CalldataYul.sol decode a (uint256,address) pair by hand with calldataload at offsets 4 and 0x24, and a dynamic bytes arg via its tuple-relative offset; test valid encoding plus truncated heads and out-of-bounds dynamic tails in test/phase08/CalldataYul.t.sol. Done when: forge test matches abi.encode on valid input, rejects each malformed low-level call, and you can explain why calldataload itself zero-pads rather than reverting.

topics.title: Reverting with data in assembly
topics.description: `revert(offset, size)` returns a memory slice as failure data, rolls back the current frame's changes, and preserves unused gas. After a failed subcall, copying `returndatasize()` bytes with RETURNDATACOPY and reverting over that exact slice bubbles the failure payload.

topics.title: Huff jump tables & when Huff pays off

Manual bytecode can optimize a known interface, but the author owns every control-flow and stack-safety decision.

topics.description: A function selector is the first 4 bytes of keccak256 of the canonical signature string — `bytes4(keccak256("transfer(address,uint256)")) == 0xa9059cbb` — using canonical types (`uint256`, not `uint`), no argument names, and no spaces. External-call calldata is this selector followed by ABI-encoded arguments. The 32-bit selector space permits collisions, which matters especially when proxy and implementation interfaces overlap.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/Selector.sol compute a selector in Solidity and cross-check with `cast sig "transfer(address,uint256)"`; record three signatures and their selectors in test/phase08/Selector.t.sol. Done when: forge test asserts your computed bytes4 equals the expected value and you can explain why `uint` vs `uint256` in the string breaks it.

requirements.purpose: Compute selectors from canonical signatures and distinguish them from encoded arguments

topics.title: The dispatcher jump table
topics.description: Compiler-generated runtime code first rejects calldata shorter than 4 bytes, then can extract a selector with `shr(0xe0, calldataload(0))`, compare it with function selectors, and jump to the matching body. The exact comparison tree and opcodes are compiler-version, pipeline, optimizer, and interface dependent, so they must be read from the actual deployed-bytecode output rather than assumed.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/Dispatch.md compile and disassemble a 3-function contract with the repository's pinned solc settings, then annotate the short-calldata guard, selector extraction, comparisons, jump destinations, and unmatched-call path. Done when: the annotations map all three selectors and explicitly record the compiler version and optimizer settings instead of generalizing the observed dispatcher shape.

requirements.purpose: Recognize selector extraction and jump routing in the actual compiler output without assuming an undocumented dispatch heuristic

topics.title: Calldata layout, fallback & receive at bytecode level
topics.description: Function-call calldata is a 4-byte selector followed by ABI head/tail encoding: static values are encoded in place, while a dynamic head word points to its tail. Empty calldata routes to `receive()` when present; otherwise a matching payable `fallback()` may handle it. Any calldata with no matching function selector routes to `fallback()` when present. Proxies use that unmatched-call path to delegate.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/Fallback.sol implement receive() and a fallback() that logs msg.data, then in test/phase08/Fallback.t.sol send (a) empty calldata, (b) 3 bytes, (c) an unknown 4-byte selector. Done when: forge test proves which handler each case hits and you can explain why <4-byte data never matches a selector.

topics.title: Sequential slot assignment & struct packing
topics.description: With the default layout base, Solidity assigns statically sized state variables from slot 0 in C3-linearized inheritance order. Value types use only their needed bytes and pack into a slot from the lower-order bytes when they fit; structs and arrays start a new slot, and their members or elements then follow packing rules. Constants and immutables do not occupy storage slots. Upgrade implementations must preserve the existing layout.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/Layout.sol declare a mix of uint256, uint64, address, and bool, deploy on anvil, then read raw slots with `cast storage <addr> <n>` and map each variable in test notes. Done when: you can predict which variables share a slot and explain why reordering them is fatal to a delegatecall/upgradeable contract.

topics.title: Mapping & dynamic-array slot derivation
topics.description: For a mapping based at slot `p`, key `k` starts at `keccak256(h(k) . p)`: `h` pads value-type keys to 32 bytes but uses unpadded data for `bytes` and `string` keys. Nested mappings apply the rule recursively. A dynamic array normally stores its length at `p`, with data from `keccak256(p)`; 32-byte elements use `keccak256(p) + i`, while smaller elements can pack. Short `bytes` and `string` values are a separate in-slot encoding.
topics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/MapSlot.sol compute a mapping entry's slot in assembly (mstore key, mstore p, keccak256) and read it back with sload; assert equality against the Solidity mapping in test/phase08/MapSlot.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and you can explain why a short `string`/`bytes` (≤31 bytes) is the exception that packs into slot p itself.

topics.title: ERC-7201 namespaced storage
topics.description: ERC-7201 documents a storage namespace as an annotated struct rooted at `keccak256(abi.encode(uint256(keccak256(bytes(id))) - 1)) & ~bytes32(uint256(0xff))`. The subtract-one location is outside Solidity's ordinary tree, the second hash keeps a multi-slot namespace disjoint under the stated assumptions, and the mask aligns the root to 256 slots. The annotation is not compiler-enforced, so code must use the claimed root correctly and namespace IDs must not collide.

topics.title: EIP-1167 minimal-proxy runtime bytecode
topics.description: ERC-1167 specifies a 45-byte deployed runtime that copies calldata, delegatecalls a fixed 20-byte implementation with all gas, copies returndata, and returns or reverts with it. Because a clone runs the implementation in the clone's storage context, the implementation constructor does not initialize clone state; initialization must be performed explicitly and atomically enough to prevent takeover.
