topics.title: Metamorphic contracts
topics.description: CREATE2 derives an address from the deployer, salt, and init-code hash, not directly from the runtime returned by that init code. Before EIP-6780, a multi-transaction pattern could delete code with `SELFDESTRUCT` and reuse the same CREATE2 inputs while mutable init-code dependencies returned different runtime. Under EIP-6780, `SELFDESTRUCT` outside the creation transaction transfers balance but does not delete code or storage, so that classic redeployment cycle no longer works.

Done when: the artifact distinguishes init code from runtime code and states the same-creation-transaction exception without claiming same-transaction destroy-and-recreate is possible.

topics.title: Symbolic execution vs fuzzing
topics.description: Fuzzing runs sampled concrete inputs and can demonstrate a counterexample but not exhaust the input domain. Symbolic execution represents inputs symbolically, forks on path conditions, and asks a solver whether an assertion can fail; a completed, sound run can establish the property for the modeled domain. Path explosion, timeouts, unsupported behavior, abstractions, and explicit bounds can leave paths unproven, so `no counterexample` is not by itself a proof result.

Done when: you can state one property fuzzing can only sample but symbolic execution can prove, and why 'no counterexample' from a bounded symbolic run is not a full proof.

topics.title: Halmos: symbolic testing in Foundry
topics.description: Halmos symbolically executes Solidity tests: `check_` parameters range over their Solidity types, `setUp()` establishes the tested state, and `svm` cheatcodes can create additional symbolic values. Assertions can be checked across the explored symbolic domain or produce counterexamples. Dynamic arrays require a fixed chosen length, assumptions restrict the domain, and non-assertion reverts are ignored by default, so those boundaries belong in the proof claim.

topics.title: AVSs & operators (EigenLayer)
topics.description: EigenLayer lets restakers extend Ethereum's economic security to new services. An AVS (Autonomous Verifiable Service) is a service that uses EigenLayer operator sets. Operators run the service's off-chain software; restakers delegate stake to an operator, and operators allocate slashable magnitude to operator sets. The AVS defines tasks, evidence, and enforcement.

topics.title: Restaking delegation & the security model
topics.description: Restakers deposit supported assets into EigenLayer strategies and delegate to one operator. For each strategy, an operator can split slashable magnitude across multiple operator sets, but total encumbered magnitude cannot exceed current max magnitude. This allocates one delegated pool across services without letting AVS allocations overcommit it. A slash reduces delegated stake and max magnitude, shrinking future security capacity.

topics.title: EigenLayer slashing
topics.description: Slashing makes allocated restaked security enforceable. An operator allocates magnitude to an AVS operator set; that set's configured slasher can reduce a bounded proportion of the operator's allocation, which proportionally reduces delegated stake. EigenLayer enforces authorization and allocation bounds, but the AVS remains responsible for safe evidence and slashing policy. Core v1.13 adds a mandatory resolution delay before burnable or redistributable shares from a recorded slash can be cleared.

STARKs use transparent public randomness and hash-based assumptions, usually trading for larger proofs. Succinctness and zero-knowledge are independent properties.

prompts.promptText: How is an Ethereum address derived from a private key, and what is irreversible about it?
prompts.answerHint: privkey → (secp256k1) pubkey → keccak256(pubkey) → last 20 bytes = address. One-way at each step; a lost private key is unrecoverable and there is no admin reset.

prompts.promptText: Name the fields of an EIP-1559 type-2 transaction and say how replay is prevented.
prompts.answerHint: chainId, nonce, maxPriorityFeePerGas, maxFeePerGas, gasLimit, to, value, data, accessList, yParity, r, s. The sender nonce blocks same-chain replay after inclusion; chainId domain-separates the signature across chains.

prompts.promptText: Break down what a sender pays per gas under EIP-1559, and where each part goes.
prompts.answerHint: base fee (burned, set by protocol from block fullness) + effective tip (to the proposer), where effectiveTip = min(maxPriorityFeePerGas, maxFeePerGas - baseFee). Total = gasUsed × (baseFee + effectiveTip).

prompts.promptText: Compare stack, memory, storage, and calldata by lifetime, mutability, and gas cost drivers.
prompts.answerHint: Stack is 256-bit operand workspace with top-16 access; memory is mutable per-call scratch with expansion cost; storage is persistent state with context-dependent SLOAD/SSTORE costs; calldata is immutable call input and avoids a memory copy for read-only external arguments.

prompts.promptText: Why is a blockchain immutable in practice, rather than by decree?
prompts.answerHint: Each block commits to its parent, so altering an old block changes descendant commitments; replacing that history must overcome honest fork choice, finality, and economic security. Pitfall: immutability is economic and consensus-backed, not absolute.

prompts.promptText: What does a Merkle root let you prove, and how large is the proof?
prompts.answerHint: A single 32-byte root commits to an entire set; membership of any leaf is provable with a branch of ~log2(n) sibling hashes, without revealing the rest. Pitfall: it proves inclusion, not exclusion (that needs a sorted/sparse variant).

prompts.promptText: Why can one seed phrase back up an unlimited number of Ethereum addresses?
prompts.answerHint: BIP-32 hierarchical-deterministic derivation expands the BIP-39 seed into a tree of child keys along a BIP-44 path (m/44'/60'/…); each index is a new keypair. Pitfall: the phrase is the master secret — leaking it compromises every derived account.

prompts.promptText: What is JSON-RPC's role, and why does Ethereum want many independent clients?
prompts.answerHint: JSON-RPC is the request/response API (eth_call, eth_sendRawTransaction, …) apps use to read and write chain state. Client diversity means one client's bug can't halt or split the network. Pitfall: a public RPC is trusted infrastructure — it can lie unless you verify.

prompts.promptText: How do EOAs and contract accounts differ in control and fields?
prompts.answerHint: EOA authority signs transaction authorizations; contract-account behavior is code-controlled and only runs when called. Both have nonce, balance, codeHash, and storageRoot fields. EIP-7702 lets an EOA delegate code without giving a contract account a private signing key.

prompts.promptText: How does the nonce prevent replay and enforce ordering?
prompts.answerHint: Each EOA tx must use its exact next sequential nonce, so a mined tx (nonce consumed) can't re-execute and txs process in order. EIP-155 adds chainId to the signature to block cross-chain replay. Pitfall: a missing lower nonce stalls all higher-nonce txs.

prompts.promptText: Name the modern Ethereum transaction types and what makes each distinct.
prompts.answerHint: Legacy wire transactions are untyped RLP (often reported by RPC as type 0x0); typed envelopes are 0x1 access-list (2930), 0x2 dynamic-fee (1559, the default), 0x3 blob (4844), and 0x4 set-code (7702). Pitfall: blob data isn't in calldata — it rides in a separate, short-lived sidecar.

prompts.topicTitle: The EVM as a state machine
prompts.promptText: In what sense is the EVM a state machine?
prompts.answerHint: Each transaction deterministically maps world state plus explicit transaction/block context to a new world state, metered by gas. Nodes agree because there is no live wall-clock input, nondeterministic RNG, or external I/O during execution.

prompts.promptText: Describe the EVM's interpreter loop and its working memory.
prompts.answerHint: Fetch opcode at PC → decode → execute against the 1024-deep stack (plus memory/storage), charge gas, advance or jump PC; halt on STOP/RETURN/REVERT or out-of-gas. Pitfall: stack overflow (>1024) or underflow reverts the whole call.

prompts.promptText: Where does the value of `mapping(k=>v) m` declared at slot p live in storage?
prompts.answerHint: At keccak256(abi.encode(k, p)); the mapping itself occupies slot p only as a placeholder. Dynamic arrays keep length at p and data at keccak256(p). Pitfall: `private` hides nothing — any slot is publicly readable.

prompts.promptText: What does the block header's stateRoot commit to, and why does it matter?
prompts.answerHint: stateRoot commits to the account trie. An account proof authenticates the account and its storageRoot against stateRoot; a separate storage proof authenticates the slot against that storageRoot along the slot key's hashed-nibble path. Changing a slot changes the storage root and ultimately stateRoot.

prompts.promptText: Compare compressed and uncompressed SEC1 public keys and identify the exact bytes Ethereum hashes for an address.
prompts.answerHint: Compressed is 33 bytes: 02/03 plus x, with the prefix encoding y parity. Uncompressed is 65 bytes: 04||x||y. Ethereum hashes the raw 64-byte x||y without 04 using Keccak-256, then takes the final 20 bytes. Pitfalls: 256 bits = 64 hex characters, and SHA3-256 is not Ethereum Keccak-256.

prompts.promptText: Write the byte pipeline that derives and validates an Ethereum address from a 32-byte private scalar.
prompts.answerHint: Reject scalar 0 or >= secp256k1 order; derive point (x,y) with an audited curve primitive; serialize 04||x||y; hash x||y with Keccak-256; slice bytes 12..31; compare against a client/cast vector. Include wrong-prefix and SHA3 negative assertions.

prompts.promptText: What does a valid Ethereum signature prove, and which practical boundaries can still fail?
prompts.answerHint: It proves control of the signing scalar authorized the exact digest. It does not prove safety or human intent. Boundaries include nonce reuse, wrong message prefix/domain, high-s malleability, parity/recovery mistakes, and accepting a zero recovered address.

prompts.promptText: Describe the complete EIP-191 sign-and-recover pipeline for a fixed message, from message bytes to checking the recovered address.
prompts.answerHint: Construct the EIP-191-prefixed digest, sign locally, enforce low-s, carry recovery parity, recover the public key/address, and compare it with the expected address. Mutating one byte or omitting the prefix must not recover the expected signer.

prompts.promptText: Trace a BIP-39 mnemonic into Ethereum child key m/44'/60'/0'/0/0 and name the silent divergence hazards.
prompts.answerHint: Entropy+checksum bits map to 11-bit word indices; NFKD mnemonic enters PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 with salt `mnemonic`+NFKD passphrase to make a 64-byte seed; BIP-32 HMAC chain codes derive hardened and normal children; BIP-44 path selects Ethereum. Wrong normalization, endian index, hardened bit, passphrase, or path yields a valid different wallet.

prompts.promptText: Write deterministic checks for one BIP-39 vector and the first two Ethereum BIP-44 addresses.
prompts.answerHint: Assert entropy checksum and word indices, PBKDF2 seed, root/child derivation, m/44'/60'/0'/0/0 and /1 addresses, checksum rejection, passphrase divergence, and hardened-index encoding against official vectors and cast.

prompts.promptText: What bytes are signed and broadcast for an EIP-1559 type-2 transaction?
prompts.answerHint: Signing digest = keccak256(0x02 || rlp([chainId, nonce, maxPriorityFeePerGas, maxFeePerGas, gasLimit, to, value, data, accessList])). Broadcast bytes append yParity, r, s inside the RLP list. Integers are minimal big-endian bytes; zero is the empty byte string.

prompts.promptText: Implement the RLP subset and type-2 signing pipeline for one fixed transaction vector.
prompts.answerHint: Cover single bytes <0x80, short/long strings and lists, minimal integer encoding, nested access lists, leading type byte, unsigned field order, signing digest, appended signature, and recovered sender; compare complete hex with cast or a maintained client.

prompts.promptText: Separate the HTTP, JSON-RPC, and Ethereum-encoding boundaries in a raw node request.
prompts.answerHint: HTTP 200 can still contain a JSON-RPC error. Match response id; require exactly result or error. QUANTITY is minimal hex parsed as bigint; DATA is even-length bytes. A block tag selects state. eth_call simulates; eth_sendRawTransaction submits signed bytes.

prompts.promptText: Given an eth_getBalance response, separate HTTP failure, JSON-RPC failure, and invalid Ethereum QUANTITY encoding.
prompts.answerHint: Check transport status first, then require exactly one of result or error in a matching JSON-RPC response. A QUANTITY must use minimal 0x-prefixed hex: 0x0 and 0x1 are valid, while 0x01 is not.

prompts.promptText: For a four-leaf Keccak Merkle tree, describe how a leaf is recomputed into the root and why each proof element needs a left or right position.
prompts.answerHint: Hash the leaf with its sibling in the declared order, then repeat with each parent-level sibling until reaching the root. Left/right position is required because swapping concatenation order generally changes the hash.

prompts.topicTitle: The EVM as a state machine
prompts.promptText: Implement the minimum interpreter needed to demonstrate deterministic execution and REVERT rollback.
prompts.answerHint: Track pc, stack, byte-addressed memory, journaled storage, remaining gas, and halt status for PUSH1/ADD/MLOAD/MSTORE/SLOAD/SSTORE/STOP/REVERT. Wrap arithmetic modulo 2^256; reject underflow/invalid opcode/out-of-gas; commit storage only on successful halt.

prompts.promptText: What replaces mining under Proof-of-Stake, and how are validators kept honest?
prompts.answerHint: Validators stake ETH and are pseudo-randomly chosen to propose/attest per 12s slot; correct attestations earn rewards, equivocation or downtime is slashed or penalized. Pitfall: security is economic — an attacker must risk stake, not buy hashpower.

prompts.promptText: How did the Merge change ETH issuance?
prompts.answerHint: It removed PoW miner rewards, leaving only the much smaller PoS validator rewards (~90% issuance drop); with EIP-1559 burn, net issuance can be negative under demand. Pitfall: the Merge changed consensus and issuance, not gas fees or throughput.

prompts.promptText: What gets a validator slashed, versus merely penalized?
prompts.answerHint: Slashing (stake burn + ejection) is for provable equivocation: a double proposal, double vote, or surround vote. Ordinary offline time loses rewards and incurs penalties; the stronger inactivity leak escalates only during prolonged failure to finalize. Pitfall: redundant setups sharing one key can double-sign and self-slash.

prompts.promptText: What does 'finalized' mean under Gasper, and how does it differ from the current head?
prompts.answerHint: Head = current heaviest-attested block (LMD-GHOST), reorg-able; finalized = a checkpoint justified in two consecutive epochs (Casper FFG), and reverting it burns ≥1/3 of stake. Pitfall: only data ~2 epochs old is finalized, not the latest block.

prompts.promptText: Optimistic vs ZK rollups — what is the core difference and its consequence?
prompts.answerHint: Optimistic assumes transactions valid and relies on fraud proofs plus a challenge window (commonly ~7 days for canonical withdrawals); ZK posts a validity proof, so it needs no fraud window but still waits for proof submission and L1 finality. Pitfall: both inherit L1 security only if the required data is available.

prompts.promptText: What is a blob (EIP-4844) and why did it cut L2 fees?
prompts.answerHint: A ~128 KiB data chunk committed to by a transaction, priced in its own blob-gas market and retained only for a limited window (initially ~18 days) — enough for rollups to establish availability without permanent calldata prices. Pitfall: the EVM can access the commitment, not the blob data itself.

prompts.promptText: What does L2Beat's Stage 0/1/2 framework measure?
prompts.answerHint: Rollup maturity, not total security: Stage 0 meets baseline rollup/proof/DA criteria; Stage 1 adds a walkaway condition, a properly configured Security Council, and exit/challenge windows; Stage 2 requires permissionless proofs, long upgrade exits, and tightly limited emergency powers. Pitfall: criteria change, so use the framework changelog.

prompts.promptText: What powers does a rollup sequencer have, and what protects users from it?
prompts.answerHint: It orders L2 txs and gives fast pre-confirmations, and can censor or reorder (MEV), but cannot make invalid state settle when the proof system and L1 contracts work. Forced inclusion via L1 limits censorship. Pitfall: broader admin and proof-system risks still matter, and a down centralized sequencer halts the L2's fast path.

prompts.promptText: Trace an ERC-4337 UserOperation from signing to execution.
prompts.answerHint: User signs a UserOperation → bundler runs view/trace simulation → packs operations into PackedUserOperation[] and submits handleOps → the compatible versioned EntryPoint singleton validates the wallet and optional paymaster, then calls account execution. No consensus change. Pitfall: clients must target a supported EntryPoint version and deployment address.

prompts.promptText: What does EIP-7702 change, and how does it differ from ERC-4337?
prompts.answerHint: 7702 lets an EOA persistently delegate code execution to a contract through a signed authorization, retaining the same address; the delegation can later be replaced or cleared. ERC-4337 defines a separate UserOperation/EntryPoint flow and can also serve delegated EOAs. Pitfall: malicious delegated code can control the account.

prompts.promptText: How does a bundler get paid, and why does it simulate UserOps first?
prompts.answerHint: The EntryPoint reimburses the bundler's gas (+ margin) from each op's prefund; simulation ensures validation won't revert on-chain, which would make the bundler eat the gas. Pitfall: storage-access rules (ERC-7562) keep simulation predictive of real execution.

prompts.promptText: What is a paymaster and what is its main risk?
prompts.answerHint: An ERC-4337 contract that funds a UserOperation's gas for sponsorship or token-denominated fees. Its EntryPoint deposit pays gas; a separate locked stake supports broader validation access. Risk: weak replay, eligibility, quota, or cost checks let attackers drain the deposit.

prompts.promptText: Name a headline change from Pectra and from Fusaka.
prompts.answerHint: Pectra (May 2025): EIP-7702 EOA delegation and EIP-7251 validator consolidation. Fusaka (December 2025): PeerDAS (EIP-7594) plus blob-parameter-only scaling machinery. Pitfall: use post-activation upgrade pages, not pre-fork candidate lists.

prompts.promptText: What did the classic Ethereum roadmap tracks mean, and how is current work organized?
prompts.answerHint: Classic taxonomy: Merge (PoS), Surge (scaling/DA), Scourge (MEV/censorship), Verge (resource-light verification), Purge (simplification), Splurge (miscellaneous). In 2026 EF Protocol work uses Scale, Improve UX, and Harden the L1, while ethereum.org tracks concrete forks. Pitfall: the classic tracks are not a release sequence or current org chart.

prompts.promptText: What did EIP-7251 (MaxEB) change and why does it help?
prompts.answerHint: It lets compounding validators have up to 2048 ETH effective balance and adds in-protocol consolidation, reducing redundant validator indices and consensus messages; the 32-ETH activation minimum remains. Pitfall: a consolidated validator places more stake behind one signing setup.

prompts.promptText: What value does an unassigned Solidity variable hold, and how does 0.8 treat integer overflow?
prompts.answerHint: Every type has a zero default: uint/int→0, bool→false, address→address(0), bytesN→zeroes. Since 0.8 arithmetic reverts on over/underflow unless wrapped in unchecked. Pitfall: there is no null — 'unset' and 'set to zero' are indistinguishable, so a zero balance can't be told from a missing one.

prompts.promptText: What are the three data locations, and what happens when you assign a storage state variable to a storage local?
prompts.answerHint: storage (persistent; a reference when local), memory (a mutable per-call copy), calldata (read-only input that avoids a memory copy). A storage local aliases the original — writes hit the state var, not a copy. Pitfall: expecting a copy and getting an alias silently mutates state.

prompts.promptText: Why is iterating a user-growable array dangerous, and what does delete do to an element?
prompts.answerHint: Loop gas grows with length, so an unbounded array can exceed the block gas limit and brick the function (DoS). delete zeroes the element without shrinking length. Pitfall: use swap-and-pop for O(1) removal and never loop over attacker-growable arrays.

prompts.promptText: Write an O(1) unordered remove for a storage uint[] arr at index i.
prompts.answerHint: arr[i] = arr[arr.length - 1]; arr.pop(); — overwrite the target with the last element, then pop. Order is not preserved.

prompts.promptText: Why can't you get a mapping's length or iterate it, and what breaks when a mapping is nested in a struct you delete?
prompts.answerHint: A mapping is a pure key→slot hash with no stored key set, so there's no length or enumeration — track keys yourself. Pitfall: delete of a struct does NOT clear a mapping inside it; those entries persist and must be cleared by key.

prompts.promptText: Write a mapping-based balance store with a deposit that credits the sender.
prompts.answerHint: mapping(address => uint256) public balanceOf; function deposit() external payable { balanceOf[msg.sender] += msg.value; }

prompts.promptText: What restriction applies to a struct that contains a mapping?
prompts.answerHint: It can only exist in storage — you cannot instantiate or pass such a struct in memory. Pitfall: trying to build a memory struct that has a mapping field is a compile error; copy field-by-field or keep the mapping outside.

prompts.promptText: What is an enum's default value and backing type, and what happens on an out-of-range cast?
prompts.answerHint: The ABI represents an enum as uint8; its default is the first member (index 0), and it has at most 256 members. Casting an out-of-range integer to the enum reverts with a Panic since 0.8. Pitfall: relying on a 'zero = unset' sentinel is impossible — index 0 is a real, valid member.

prompts.promptText: How many wei is 1 ether, and what unit are msg.value and address.balance in?
prompts.answerHint: 1 ether = 1e18 wei; 1 gwei = 1e9 wei. msg.value and balances are always in wei. Pitfall: mixing 'human' ether with raw wei is an off-by-1e18 error — always scale explicitly.

prompts.promptText: How do named returns differ from an explicit return, and how does a caller take just the third of three returns?
prompts.answerHint: Named returns pre-declare variables that can be assigned and implicitly returned; an explicit return supplies its expressions directly. Destructure with (, , c) = f(); to skip fields. Pitfall: mixing implicit named returns with explicit return expressions is easy to misread.

prompts.promptText: What does view promise versus pure, and are they free to call?
prompts.answerHint: view reads state but never writes; pure neither reads nor writes; the compiler enforces both, and external view calls use STATICCALL. Free only via off-chain eth_call — inside a transaction they still cost gas. Pitfall: view doesn't mean gasless when reached on-chain.

prompts.promptText: Name the four visibility levels and correct the myth that private data is hidden.
prompts.answerHint: Functions can be public (internal or external calls), external (message calls, including this.f()), internal (this contract and derived contracts), or private (only the declaring contract). State variables use public, internal, or private; public variables receive generated getters. Pitfall: private/internal restrict Solidity access only — storage remains readable on-chain.

prompts.promptText: What does the _ in a modifier do, and what happens if it's missing?
prompts.answerHint: _ marks where the wrapped function body executes; code before/after _ runs around it. Pitfall: a modifier with no _ silently skips the entire function body (the call succeeds but does nothing) — and when several modifiers apply, their order matters.

prompts.promptText: Write an onlyOwner modifier using a custom error.
prompts.answerHint: error NotOwner(); modifier onlyOwner() { if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner(); _; }

prompts.promptText: When does the constructor run, and why can't it be called later?
prompts.answerHint: Once, during deployment, to init state and set immutables; it's part of the creation code, not the deployed runtime bytecode, so it no longer exists to call. Pitfall: forgetting to initialize an owner/immutable in the constructor leaves it at its zero default with no second chance.

prompts.promptText: Which control-flow construct does Solidity NOT have, and what's the danger of loops?
prompts.answerHint: No switch (that's Yul-only); it has if/else, for, while, do-while, break, continue. Pitfall: an unbounded loop over an attacker-growable array can exceed the block gas limit and permanently DoS the function — bound loops or use pull payments.

prompts.promptText: Compare the gas of a cold SLOAD, a warm SLOAD, and a zero→non-zero SSTORE.
prompts.answerHint: A cold SLOAD costs 2100 gas and a warm SLOAD 100. A warm zero→non-zero SSTORE has a 20000-gas base cost; a first cold touch adds 2100. Other SSTORE costs depend on the original, current, and new values, and eligible refunds are capped. Pitfall: cache repeated storage reads in a local.

prompts.promptText: Write a loop that sums a storage uint[] without re-reading the array length from storage each iteration.
prompts.answerHint: uint256 len = arr.length; uint256 s; for (uint256 i; i < len; ++i) { s += arr[i]; } — cache length in a local so the loop test doesn't SLOAD each time.

prompts.promptText: How does the compiler pack state variables, and when does packing NOT help?
prompts.answerHint: It lays variables out sequentially from slot 0 and packs adjacent sub-32-byte types into one slot. Packing reduces occupied slots and can combine work when neighboring fields are accessed together. Pitfall: writing one packed field alone requires a full-slot read-modify-write, so packing separately accessed fields can cost more.

prompts.promptText: How do constant and immutable differ, and what do they share?
prompts.answerHint: constant is fixed at compile time and substituted at each use; immutable can be assigned during construction from values such as constructor arguments and is substituted into runtime code. Neither occupies a storage slot, though a constant can sometimes be cheaper. Pitfall: an immutable cannot be assigned after construction.

prompts.promptText: What must a base and child mark to override, and how is multiple inheritance resolved?
prompts.answerHint: Base marks virtual and child marks override. With multiple inheritance, the override list names the relevant bases unless the documented common-base exception applies. Direct bases are declared from most base-like to most derived, and lookup searches them right-to-left. Pitfall: reordering bases can change resolution.

prompts.promptText: Write the signature of a child function that overrides a foo() declared virtual in both A and B.
prompts.answerHint: function foo() public override(A, B) { ... } — when both A and B independently declare foo, the override list names both; Solidity documents an exception when one base inherits the declaring function from another.

prompts.promptText: How does super.foo() choose which parent runs in a diamond hierarchy?
prompts.answerHint: It calls the next contract in the C3-linearized method resolution order, not a single literal parent — so a chain of super calls walks every mixin once. Pitfall: assuming super means 'my declared parent' breaks in multiple inheritance; trace the MRO.

prompts.promptText: Can a child redeclare an inherited state variable? How should it set the base's value?
prompts.answerHint: A child cannot redeclare a visible inherited state variable; assign that inherited variable directly. A private base variable is not visible, so the child may use the same name for a distinct variable. Pitfall: local variables can shadow state variables and compile with a warning.

prompts.promptText: What makes a contract abstract, and how does it differ from an interface?
prompts.answerHint: A contract must be abstract if it has an unimplemented function or lacks required base-constructor arguments; a fully implemented contract may also be marked abstract intentionally. It cannot be deployed directly. Unlike an interface, it may hold state, constructors, and implemented functions.

prompts.promptText: How many event parameters can be indexed, and what is lost by indexing a string?
prompts.answerHint: A non-anonymous event may index up to three parameters; an anonymous event may index four. The rest go into ABI-encoded data. Pitfall: an indexed dynamic or complex value stores Keccak-256 of its special in-place encoding, so the original is not decodable from the topic alone.

prompts.promptText: Write an ERC-20-style Transfer event declaration with the correct indexing.
prompts.answerHint: event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value); — addresses indexed for filtering, value in data.

prompts.promptText: What is topic0 of a normal event, and what changes for an anonymous event? Can a contract read logs?
prompts.answerHint: topic0 = keccak256 of the event signature; indexed args fill topics 1–3, non-indexed args go in data. An anonymous event omits topic0 (gaining a 4th indexed slot) but is unfilterable by signature. Pitfall: contracts cannot read logs at all — logs are output for off-chain consumers only.

prompts.promptText: Why are custom errors cheaper than revert strings, and what data does a caller get?
prompts.answerHint: Revert data is a 4-byte selector + ABI-encoded args instead of a stored string, cutting deploy and revert gas; the caller gets structured, decodable failure data. Pitfall: the caller must decode the selector/args to read it — plain string tooling won't show the values.

prompts.promptText: Write a custom error carrying the shortfall and the revert that uses it.
prompts.answerHint: error InsufficientBalance(uint256 have, uint256 want); ... if (bal < amt) revert InsufficientBalance(bal, amt);

prompts.promptText: When do you use require vs assert, and what does each return on failure?
prompts.answerHint: Use require for preconditions and revert for unconditional/complex exits; either can return empty data, Error(string), or a custom error. assert is for unreachable invariants and returns Panic(uint) (0x11 overflow, 0x12 divide-by-zero, 0x32 OOB). Pitfall: a triggered assert signals a contract bug, not bad user input.

prompts.promptText: What must a function be to receive ETH, and in what unit is msg.value?
prompts.answerHint: It must be marked payable, else sending value reverts; msg.value is the attached amount in wei for the current call. Pitfall: msg.value is the same across internal calls in one context — summing it per internal call double-counts the actual ETH received.

prompts.promptText: Compare transfer, send, and call for sending ETH, and state today's recommendation.
prompts.answerHint: transfer: 2300-gas stipend, reverts on failure. send: same stipend, returns bool. Both are deprecated in current Solidity docs. call{value:}("") forwards available gas by default and returns (bool, bytes); check success. Pitfall: call hands over control, so use checks-effects-interactions or a guard.

prompts.promptText: Write a safe ETH send using call that reverts on failure.
prompts.answerHint: (bool ok, ) = to.call{value: amount}(""); require(ok, "send failed"); — forward the available gas by default and check success.

prompts.promptText: Which of receive/fallback runs for a given call, and can a contract with neither accept ETH?
prompts.answerHint: Empty calldata + a receive present → receive; otherwise (data, or no receive) → fallback, which must be payable to accept value. A contract with neither rejects plain transfers, though selfdestruct or protocol balance credits can force ETH. Pitfall: transfer/send provide only their fixed stipend to receive/fallback.

prompts.promptText: What does addr.call return, and what two things does it NOT do for you?
prompts.answerHint: Returns (bool success, bytes returndata). It does NOT revert on failure (you must check success) and does NOT verify the target has code — a call to an EOA/empty address returns success = true. Pitfall: ignoring the returned bool silently swallows the callee's revert.

prompts.promptText: In a delegatecall, whose storage and msg.sender are used, and what is the critical safety requirement?
prompts.answerHint: The caller's storage is read/written and msg.sender/msg.value are preserved from the original call; the target's code runs but address(this) is the caller. Requirement: proxy and implementation storage layouts must match slot-for-slot. Pitfall: a layout mismatch makes the implementation write to the wrong slots and corrupt state.

prompts.promptText: Write a delegatecall that forwards a payload and reverts on failure.
prompts.answerHint: (bool ok, bytes memory data) = impl.delegatecall(msg.data); require(ok); — runs impl's code against this contract's storage.

prompts.promptText: What does staticcall guarantee, and what happens if the callee tries to write state?
prompts.answerHint: It runs the sub-call read-only; any state change — SSTORE, LOG, CREATE, selfdestruct, or value-call — makes the EVM revert the sub-call. Pitfall: invoking a 'view' function through a plain call instead of staticcall loses the read-only guarantee entirely.

prompts.promptText: What can try/catch handle, and how do you separate a revert string from an arithmetic panic?
prompts.answerHint: Only external calls and new-contract creation (not internal/private). catch Error(string reason) captures require/revert strings; catch Panic(uint code) captures asserts/arithmetic; catch (bytes) catches custom errors; bare catch is the fallback. Pitfall: it cannot catch failures in internal calls, so wrapping your own function in try does nothing.

prompts.promptText: How do abi.encode and abi.encodePacked differ, and why is encodePacked dangerous for hashing?
prompts.answerHint: abi.encode uses standard 32-byte-word head/tail encoding and is decodable with the schema; encodePacked omits dynamic lengths and concatenates compactly. Pitfall: adjacent dynamic values are ambiguous — ("a","bc") and ("ab","c") have the same packed preimage. Use abi.encode for security-relevant structured hashes.

prompts.promptText: Write the hash of two strings in a way that is NOT vulnerable to the packed collision.
prompts.answerHint: keccak256(abi.encode(a, b)) — standard ABI encoding gives distinct pairs distinct preimages, unlike the ambiguous packed concatenation (apart from the hash function's negligible collision probability).

prompts.promptText: How is a function selector computed, and why prefer abi.encodeCall over abi.encodeWithSignature?
prompts.answerHint: Selector = bytes4(keccak256("name(type1,type2)")) using canonical types (uint256, not uint); calldata is selector ++ abi.encode(args). Pitfall: encodeWithSignature takes a string that the compiler can't type-check, so a typo mis-encodes silently — encodeCall(IFoo.f, (args)) is verified at compile time.

prompts.promptText: What kind of hash is keccak256, and what does the encode-vs-packed choice affect?
prompts.answerHint: The pre-standard Keccak-256 (not NIST SHA3-256): deterministic, one-way, collision-resistant, 32-byte output; used for mapping slots, merkle roots, selectors, commit-reveal. Pitfall: hashing abi.encodePacked of dynamic inputs can collide, and keccak256(encode(x)) ≠ keccak256(encodePacked(x)) — pick one deliberately.

prompts.promptText: What does ecrecover return on failure, and name two ways signature verification is abused.
prompts.answerHint: It returns address(0) on failure — you must reject that or a bad sig 'authorizes' the zero address. Pitfall: (1) signature malleability — (r, n−s) is a second valid signature — enforce low-s; (2) replay — reuse the same signature — bind a nonce/deadline and the verifying contract/chain (EIP-712). Prefer OpenZeppelin's ECDSA.

prompts.promptText: Write the recovery of a signer from an EIP-191 personal-signed 32-byte hash.
prompts.answerHint: bytes32 d = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n32", hash)); address signer = ecrecover(d, v, r, s); require(signer != address(0));

prompts.promptText: What goes into an EIP-712 domain separator, and why does it matter for replay?
prompts.answerHint: Common domain fields are name, version, chainId, and verifyingContract; the digest is keccak256("\x19\x01" ++ domainSeparator ++ hashStruct(msg)). These fields separate chains/contracts, but EIP-712 alone does not stop same-domain replay — include a nonce/deadline or make the action idempotent.

prompts.promptText: Write the final EIP-712 digest given domainSeparator and structHash.
prompts.answerHint: bytes32 digest = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("\x19\x01", domainSeparator, structHash));

prompts.promptText: How do internal and external library functions differ, and what can a library not do?
prompts.answerHint: internal library functions are compiled into the caller and use the internal calling convention; public/external ones use a separately deployed library through DELEGATECALL. A library declares no state, cannot normally receive ETH, and cannot be destroyed. Pitfall: deployed library code runs in the caller's context and must be linked.

prompts.promptText: What can an interface contain, and what does IToken(addr).f() assume?
prompts.answerHint: Interfaces contain external function signatures and may declare ABI-visible types, events, and errors, but no implementations, state variables, constructor, or modifiers; functions are implicitly virtual. IToken(addr).f() assumes runtime conformance. Pitfall: the type is a compile-time promise, not proof about the address.

prompts.promptText: What does the high-level Contract(addr).f() do that raw call doesn't?
prompts.answerHint: It ABI-encodes from declared types, performs CALL, checks code when needed (or lets return decoding reject empty data), decodes returns, and bubbles failures. A codeless target therefore reverts through a check or decoding. Pitfall: a wrong interface still encodes and interprets data using the wrong schema.

prompts.promptText: What safety do you give up in an assembly block, and what memory regions must you respect?
prompts.answerHint: You lose normal type and checked-arithmetic guarantees and can touch memory/storage/calldata directly. Respect scratch 0x00–0x3f, the free-pointer word at 0x40–0x5f, and the zero slot at 0x60–0x7f. Pitfall: corrupting the pointer or zero slot breaks surrounding Solidity allocations.

prompts.promptText: In Yul, which opcodes read/write storage and memory, and how is a mapping entry's slot located?
prompts.answerHint: sload/sstore access storage; mload/mstore/mstore8 access memory; keccak256(ptr,len) hashes memory. For a value-type key, mapping m at slot p uses keccak256(abi.encode(key, p)): 32-byte key then 32-byte slot. Pitfall: reversed order, wrong padding, or a bad slot touches unrelated state.

prompts.promptText: Write the Yul that computes the storage slot of mapping entry m[key] where m is at baseSlot.
prompts.answerHint: mstore(0x00, key); mstore(0x20, baseSlot); let slot := keccak256(0x00, 0x40); — uses scratch space for the keccak input.

prompts.promptText: What is the lifetime and cost of transient storage, and why is it a good reentrancy lock?
prompts.answerHint: TSTORE and TLOAD each currently cost 100 gas; contract-private transient values survive owned nested frames and are discarded at transaction end. That makes a lock visible to reentrant calls without persistent-storage/refund costs. Pitfall: reset it before a successful return so later calls in the same transaction remain composable.

prompts.promptText: Write a reentrancy guard modifier using the transient keyword (0.8.28+).
prompts.answerHint: bool transient locked; modifier nonReentrant() { require(!locked); locked = true; _; locked = false; } — the transient bool auto-clears at tx end.

prompts.promptText: What does a user-defined value type give you, and what does it NOT do?
prompts.answerHint: type Duration is uint256 creates a distinct compile-time type converted via Duration.wrap/unwrap, preventing accidental mixing of same-underlying values (Price vs Quantity) at zero runtime cost. Pitfall: it has no operators or implicit conversions by default (add them via using-for since 0.8.19) and adds no runtime checks — only compile-time distinctness.

prompts.promptText: What do src/, test/, lib/, script/, and out/ each hold in a Foundry project, and which one is safe to delete/regenerate?
prompts.answerHint: src/ = contracts, test/ = .t.sol tests, lib/ = installed dependencies, script/ = deploy/interaction scripts, out/ = compiled artifacts (ABI+bytecode), and cache/ = compiler cache. Pitfall: out/ and cache/ are generated and normally gitignored, but they are not the same directory or the same data.

prompts.promptText: Name three things cast can do without writing a Solidity script, and why cast call can never change state.
prompts.answerHint: cast call (read), cast send (write tx), cast storage (raw slot read), plus abi-encode/logs/etc. — all from the terminal against any RPC. Pitfall: cast call behaves like eth_call — it never actually mines a tx, even against a live node, so it can't be used to change state.

prompts.promptText: What makes anvil faster to iterate against than a public testnet, and what happens to its state on restart?
prompts.answerHint: Instant mining, pre-funded accounts, and development RPC extensions (anvil_setBalance, snapshot/revert) make resets cheap. Pitfall: state is in memory by default; use --state (load if present, dump on exit) or the separate --load-state/--dump-state flags when persistence is intentional.

prompts.promptText: Why is chisel faster than forge test for checking a one-line Solidity/assembly idea, and what does it share with real tests?
prompts.answerHint: It evaluates each statement immediately in an interactive session instead of a full compile+run cycle, with full access to Foundry cheatcodes just like a test. Pitfall: a working chisel snippet doesn't automatically become a committed test — copy it into a real test file.

prompts.promptText: Why does each Foundry test function run against its own isolated EVM state, and what does that mean for relying on test execution order?
prompts.answerHint: Every test* function gets setUp() re-run and a fresh state snapshot, so tests can't leak state into each other regardless of order. Pitfall: a test that depends on state created by an earlier test's body (not its own setUp()) will break — each test only sees its own setUp() plus its own body.

prompts.promptText: Write a minimal Foundry test file skeleton testing a Counter contract's increment().
prompts.answerHint: import {Test} from "forge-std/Test.sol"; import {Counter} from "../src/Counter.sol"; contract CounterTest is Test { Counter c; function setUp() public { c = new Counter(); } function test_Increment() public { c.increment(); assertEq(c.count(), 1); } }

prompts.promptText: What's the difference between vm.prank and vm.startPrank/stopPrank, and what does vm.deal NOT do?
prompts.answerHint: prank affects only the next external call; startPrank/stopPrank affects every call until stopPrank. vm.deal sets a balance directly — it runs no real transfer logic (no receive/fallback triggered). Pitfall: forgetting stopPrank leaves impersonation active for later, unrelated calls in the same test.

prompts.promptText: Write cheatcode calls making the next call appear from address(0xBEEF) with a 10 ether balance.
prompts.answerHint: vm.deal(address(0xBEEF), 10 ether); vm.prank(address(0xBEEF)); target.doSomething();

prompts.promptText: Where must vm.expectRevert/vm.expectEmit be placed relative to the call they check, and what's the risk of a bare vm.expectRevert() with no arguments?
prompts.answerHint: Immediately before the call being tested — the cheatcode applies only to the very next external call. Pitfall: vm.expectRevert() with no args matches ANY revert reason, which can hide a wrong-reason bug — pass the specific selector/string when you can.

prompts.promptText: What do vm.warp and vm.roll each control, and does setting one automatically advance the other?
prompts.answerHint: vm.warp(ts) sets block.timestamp; vm.roll(n) sets block.number — instantly, for all subsequent calls in the test. Pitfall: warping doesn't advance block.number and vice versa; a contract checking both may need both cheatcodes set consistently.

prompts.promptText: What does Foundry do when a fuzz test fails, and why does fuzzing catch bugs example-based unit tests often miss?
prompts.answerHint: It reports the failing calldata and arguments as a counterexample. Fuzzing samples many typed inputs instead of the few a human thinks to write. Pitfall: constrain the intended domain with bound() or vm.assume(); excessive assumptions discard runs and can exhaust the rejection limit.

prompts.promptText: Write a fuzz test asserting a Vault's deposit always credits the exact amount deposited.
prompts.answerHint: function testFuzz_Deposit(uint96 amount) public { vm.assume(amount > 0); vault.deposit{value: amount}(); assertEq(vault.balanceOf(address(this)), amount); }

prompts.promptText: Why does pinning a fork to a specific block number matter for test determinism?
prompts.answerHint: Without a pinned block, forking 'latest' means the exact state (balances, oracle prices) differs run to run, so a passing test today could fail tomorrow for reasons unrelated to your code. Pitfall: forking without a rate-limit-safe RPC can hit limits mid-suite — use a dedicated fork RPC or cache.

prompts.promptText: What is a 'handler' in Foundry invariant testing, and what does it catch that a single fuzz test doesn't?
prompts.answerHint: A handler wraps the target's functions with bounded/valid inputs; the fuzzer calls handler functions in random sequences and order, then checks the invariant after each — catching bugs that only surface after a specific multi-call history. Pitfall: an unconstrained handler wastes runs on reverting calls — bound inputs inside the handler, not just the invariant.

prompts.promptText: What do `-vvv` and `-vvvv` add to `forge test` output, and when would you choose each?
prompts.answerHint: `-vvv` prints execution traces for failing tests. `-vvvv` prints traces for all tests and setup traces for failures. Start with `-vvv` to isolate a failure; use `-vvvv` when a passing path or setup needs comparison. Pitfall: broad trace output becomes noisy on fuzz or invariant campaigns, so combine it with a test filter.

prompts.promptText: How do you launch Foundry's interactive debugger for one specific test, and what do `C`, `s`, and `G` navigate to?
prompts.answerHint: Run `forge test --debug --match-test "<regex>"` with a pattern that selects one function. `C` moves to the next call-type instruction, `s` to the next `JUMPDEST`, and `G` to the end of the transaction. Pitfall: `s` is not a source-level step-into command, and the current debugger has no documented `o` step-out binding.

prompts.promptText: What does `forge snapshot --check` actually fail the build on, and what must you do after an intentional gas increase?
prompts.answerHint: It diffs the current run's gas-per-test against the committed .gas-snapshot file and fails if it changed. Pitfall: an intentional increase (e.g. added a safety check) needs .gas-snapshot regenerated and committed, or every future CI run fails on that line forever.

prompts.promptText: What can branch/line coverage from forge coverage reveal that 'all tests pass' doesn't?
prompts.answerHint: An untested revert branch, an unreached else, or a function only ever exercised on one code path. Pitfall: 100% line coverage doesn't mean every input combination or invariant is tested — coverage measures reached code, not correctness.

prompts.promptText: What's the difference between running a forge script with and without --broadcast?
prompts.answerHint: Without `--broadcast`, Forge collects and simulates the marked transactions but sends nothing. With it, calls and creations at the broadcast call depth between `vm.startBroadcast()` and `vm.stopBroadcast()` are signed and sent after simulation succeeds. Pitfall: a dry run uses remote state only when an RPC/fork URL is supplied; otherwise it is a local EVM simulation.

prompts.promptText: Write a minimal forge script deploying a Counter with a constructor arg of 42.
prompts.answerHint: function run() external { vm.startBroadcast(); new Counter(42); vm.stopBroadcast(); }

prompts.promptText: Why must compiler settings match exactly for forge verify-contract to succeed, even when the source is 'the same'?
prompts.answerHint: The verifier recompiles the submitted sources with the supplied compiler version, optimizer, EVM, and other settings, then compares the result with deployed bytecode. Sourcify calls byte-for-byte agreement including metadata an exact match and agreement excluding metadata a match. A setting that changes executable bytecode fails both. Pitfall: constructor arguments must be ABI-encoded exactly as deployed with `cast abi-encode`, and match labels vary by verifier.

prompts.promptText: What breaks if a fresh clone of a Foundry repo skips `git submodule update --init --recursive` before `forge build`?
prompts.answerHint: The superproject has gitlinks but the dependency working trees under `lib/` are absent, so imports fail; `--recursive` also initializes nested submodules. The recorded gitlink identifies a commit, while `foundry.lock` preserves requested tag/revision intent. Pitfall: an unqualified first install follows the repository's default ref at install time, so choose a reviewed tag or revision explicitly.

prompts.promptText: What does a line like `@openzeppelin/=lib/openzeppelin-contracts/` in remappings.txt do, and what does `forge remappings` show beyond what you wrote by hand?
prompts.answerHint: It rewrites any import starting with @openzeppelin/ to resolve under lib/openzeppelin-contracts/. forge remappings prints the FULL resolved table, including entries auto-inferred from installed dependencies. Pitfall: a typo'd prefix fails silently as 'file not found', not as a remapping error.

prompts.promptText: Write a remappings.txt line mapping forge-std imports to lib/forge-std/src/.
prompts.answerHint: forge-std/=lib/forge-std/src/

prompts.promptText: How does installing a dependency with soldeer differ from forge install for a git submodule, in terms of where the dependency's version is recorded?
prompts.answerHint: Soldeer records a version requirement under `[dependencies]`, resolves source under `dependencies/`, and records the exact resolution in `soldeer.lock`; default `forge install` uses a Git submodule under `lib/`, with `.gitmodules`, a gitlink commit, and `foundry.lock`. Pitfall: the managers can coexist, but do not install the same package twice or let their remappings collide.

prompts.promptText: How does FOUNDRY_PROFILE change which foundry.toml settings apply, and why give [profile.ci] more fuzz runs than [profile.default]?
prompts.answerHint: FOUNDRY_PROFILE=ci makes Foundry read [profile.ci], falling back to [profile.default] for any key it doesn't override. Fewer runs locally means fast iteration; more runs in CI means a fuller check before merge, without changing test code. Pitfall: a key missing from [profile.ci] silently inherits from [profile.default] — an incomplete profile isn't an error, just a partial override.

prompts.promptText: Write a foundry.toml block giving the ci profile 1024 fuzz runs.
prompts.answerHint:
[profile.ci]
fuzz = { runs = 1024 }

prompts.promptText: What class of bug can Slither/Aderyn catch that a passing test suite might miss, and why?
prompts.answerHint: Static analyzers flag patterns like reentrancy-prone external calls before state updates, unchecked low-level call returns, or uninitialized state — by reading code structure, not executing it, so they catch a bug class even if no test happens to exercise that exact path. Pitfall: static analysis produces false positives routinely — triage findings, don't blindly 'fix' every warning.

prompts.promptText: What does hardhat.config.ts declare, and what testing option does Hardhat 3 add that Hardhat 2 didn't have?
prompts.answerHint: The Solidity compiler version/settings, source/test paths, and networks. Hardhat 3 adds first-class Foundry-compatible Solidity tests (.t.sol, forge-std style) alongside the original TypeScript test runner. Pitfall: both test styles still compile from ONE shared contracts/ tree — a config mistake there breaks both.

prompts.promptText: Complete Speedrun Ethereum challenges 0–2 (Simple NFT Example, Decentralized Staking App, Token Vendor).
prompts.answerHint: Each challenge scaffolds a Scaffold-ETH 2 (Hardhat-based) project with a contract plus a Next.js frontend; deploy locally with Hardhat, pass the contract's own test suite, then follow the challenge's deploy/verify steps.

prompts.promptText: Why write a TS integration test with viem in addition to a Foundry Solidity test for the same contract?
prompts.answerHint: A TS test exercises the viem-facing ABI, typing, accounts, and multi-contract wiring used by clients and scripts, complementing contract-internal Solidity tests. Use each style for the boundary it can actually observe instead of assuming one runner replaces the other.

prompts.promptText: Write a viem-based Hardhat TS test deploying a contract and asserting a read call.
prompts.answerHint: import assert from "node:assert/strict"; const counter = await viem.deployContract("Counter"); await counter.write.increment(); assert.equal(await counter.read.count(), 1n);

prompts.promptText: What does Ignition's deployment journal let you safely do that a plain imperative deploy script can't?
prompts.answerHint: Resume a partially-failed multi-contract deployment without re-deploying contracts that already succeeded, because Ignition tracks what's been deployed against a module's declared dependency graph. Pitfall: Ignition modules are declarative, so imperative control flow (loops/conditionals over deploys) doesn't work the way a hand-written script would.

prompts.promptText: Write a minimal Hardhat Ignition module deploying a Counter with a constructor arg of 0.
prompts.answerHint: import { buildModule } from "@nomicfoundation/hardhat-ignition/modules"; export default buildModule("Phase03", (m) => { const counter = m.contract("Counter", [0]); return { counter }; });

prompts.promptText: What's the difference between an edr-simulated network and an http network in Hardhat 3's config, and why keep RPC URLs as configuration variables?
prompts.answerHint: edr-simulated runs an in-memory local chain (optionally forking a real one); http points at a real JSON-RPC endpoint. Configuration variables keep secrets (RPC URLs, keys) out of the committed hardhat.config.ts. Pitfall: a forking config still needs a valid url — without one, forking is disabled.

prompts.promptText: What does a Hardhat plugin actually add to a project, beyond 'more npm packages'?
prompts.answerHint: A plugin can add CLI tasks, hooks, config fields, global options, or runtime extensions (for example, hardhat-viem exposes viem helpers on a network connection). Check the installed plugin's documented capability instead of assuming every plugin adds every kind of surface.

prompts.promptText: What does Hardhat 3 actually read to resolve a remapped Solidity import, and what does it NOT parse directly?
prompts.answerHint: Hardhat 3 natively loads scoped remappings.txt files from the project and imported npm packages. If a Foundry project relies on Forge-autogenerated remappings instead, add @nomicfoundation/hardhat-foundry; otherwise an import can resolve under Forge but fail under Hardhat.

prompts.promptText: Why can a Foundry .t.sol test run unmodified under Hardhat's own test runner, without either tool 'owning' it?
prompts.answerHint: Hardhat treats Solidity files under test/ as tests and .t.sol files under contracts/ as tests, supports forge-std, and can execute Foundry-origin tests within its documented compatibility surface. The source can be shared, but generated test artifacts and compiler settings remain tool-specific.

prompts.topicTitle: When to reach for Foundry vs Hardhat
prompts.promptText: Give the one-line decision rule for choosing Foundry vs Hardhat for a given task in this curriculum.
prompts.answerHint: Use Forge when the task specifically needs Forge commands or analysis; use Hardhat for Ignition, viem-facing TypeScript integration, or a Hardhat plugin surface. Hardhat 3 also runs Solidity unit/fuzz/invariant tests, so choose from the concrete workflow rather than an old language-only split.

prompts.promptText: Name the core ERC-20 functions and one way a real token can break code that assumes 'standard' behaviour.
prompts.answerHint: totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, transferFrom, approve, allowance (+ Transfer/Approval events). Pitfall: some tokens don't return the bool the spec mandates (old USDT), and fee-on-transfer/rebasing tokens deliver a different amount than requested — always use SafeERC20 and measure balance deltas.

prompts.promptText: Explain the ERC-20 approval race and what SafeERC20 does and does not solve.
prompts.answerHint: If an owner replaces allowance N with M, the spender can spend N before the update and later spend M. SafeERC20 handles false or empty returns; forceApprove handles tokens that require zero before non-zero, but neither makes separate owner transactions race-free. Prefer allowance deltas where applicable, or revoke and wait while accounting for value already spent.

prompts.promptText: Use SafeERC20 to set an allowance on a token that requires zero before non-zero approval.
prompts.answerHint: token.forceApprove(spender, newAmount); forceApprove performs the compatibility sequence for tokens that require zero before a new non-zero approval. Avoid presenting two forceApprove calls as necessary, and remember that zero-first reduces token compatibility problems but cannot make two separate pending transactions atomic.

prompts.promptText: How is an ERC-165 interface id computed, and what does supportsInterface actually guarantee?
prompts.answerHint: The id is the XOR of the interface's 4-byte function selectors; supportsInterface(id) returns whether the contract claims to implement it. Pitfall: it's a self-declaration, not a proof — a contract can return true and still not honour the behaviour, so keep guarding the real calls.

prompts.promptText: Why does safeTransferFrom call onERC721Received, and what risk does that introduce during _safeMint?
prompts.answerHint: It checks a contract recipient can handle NFTs (returns the magic selector) so tokens don't get stranded. Pitfall: the callback hands execution to the recipient mid-transaction — if _safeMint runs before state is finalized, the recipient can re-enter and mint again. Follow checks-effects-interactions or add nonReentrant.

prompts.promptText: Ethernaut-style: exploit a mint function that calls _safeMint before updating its per-address mint cap.
prompts.answerHint: Deploy a contract whose onERC721Received calls mint again; because the cap is written after _safeMint, the callback sees the stale count and mints past the limit. Fix by writing the count before the external _safeMint (CEI) or guarding with nonReentrant.

prompts.promptText: What does ERC-1155 do that needing a separate ERC-20/721 deployment per asset would not?
prompts.answerHint: One contract holds many token types addressed by id, with batch balance queries and safeBatchTransferFrom for atomic multi-transfers; the optional metadata extension uses an {id}-templated URI. Pitfall: recipients' acceptance callbacks are a reentrancy surface — finalize application state before the external callback.

prompts.promptText: Which way must ERC-4626 conversions and previews round?
prompts.answerHint: Both convert methods round down. User outputs round down: previewDeposit returns no more shares than deposit and previewRedeem no more assets than redeem. Required inputs round up: previewMint returns no fewer assets and previewWithdraw no fewer shares. The standard does not require every vault's conversion estimate to equal totalAssets/totalSupply.

prompts.promptText: Walk through the ERC-4626 first-depositor inflation attack and OZ's defense.
prompts.answerHint: Against a naive empty vault, an attacker deposits dust then donates assets, raising the rate until a victim deposit rounds to zero shares. OpenZeppelin includes virtual assets and shares; these capture part of the donation, so even offset zero makes the attack unprofitable. A positive _decimalsOffset increases precision and makes dilution increasingly wasteful.

prompts.promptText: Practice the inflation/donation class of vault bug on a wargame vault.
prompts.answerHint: Reproduce it: deposit a dust amount, donate directly to inflate the share price, then let a victim deposit and round to zero shares. Then patch with virtual-offset shares and prove the exploit no longer profits. Damn Vulnerable DeFi has share/price-manipulation challenges in this family.

prompts.promptText: In a proxy, whose storage does the implementation's code modify, and what must the two contracts agree on?
prompts.answerHint: delegatecall runs the implementation's code in the PROXY's storage context (msg.sender/msg.value preserved), so all state lives in the proxy. They must agree exactly on storage layout. Pitfall: if the proxy stores its implementation pointer at a slot the logic also uses, a write collides and can brick or hijack the proxy — hence ERC-1967's reserved slots.

prompts.promptText: Why does ERC-1967 store the implementation address at keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation') - 1 instead of slot 0?
prompts.answerHint: Sequential variable layout starts at slot 0 and grows up, so a pseudo-random high slot is astronomically unlikely to collide with the logic contract's variables, keeping the pointer safe. The '- 1' avoids the address being a known keccak preimage. Pitfall: rolling your own proxy with the pointer at slot 0 invites a storage collision.

prompts.promptText: What problem does the Transparent proxy solve, and how?
prompts.answerHint: The selector-clash problem: proxy and implementation functions can share four-byte selectors. Transparent routing delegates every non-admin call, while the admin may upgrade but cannot fall back to implementation functions. In OpenZeppelin v5 the associated ProxyAdmin address is immutable; its owner holds the upgrade authority.

prompts.promptText: Where does UUPS put upgrade logic, and what must protect and preserve it?
prompts.answerHint: UUPSUpgradeable puts upgradeToAndCall in the implementation behind ERC1967Proxy. _authorizeUpgrade must restrict callers, and OpenZeppelin checks proxiableUUID compatibility before installing the new implementation. A custom or deliberately bypassed check can still remove upgradeability; the current default rejects a plain non-UUPS implementation.

prompts.promptText: Legacy Ethernaut Motorbike: how did an unlocked implementation enable the historical pre-EIP-6780 bricking path?
prompts.answerHint: The attacker initialized the implementation directly, gained its upgrade authority, then made it delegatecall code containing SELFDESTRUCT, historically deleting the implementation and leaving the proxy with no code target. _disableInitializers() prevents the takeover. Current EIP-6780 SELFDESTRUCT semantics no longer generally delete old contract code, so treat the destruction step as historical.

prompts.promptText: How does a Beacon proxy let you upgrade thousands of instances at once, and what's the trade-off?
prompts.answerHint: Each proxy reads its implementation from a shared UpgradeableBeacon rather than storing it; upgrading the beacon once changes the logic for every proxy simultaneously, while each proxy keeps its own state. Pitfall: the beacon is a single fleet-wide upgrade point — compromising its owner upgrades (and can drain) every instance at once.

prompts.promptText: How does a Diamond route calls and keep facets from corrupting each other's storage?
prompts.answerHint: diamondCut maps each function selector to a facet; the fallback delegatecalls the facet owning the called selector, letting the system exceed 24 KB and upgrade per-facet. Facets share the proxy's storage, so each uses Diamond Storage — a struct at a namespaced slot keccak(unique string). Pitfall: two facets claiming the same selector, or reusing a storage namespace, corrupts state.

prompts.promptText: State the storage-layout rule for upgrades, then contrast storage gaps with ERC-7201 namespaces.
prompts.answerHint: For a sequential layout, append only: do not reorder, remove, insert before, or change existing variable types. A fixed __gap reserves base-contract slots and must shrink as the base consumes them. ERC-7201 instead isolates annotated namespaced structs; OpenZeppelin Contracts Upgradeable v5 uses this namespaced approach.

prompts.promptText: Why can't upgradeable contracts use constructors, and why must the implementation call _disableInitializers()?
prompts.answerHint: An implementation constructor writes only implementation state, not proxy state, so proxy setup goes in a guarded initialize function and must call parent initializers explicitly. The implementation constructor calls _disableInitializers() to stop anyone taking over that separate instance. Keep this distinct from the historical Parity library incident.

prompts.promptText: What changed about Ownable's constructor in OpenZeppelin v5, and what does renouncing ownership do?
prompts.answerHint: v5's constructor takes an explicit initialOwner (constructor(address initialOwner) Ownable(initialOwner)) and reverts on address(0), instead of v4's implicit msg.sender. renounceOwnership sets owner to address(0), permanently disabling every onlyOwner path. Pitfall: passing the wrong initialOwner at deploy, or renouncing while admin-only functions are still needed, is unrecoverable.

prompts.promptText: How does AccessControl enforce least privilege, and what is the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE risk?
prompts.answerHint: Capabilities are separate bytes32 roles gated by onlyRole (MINTER_ROLE can't pause, etc.), granted/revoked independently via grantRole/revokeRole. Pitfall: DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE administers all roles, so one compromised admin can grant itself everything — protect it (AccessControlDefaultAdminRules for a delayed two-step admin handoff) and never leave a privileged function without its onlyRole check.

prompts.promptText: Why is Ownable2Step safer than single-step transferOwnership?
prompts.answerHint: Single-step hands control to whatever address you pass — a typo or an address nobody controls loses the contract permanently. Ownable2Step records a pendingOwner and only completes when that address calls acceptOwnership, proving it exists and is controllable. Pitfall: even two-step can't save you if you set the pending owner to a contract that can't call acceptOwnership.

prompts.promptText: What does Pausable give you, and which functions should you be careful NOT to gate?
prompts.answerHint: Pause state, whenNotPaused/whenPaused modifiers, and internal _pause/_unpause functions that you authorize and apply to selected entry points. Pitfall: Pausable does not pause functions automatically, and gating withdrawals/exits can trap user funds — pause deposits and risky actions but leave an emergency exit open.

prompts.promptText: State the checks-effects-interactions order and why nonReentrant alone isn't enough.
prompts.answerHint: Checks (validate) → Effects (update state) → Interactions (external calls), so a re-entrant call sees finalized state. OZ nonReentrant uses one contract-wide guard, so reentry into any protected entry point fails; it cannot protect an unguarded sibling or prevent another protocol from reading transiently inconsistent state during a callback. Pitfall: apply CEI first and guard every exposed mutation that shares the invariant.

prompts.promptText: Rewrite a vulnerable withdraw to be reentrancy-safe with CEI.
prompts.answerHint: uint256 amt = balance[msg.sender]; balance[msg.sender] = 0; (bool ok,) = msg.sender.call{value: amt}(""); require(ok); — zero the balance (effect) BEFORE the external call (interaction), so a re-entrant withdraw sees 0.

prompts.promptText: Solve the Ethernaut Reentrancy level: drain a contract whose withdraw sends before it debits.
prompts.answerHint: Deposit a small amount, then in your attacker's receive/fallback call withdraw again while your recorded balance is still non-zero; the contract sends ETH before zeroing your balance, so each re-entry pays you again until it's empty. Fix is CEI + nonReentrant.

prompts.promptText: Why is looping to push payments dangerous, and what does the pull pattern change?
prompts.answerHint: One recipient that reverts (no receive, or a griefer) makes the whole loop revert, and each send is a reentrancy opening — a push refund can DoS everyone. Pull payments credit a mapping and let each account withdraw itself, isolating failures and reducing external calls to one guarded path. Pitfall: still apply CEI on the withdraw.

prompts.promptText: How does permit avoid a separate approve tx, and what stops the signature being replayed?
prompts.answerHint: The owner signs an EIP-712 permit(owner,spender,value,deadline) off-chain; anyone submits it and the token sets the allowance, so approve+action fit in one tx. A per-owner nonce (included and incremented) blocks replay and the deadline bounds validity. Pitfall: anyone can submit the permit first, so an integration should tolerate its permit call failing when the intended allowance is already set.

prompts.promptText: In an ERC-2771 contract, why read _msgSender() instead of msg.sender, and where is the trust?
prompts.answerHint: For a forwarded call msg.sender is the relayer/forwarder; the real user is appended to the last 20 bytes of calldata and recovered by _msgSender(). Trust rests entirely on only whitelisting a vetted forwarder. Pitfall: trusting an untrusted contract lets it append any address and impersonate anyone, and mixing raw msg.sender into logic breaks the abstraction.

prompts.promptText: Why does ERC-1271 exist, and how should a verifier support both EOAs and contract wallets?
prompts.answerHint: ecrecover only validates EOA ECDSA sigs, so smart-contract wallets expose isValidSignature(hash,sig) returning the magic value 0x1626ba7e when they accept a signature. Use OZ SignatureChecker, which uses ECDSA for an EOA signer and ERC-1271 when the signer has code. Pitfall: an isValidSignature that doesn't bind hash to a nonce/domain lets a signature be replayed.

prompts.promptText: Name the three ways a signed message can be replayed and the defense for each.
prompts.answerHint: Same-contract replay → a per-signer nonce the contract consumes; cross-chain replay → chainId in the EIP-712 domain separator; cross-contract replay → verifyingContract in the domain separator (plus a deadline to bound the window). Pitfall: omitting any one — especially the nonce — turns a signature into a reusable bearer token.

prompts.promptText: How does a Merkle airdrop scale, and what two disciplines keep it safe?
prompts.answerHint: Store one root instead of preloading every allocation; each claim submits a recipient-and-amount leaf plus a logarithmic proof and records replay state only when claimed. Use an unambiguous leaf encoding (StandardMerkleTree double-hashes) so an internal node cannot masquerade as a leaf, and pay the recipient encoded in the leaf so a caller cannot redirect funds. Pitfall: forgetting replay tracking allows double claims.

prompts.promptText: Write the core of an OZ MerkleProof airdrop claim check.
prompts.answerHint: bytes32 leaf = keccak256(bytes.concat(keccak256(abi.encode(msg.sender, amount)))); require(!claimed[msg.sender]); require(MerkleProof.verify(proof, root, leaf)); claimed[msg.sender] = true; — double-hashed leaf, claimed flag set before transfer.

prompts.promptText: How does a signature airdrop differ from a Merkle airdrop, and what's its main risk?
prompts.answerHint: Instead of an on-chain root + proof, an off-chain signer issues an EIP-712 signature authorizing (address, amount); the contract verifies it and pays out — no root needed, eligibility computed lazily. Risk: it centralizes trust in the signer's key (a leak mints unlimited claims). Pitfall: needs a per-claim nonce + deadline or the signature is replayable.

prompts.promptText: What security property does an M-of-N multisig provide, and what are its dangerous settings?
prompts.answerHint: It requires M of N owner approvals to execute; when M > 1, no single owner key is sufficient. Pitfall: 1-of-N keeps a single-key failure mode, owner and threshold changes are security-critical, and an enabled Safe module can execute arbitrary transactions without the normal signature check. Guards inspect transactions but are not the same authority path as modules.

prompts.promptText: Give the CREATE2 address formula and one thing it enables that CREATE does not.
prompts.answerHint: address = keccak256(0xff ‖ deployer ‖ salt ‖ keccak256(init_code))[12:]. Independent of the deployer's nonce, so you can compute the address before deployment; matching deployer, salt, and init code can produce the same address across chains. Pitfall: a precomputed address may have no code yet, and EIP-6780 ended general CREATE2 redeployment after later SELFDESTRUCT.

prompts.promptText: What is an EIP-1167 clone, and why must you initialize it after deploying?
prompts.answerHint: A ~45-byte proxy that delegatecalls a hard-coded implementation, so deploying the Nth identical instance is cheap (OZ Clones.clone / cloneDeterministic). Because it's a proxy, the implementation's constructor never runs against the clone's storage — you must call an initializer after cloning. Pitfall: leaving a clone uninitialized lets anyone initialize (and hijack) it, so initialize atomically in the factory.

prompts.promptText: Why doesn't holding ERC20Votes tokens give you voting power, and how does it resist flash-loan voting?
prompts.answerHint: Voting power is tracked by delegation, so you must delegate to yourself or another account before tokens count. getPastVotes fixes weight at the proposal snapshot, preventing later transfers from reusing the same tokens; power acquired after the snapshot cannot affect that vote. Pitfall: snapshotting does not stop power acquired or borrowed before the snapshot, and current balance is not a safe vote source.

prompts.promptText: Walk the OZ Governor proposal lifecycle and name what weights the votes.
prompts.answerHint: propose() → votingDelay → holders cast For/Against/Abstain over votingPeriod, weighted by getPastVotes at the snapshot → if quorum + majority, execute the encoded calls, queueing first when a timelock module is configured. proposalThreshold gates who can propose. Pitfall: tokens must be delegated before the snapshot block/timestamp to count.

prompts.promptText: What does a governance Timelock protect against, and who holds the protocol in a Governor+Timelock setup?
prompts.answerHint: It enforces minDelay between scheduling and execution, creating a reaction window. In a Governor integration the Timelock owns governed assets and permissions because it executes the proposal calls; the Governor is normally a proposer. PROPOSER, EXECUTOR, and CANCELLER roles separate duties, and granting EXECUTOR_ROLE to address(0) permits anyone to execute ready operations. Pitfall: zero delay or unsafe role grants remove the intended control.

prompts.promptText: How does declaration order of small state variables affect gas, and why?
prompts.answerHint: Adjacent value types smaller than 32 bytes pack when they fit, so fields used together can require fewer slot accesses. Pitfall: updating only one packed field needs a read-modify-write, and interleaving a full-word field can force another slot.

prompts.promptText: Write a two-field storage layout (a uint128 and a uint128) that the compiler packs into one slot.
prompts.answerHint: uint128 a; uint128 b; // declared consecutively, both occupy slot 0 at offsets 0 and 16. Verify with the compiler's storageLayout output rather than inferring opcode count from layout alone.

prompts.promptText: Solve the storage-packing gas puzzle in the RareSkills gas-puzzles repo.
prompts.answerHint: Reorder fields so hot ones pack into a single slot; measure with forge snapshot until under target.

prompts.promptText: Under EIP-2929, what do cold and warm access cost for a storage slot and for an account?
prompts.answerHint: Slot: cold SLOAD 2100, warm 100. Covered account access: cold 2600, warm 100. An access is cold only when absent from the transaction-wide accessed sets; the sender, destination, precompiles, and EIP-2930 entries start warm, with access-list entries charged intrinsically.

prompts.promptText: Write a snippet that reads the same storage variable twice so only the first read pays cold cost.
prompts.answerHint: uint256 x = s; // cold if this key was not prewarmed or touched ... uint256 y = s; // the key is warm afterward. An optimizing compiler may eliminate the second SLOAD, so confirm the intended accesses in a trace.

prompts.promptText: Solve a warm/cold access gas puzzle from the RareSkills gas-puzzles repo.
prompts.answerHint: Reorder or dedupe accesses so repeat touches are warm (100) not cold (2100/2600); snapshot under target.

prompts.promptText: Why can SLOAD be quoted with warm/cold prices while SSTORE needs original, current, and new values?
prompts.answerHint: EIP-2929 sets SLOAD to 100 warm or 2100 cold. EIP-2200 branches SSTORE metering on original/current/new values, with later fork rules adding cold surcharges and changing refunds; there is no single universal update price.

prompts.promptText: Write a loop that accumulates into a local and writes storage once at the end.
prompts.answerHint: uint256 sum; for (uint256 i; i < n; ++i) { sum += a[i]; } total = sum; // one SSTORE instead of one per iteration.

prompts.promptText: Why is caching a storage variable in a local worth it even for warm reads?
prompts.answerHint: A local snapshot can let the optimizer reuse a value instead of issuing another SLOAD. Exact placement and savings depend on generated code. Pitfall: relevant state can change across an external call, making a cache stale.

prompts.promptText: Write a loop condition and body that read a state variable `count` only once.
prompts.answerHint: uint256 c = count; for (uint256 i; i < c; ++i) { ... } // read `count` into c once, use c throughout.

prompts.promptText: How do `constant` and `immutable` each avoid an SLOAD, and when do you use which?
