Then explain the smallest CEI or reentrancy-guard mitigation that closes that specific path; do not assume every incident runs on mainnet or at the block immediately before the exploit transaction.

prompts.promptText: Replay a real oracle-manipulation incident from DeFiHackLabs (e.g. a spot-price or flash-loan-funded manipulation).
prompts.answerHint: Run the selected incident's documented command and recorded chain/fork setup, confirm the PoC's price-moving sequence and observed victim balance change, then explain whether a sufficiently configured TWAP, independent oracle, or another incident-specific control would reject it. Do not substitute one generic pre-exploit-block recipe for the repository entry's actual setup.

prompts.promptText: What's the difference in what DeFiHackLabs and DeFiVulnLabs each teach, given they cover overlapping incidents?
prompts.answerHint: DeFiHackLabs teaches EXECUTION against a real, messy, specific deployed system (forked PoCs); DeFiVulnLabs teaches RECOGNITION — the minimal abstracted shape of the bug, stripped of one incident's specific noise, so you can spot the same pattern in a codebase that looks nothing like the original victim. Pitfall: doing only one of the two leaves a gap — pattern recognition without execution practice doesn't build the muscle to actually write a working exploit under contest time pressure, and vice versa.

prompts.promptText: Map DeFiVulnLabs's read-only-reentrancy and price-oracle-manipulation patterns to the exact 06b/06c leaves that cover them.
prompts.answerHint: Read-only reentrancy pattern → 'Read-only reentrancy' and 'Read-only reentrancy into oracles'; price-manipulation patterns → 'Spot-price oracle manipulation', 'TWAP oracle manipulation', 'Flash-loan price manipulation' — note any DeFiVulnLabs pattern (e.g. a specific rebasing-token quirk) that doesn't already have a home leaf.

prompts.topicTitle: Real-exploit replays: rekt.news & BlockThreat incident intuition
prompts.promptText: Why is skimming 10 incident writeups a week different in kind from replaying one incident in Foundry, and why do you need both?
prompts.answerHint: Breadth (rekt/BlockThreat) trains fast classification — recognizing 'this smells like a first-depositor inflation bug' from a headline-level description before digging in; depth (DeFiHackLabs replay) trains the actual exploit-writing muscle. An auditor needs both: breadth to triage what to look at first in a real codebase, depth to actually prove the finding. Pitfall: breadth without ever replaying anything produces false confidence — you recognize the shape but haven't proven you can exploit it under time pressure.

prompts.topicTitle: Real-exploit replays: rekt.news & BlockThreat incident intuition
prompts.promptText: Read this week's BlockThreat digest (or a recent rekt.news post-mortem) and classify the top incident by attack family.
prompts.answerHint: Identify the root-cause category (reentrancy / access-control / oracle-price / arithmetic / business-logic / etc.), name the matching 06b/06c taxonomy leaf, and state the one design decision (a check, an invariant, a timelock) that would have prevented the loss.

prompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks First Flights: beginner audit contests
prompts.promptText: Why does competing in a real First Flight teach something Ethernaut/DVD wargames structurally can't?
prompts.answerHint: Wargames have ONE known bug and a clear win condition (drain the contract); a First Flight codebase may have zero, one, or several bugs of unknown location and severity, on a fixed clock, judged by a human against a rubric — you must decide what's worth reporting, not just whether you can exploit something. Pitfall: treating a First Flight like a wargame ('find THE bug') under-reports; treating a wargame like an audit ('write up every theoretical issue') over-reports — First Flights calibrate that judgment.

prompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks First Flights: beginner audit contests
prompts.promptText: Enter a CodeHawks First Flight contest and submit at least one finding before the contest closes.
prompts.answerHint: Scope the codebase during the review window, write findings in CodeHawks' report format as you go (don't wait until the end), and submit before the deadline — late submissions aren't judged regardless of quality.

prompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks First Flights: writing a finding that survives judging
prompts.promptText: What are the most common reasons a technically-correct finding gets downgraded or rejected in CodeHawks judging?
prompts.answerHint: No runnable PoC (a claim without proof), severity asserted without justification against the actual impact + likelihood, an impact statement broader than what the PoC actually demonstrates, or duplicate/near-duplicate of an already-submitted finding. Pitfall: 'this could theoretically lead to X' without a PoC reads as speculation to a judge — always show the concrete path from bug to loss, even if the PoC is minimal.

prompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks First Flights: writing a finding that survives judging
prompts.promptText: Rewrite a First Flight finding you submitted informally into the full CodeHawks report format and resubmit/record its verdict.
prompts.answerHint: Use the current contest's live form rather than assuming one immutable template. Supply its required title, severity, and detailed description/reproduction fields; ground severity in impact and likelihood, keep within scope, add a runnable test when applicable, separate attacker/victim/protocol roles, and propose a specific mitigation.

prompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks AI First Flights: standalone AI-graded practice
prompts.promptText: How do CodeHawks AI First Flights differ from the scheduled human-judged First Flights, and how should you use them?
prompts.answerHint: AI First Flights let you choose when to start, then give you one week and instant AI evaluation with no appeals; regular First Flights run on scheduled platform windows and proceed through professional judging and appeals. Use AI First Flights for fast iteration between regular competitions, not as a substitute for judged scope, duplication, and severity decisions.

prompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks AI First Flights: standalone AI-graded practice
prompts.promptText: Complete one standalone CodeHawks AI First Flight practice audit end-to-end and act on the AI's grading.
prompts.answerHint: Pick an AI First Flight, review its codebase, submit your findings, and read the AI's instant grading; note every gap it flags (missing PoC, unjustified severity, vague impact) and record one concrete lesson to carry into your next real contest.

prompts.promptText: Why keep doing wargame-style practice after finishing Ethernaut and DVD, instead of moving straight to real audits?
prompts.answerHint: Pattern-recognition speed and exploit-writing fluency both degrade without repetition, and a fixed, exhaustive ladder (Ethernaut/DVD) eventually runs out — ongoing platforms with a growing challenge set (ONLYPWNER, Node Guardians) keep the reps coming without waiting for a new CTF season. Pitfall: novelty-seeking across platforms without ever writing up WHAT was learned (unlike the taxonomy-mapping discipline in the required ladders) turns practice into pure entertainment — keep the one-line bug-class note per challenge.

prompts.promptText: Solve at least one ONLYPWNER challenge and record which bug class it drilled.
prompts.answerHint: Pick a challenge near your current level on the leaderboard's difficulty signal, solve it, and note the bug class (it will usually map to a 06b/06c taxonomy leaf) in security/campaigns/.

prompts.promptText: Complete a Node Guardians security-themed quest or campaign chapter.
prompts.answerHint: Node Guardians' CTF-on-testnet mode replays famous hacks in a gamified quest chain — pick a security campaign, complete its chapters, and log the bug class(es) drilled in security/campaigns/.

prompts.promptText: For a constant-product pool with reserves x, y and a fee-free input dx, derive the output dy and explain why large trades slip.
prompts.answerHint: Keep x*y=k: after adding fee-free dx, x'=x+dx, so y'=k/x' and dy=y-y'=y*dx/(x+dx). The marginal price moves continuously against a larger trade on the convex curve. With Uniswap V2's fee, getAmountOut prices as though 997/1000 of input entered, but the pair receives the full input; its adjusted-balance check therefore permits and normally produces reserve-product growth. Pitfall: confusing the priced input with the final token balance gives the wrong invariant explanation.

prompts.promptText: Write Uniswap's getAmountOut with the 0.3% fee baked in.
prompts.answerHint: function getAmountOut(uint amountIn, uint rIn, uint rOut) pure returns (uint) { uint inWithFee = amountIn * 997; uint num = inWithFee * rOut; uint den = rIn * 1000 + inWithFee; return num / den; } // fee taken from input, division truncates in the pool's favor

prompts.promptText: Ethernaut level 22 (Dex): drain almost all of one token from the two-token AMM.
prompts.answerHint: The Dex prices swaps as amount*toReserve/fromReserve with integer truncation and no invariant guard; swap the full balance back and forth so the ratio skews further each round until one side rounds enough in your favor to take nearly the entire reserve. It shows why a naive spot-price AMM without a k check is drainable.

prompts.promptText: Why is a pure constant-sum (x+y=k) pool unusable on its own, and what does a hybrid curve fix?
prompts.answerHint: x+y=k gives a fixed 1:1 price and zero price impact, so an arbitrageur can swap until one reserve hits zero — there is no rising marginal price to stop them. StableSwap approximates constant-sum near balance but bends toward constant-product as reserves skew. Pitfall: the flat region assumes correlated assets; after a depeg it lets arbitrageurs exchange the impaired asset for the good one cheaply.

prompts.promptText: What does the amplification coefficient A control in Curve's stableswap, and what is its hidden risk?
prompts.answerHint: A interpolates between constant-sum (high A: prices pinned near 1:1 across a wide balance range, great for pegged pairs) and constant-product (low A: more slippage but reserves never exhaust). The invariant has no closed form, so D and outputs are solved by on-chain Newton iteration. Pitfall: high A assumes the peg holds — if an asset depegs, the flat low-slippage region becomes a trap where arbitrage drains the good asset cheaply, exactly what happened in stablecoin depeg events.

prompts.promptText: What is impermanent loss, and on what does it actually depend?
prompts.answerHint: It is the shortfall between holding LP position value and just holding the two tokens, caused by the pool auto-rebalancing along x*y=k so you end up heavier in the asset that dropped. It depends on the RATIO of price change, not volatility alone: IL = 2*sqrt(r)/(1+r) - 1 where r is the price ratio (r=2 -> ~5.7%, r=4 -> ~20%). Pitfall: it is only 'impermanent' if price returns; if you withdraw after a permanent move, the loss is realized and only offset if accrued fees exceeded it.

prompts.promptText: How does Uniswap V2's swap() enforce the invariant and the fee without computing an output amount itself?
prompts.answerHint: It optimistically transfers the caller-requested outputs, infers input from post-callback balances, then requires (balance0*1000-amount0In*3)*(balance1*1000-amount1In*3) >= reserve0*reserve1*1000^2. Underpayment reverts. Reserves are cached: sync() sets reserves to current balances, while skim() transfers only balance excess and leaves reserves unchanged. Pitfall: treating skim and sync as equivalent reconciliation operations reverses their intended effects.

prompts.promptText: How many LP shares does the first vs a subsequent depositor mint in Uniswap V2, and why the MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY burn?
prompts.answerHint: First: sqrt(amount0*amount1) - MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY, with 1000 raw share units permanently sent to address(0). Subsequent: min(amount0*totalSupply/reserve0, amount1*totalSupply/reserve1), so only the limiting side is credited and division rounds down. Locking the initial 1000 shares raises the cost of donation-driven share-value inflation; it is not a universal proof against every vault inflation path. Pitfall: an imbalanced deposit gifts the uncredited excess to existing LPs.

prompts.promptText: Write the subsequent-deposit LP mint amount for Uniswap V2.
prompts.answerHint: uint liquidity = Math.min(amount0 * totalSupply / reserve0, amount1 * totalSupply / reserve1); // MIN over both assets, integer division rounds down (pool-favorable); the excess of the over-supplied token is not credited

prompts.promptText: How is a Uniswap V2 TWAP computed, and what makes it manipulation-resistant (and where does it still fail)?
prompts.answerHint: The pair accumulates price*timeElapsed into priceCumulativeLast (UQ112.112) before reserves change; a consumer takes (cumulative_t2-cumulative_t1)/(t2-t1). If no pair write occurs at t2, extend the cumulative counterfactually from current reserves or the endpoint is stale. Sustaining distortion across time is costlier than an atomic spot move, but thin liquidity or a short window remains weak. Pitfall: stored cumulative values do not advance merely because time passes.

prompts.promptText: What makes a Uniswap V2 flash swap possible, and what enforces repayment?
prompts.answerHint: swap() sends output before its adjusted-k check and calls uniswapV2Call when data is non-empty, so the recipient can act before payment. Returning the same token requires returned >= ceil(amountOut*1000/997), about 0.3009% of amountOut; payment in the other token is also allowed if the final invariant passes. Pitfall: amountOut plus 0.3% can underpay because the fee is charged on input and integer repayment must round up.

prompts.promptText: How does Uniswap V2 collect its 1/6 protocol fee, and why lazily via sqrt(k)?
prompts.answerHint: When feeTo is on, the protocol targets one-sixth of the 30-bp LP fee (5 bp) by minting shares on the next mint/burn: liquidity = totalSupply*(sqrt(k)-sqrt(kLast))/(5*sqrt(k)+sqrt(kLast)). Measuring sqrt(k) growth avoids per-swap accounting. kLast is refreshed after liquidity events while fees are on; if fees are off and kLast is nonzero, _mintFee clears it. Pitfall: it mints LP shares rather than transferring reserve tokens per swap.

prompts.promptText: Write the conversions between a price and sqrtPriceX96 (Q64.96).
prompts.answerHint: // price1e18 is token1/token0 scaled by 1e18; this compact forward form has an explicit shift bound\nfunction priceToSqrtX96(uint price1e18) pure returns (uint160) { require(price1e18 <= type(uint64).max); return uint160(Math.sqrt(price1e18 << 192) / 1e9); }\nfunction sqrtX96ToPrice1e18(uint160 s) pure returns (uint) { uint q96 = 1 << 96; return FullMath.mulDiv(FullMath.mulDiv(s, s, q96), 1e18, q96); } // same 1e18 scale; use a 512-bit sqrt design when the bound is too narrow

prompts.promptText: Write getAmount1 for a Uniswap V3 position (amount of token1 for liquidity L over a sqrt-price range).
prompts.answerHint: // amount1 = L * (sqrtP - sqrtPa), clamped so sqrtP stays within [sqrtPa, sqrtPb]\nfunction getAmount1(uint128 L, uint160 sqrtA, uint160 sqrtB, uint160 sqrtP) pure returns (uint) { if (sqrtP < sqrtA) sqrtP = sqrtA; if (sqrtP > sqrtB) sqrtP = sqrtB; return uint(L) * (sqrtP - sqrtA) / (1 << 96); }

prompts.promptText: In Uniswap V3, what does liquidity L represent and what happens when price leaves a position's range?
prompts.answerHint: L is the concentrated liquidity active within [pa, pb]; inside the range the position holds amount0 = L*(sqrt(pb)-sqrt(P))/(sqrt(P)*sqrt(pb)) and amount1 = L*(sqrt(P)-sqrt(pa)), acting like a constant-product pool with virtual reserves so the same capital gives deeper liquidity near P. Outside the range it is entirely one asset and earns no swap fees until price re-enters. Pitfall: concentration increases in-range capital efficiency while concentrating price exposure; it does not apply one universal multiplier to fee yield or impermanent loss.

prompts.promptText: What is a tick in Uniswap V3, and why does each fee tier have a tickSpacing?
prompts.answerHint: Tick i maps to price 1.0001^i; a position's bounds must be divisible by that pool's immutable tickSpacing. The factory initially enabled 0.05%/10, 0.3%/60, and 1%/200, and governance later enabled 0.01%/1; more fee/spacing pairs can be enabled, so the list is not a protocol constant. Pitfall: only crossing an initialized tick applies liquidityNet; an aligned but uninitialized tick does not change active liquidity.

prompts.promptText: Why does Uniswap V3 store sqrt(price) as a Q64.96 number, and how do you convert back to price?
prompts.answerHint: sqrtPriceX96 = floor(sqrt(price) * 2^96) where price is token1/token0; recover price = (sqrtPriceX96 / 2^96)^2. Tracking sqrt(price) makes each swap step linear in sqrt-price along a tick (no per-step square root), and Q64.96 (64 integer + 96 fractional bits) preserves precision across the whole price range. Pitfall: forgetting the 2^96 scale or flipping the token0/token1 direction inverts or mis-scales the price by huge factors — a very common integration bug.

prompts.promptText: How does Uniswap V3 attribute fees to a specific position's range?
prompts.answerHint: It tracks feeGrowthGlobalX128 (fees per unit liquidity, Q128.128) and, per tick, feeGrowthOutside; feeGrowthInside(lower, upper) = global - outside(lower) - outside(upper) (adjusted by which side the current tick is on). Owed fees = liquidity * (feeGrowthInside_now - feeGrowthInside_last), so only fees earned while price was inside the range count. Pitfall: this per-range accounting is why V3 positions are NFTs — fees aren't a fungible pro-rata claim like V2 LP tokens, and an out-of-range position accrues nothing.

prompts.promptText: What changes when every Uniswap V4 pool lives inside one singleton PoolManager?
prompts.answerHint: All pools' tokens are custodied by one contract and pool state is keyed by PoolId, so creating a pool is a cheap state write (not a deployment) and multi-hop swaps net internally instead of transferring tokens between separate pool contracts. The concentrated-liquidity math is identical to V3; the gain is architectural — shared custody plus flash accounting cuts gas sharply. Pitfall: a single custody contract concentrates risk, so V4's core is heavily audited and hooks (not the manager) carry the customizable — and riskier — logic.

prompts.promptText: Explain V4's flash accounting: how do lock/unlock and currency deltas guarantee solvency?
prompts.answerHint: Operations run inside PoolManager.unlock(): swaps/liquidity changes accrue signed currency deltas in EIP-1153 transient storage, and unlock reverts unless every delta returns to zero. settle() pays a negative delta and take() withdraws a positive one. Net settlement can avoid intermediate pool-to-pool transfers, but the exact transfer count depends on router behavior. Pitfall: any unsettled non-zero delta reverts the whole transaction.

prompts.promptText: How does Uniswap V4 know which callbacks a hook implements, and why is that encoded in the address?
prompts.answerHint: The hook's ADDRESS low bits are permission flags (beforeSwap, afterSwap, before/afterAddLiquidity, etc.); the PoolManager reads those bits to decide which callbacks to invoke, so hooks are CREATE2-mined to an address whose bits match their implemented functions. This makes permissions immutable and gas-cheap to check. Pitfall: a hook is untrusted code the pool calls mid-operation — a malicious or buggy hook can tax, block, or reorder swaps, so hook trust is part of a pool's risk profile, not an afterthought.

prompts.promptText: What do ERC-6909 claim tokens let a Uniswap V4 trader avoid, and when does it pay off?
prompts.answerHint: Instead of withdrawing ERC-20s after each action, a trader can hold CLAIM balances (ERC-6909, a minimal multi-token standard without transfer callbacks) inside the PoolManager and settle later swaps from them — pure internal ledger updates, no real token transfers. It pays off for high-frequency traders/MEV bots and routers doing many actions per block. Pitfall: 6909 balances live inside the manager, so they carry the manager's custody risk and must eventually be redeemed to real tokens to leave the system.

prompts.promptText: What must a Chainlink consumer validate on latestRoundData(), and why is a 'push' feed shaped this way?
prompts.answerHint: Validate answer > 0, reject updatedAt==0 or an age beyond your policy, and normalize using the proxy's decimals() rather than assuming 8. Each feed updates when its configured deviation threshold or heartbeat is met, so retrieve those parameters from the official feed directory and choose an application limit. Pitfall: answer>0 alone accepts a healthy-looking value indefinitely after updates stop.

prompts.topicTitle: Uniswap V3 TWAP from tick cumulatives
prompts.promptText: How do you derive a TWAP from a Uniswap V3 pool's observations?
prompts.answerHint: Call observe([window,0]); arithmeticMeanTick=(tickCumulativeNow-tickCumulativePast)/window, correcting a negative non-exact quotient down by one because Solidity division truncates toward zero. Quote at that tick to obtain the geometric-mean price. increaseObservationCardinalityNext only schedules capacity that subsequent writes populate; requesting older-than-initialized history reverts OLD. Pitfall: capacity, initialized history, liquidity, and window length all matter to safety.

prompts.promptText: How does a Pyth pull oracle differ from a Chainlink push feed in the consumer's flow?
prompts.answerHint: In Pyth's EVM pull integration, submit updateData, pay getUpdateFee to updatePriceFeeds, then call getPriceNoOlderThan(id,maxAge). Price and conf both scale by 10^expo, so compare conf/abs(price) without losing precision. Unlike this caller-submitted path, push integrations update independently. Pitfall: Pyth supports both pull and push; regardless of path, enforce freshness and a protocol-specific confidence policy.

prompts.promptText: What is the single question that decides whether a price source is safe to trust for collateral?
prompts.answerHint: Manipulation cost relative to value at risk is necessary, not sufficient. Also model source independence, market liquidity, averaging duration, update and liveness behavior, freshness, divergence handling, and failure policy. An atomic AMM spot read is weak because an attacker can move and reverse it in one transaction while paying trading costs; a TWAP raises the cost by requiring distortion over time but is not absolute protection. Pitfall: decentralization alone says nothing about manipulation resistance.

prompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Puppet: drain the lending pool that prices collateral from a Uniswap spot pool.
prompts.answerHint: The lending pool computes required collateral from a manipulable Uniswap spot price; sell enough token into the AMM to crater that quote, then borrow against the artificially cheap valuation. Puppet variants change the AMM and collateral mechanics but preserve the same unsafe spot-oracle root. The fix is a manipulation-resistant oracle and explicit risk bounds, not merely blocking flash loans.

prompts.promptText: How does an aToken's balance grow without any transfer, and how is that implemented?
prompts.answerHint: An aToken is a scaled-balance token: your stored scaledBalance is fixed at deposit, but balanceOf = scaledBalance * liquidityIndex / RAY, and the liquidity index rises continuously with accrued interest — so balanceOf increases over time with no transfer. Debt uses the same trick with a borrow index. Pitfall: because the balance rebases, integrating aTokens like a static ERC-20 (caching a balance, or treating it as fee-on-transfer-free) silently mis-accounts interest.

prompts.promptText: Write Aave's health-factor formula and state exactly when a position becomes liquidatable.
prompts.answerHint: HF = sum(collateral_i * liquidationThreshold_i) / totalDebt, all valued in one base currency; the position is liquidatable the moment HF < 1. Borrowing is capped at the lower max-LTV, and the liquidation threshold sits above LTV to leave a buffer. A liquidator repays up to the close factor of the debt and seizes collateral plus a liquidation bonus. Pitfall: use the LIQUIDATION THRESHOLD, not the LTV, in the HF numerator — mixing them up either blocks valid liquidations or lets bad debt accrue.

prompts.promptText: Implement computeHealthFactor for a single collateral/debt pair (18-decimal base).
prompts.answerHint: function healthFactor(uint collUsd, uint liqThresholdBps, uint debtUsd) pure returns (uint) { if (debtUsd == 0) return type(uint).max; uint weighted = Math.mulDiv(collUsd, liqThresholdBps, 10_000); return Math.mulDiv(weighted, 1e18, debtUsd); } // HF < 1e18 means liquidatable

prompts.promptText: How did Aave v3.7 replace legacy isolation mode with isolated e-mode?
prompts.answerHint: E-mode applies governance-configured category LTV, liquidation, and borrowing permissions. In v3.7 an isolated e-mode lets only category collateral contribute LTV, blocks entry while outside collateral is enabled, and prevents enabling outside collateral after entry. It replaces the legacy isolated-collateral mechanism with approved debt assets and a debt ceiling, which v3.7 removes. Pitfall: rollout and category parameters are market configuration, and correlation assumptions can fail.

prompts.promptText: How does Compound V3 (Comet) differ structurally from a pooled Aave-style market?
prompts.answerHint: Comet has a SINGLE borrowable base asset per deployment (e.g. USDC): you earn/borrow only the base asset, and every other supported asset is collateral ONLY — it backs your borrow, earns no supply interest, and cannot itself be borrowed. This isolates each market's risk to one base asset and its curated collateral, versus Aave's shared multi-asset pool. Pitfall: don't expect to earn yield on collateral in Comet — supplying a collateral asset is not the same as supplying the base asset.

prompts.promptText: How does an overcollateralized CDP mint a stablecoin and keep it near $1?
prompts.answerHint: Lock collateral worth more than the debt and mint the coin up to a minimum collateralization ratio (e.g. 150% -> max ~66% of collateral value as debt); burn the coin to unlock collateral. The peg holds via overcollateralization plus arbitrage: below $1 the coin is cheap to buy and repay debt at par (worth $1 of collateral release), above $1 it's profitable to mint and sell. Pitfall: the whole system's solvency rides on the collateral PRICE FEED — a manipulated or stale oracle either mis-mints or hides insolvent vaults.

prompts.promptText: Cyfrin Updraft (Advanced Foundry) — build the DecentralizedStableCoin + DSCEngine and pass the invariant suite.
prompts.answerHint: Implement an ERC-20 stablecoin plus an engine that deposits collateral, mints DSC bounded by a health factor derived from a Chainlink feed, redeems, and liquidates undercollateralized positions with a bonus; write an invariant test asserting protocol collateral value always exceeds total DSC supply. It is the canonical from-scratch CDP exercise.

prompts.promptText: Define a CDP's collateralization ratio and explain why the oracle is its most critical dependency.
prompts.answerHint: Ratio = collateralValueUSD / debtValueUSD; below the protocol's liquidation ratio a keeper liquidates — repaying debt from collateral and taking a penalty/bonus. Both values come from an oracle, so a stale or manipulated price can trigger unfair liquidations (price reads too low) or hide insolvent vaults (price reads too high), directly threatening the peg and solvency. Pitfall: liquidations must stay incentive-compatible even in a gas spike / price crash, or nobody liquidates and the protocol accrues bad debt.

prompts.promptText: Why are seigniorage-style algorithmic stablecoins structurally fragile, using UST/LUNA as the example?
prompts.answerHint: Terra Classic's market module burned the offered native coin and minted the requested coin at oracle exchange rates. When stablecoin exits require minting a volatile sister asset, falling sister-asset price means each redemption requires more issuance, which can further weaken price and redemption capacity. After the May 2022 collapse, market-module swaps were disabled on Terra Classic and the new Terra chain launched without native stablecoins or that module. Pitfall: mint/burn convertibility is not collateral; it depends on demand for the asset being issued.

prompts.promptText: What is the relationship between DAI and USDS after MakerDAO's rebrand to Sky?
prompts.answerHint: USDS is a distinct upgradeable ERC-20. The permissionless DaiUsds convenience contract converts DAI and USDS both ways at 1:1 by using DaiJoin and UsdsJoin; it does not make their token addresses or implementation surfaces identical. The canonical USDS repository documents permit, EIP-1271 signatures, and UUPS upgradeability, but no account-freeze function. Pitfall: parity through a converter is not ERC-20 identity—integrations must configure each address and its actual contract behavior.

prompts.promptText: Why does DeFi prefer wstETH over stETH, given they represent the same staked ETH?
prompts.answerHint: stETH is share-accounted and normally rebases when Lido's oracle report changes pooled ether; balances can rise with rewards or fall with penalties. wstETH represents those shares with a non-rebasing ERC-20 balance, while stETH-per-wstETH changes. That is safer for systems that cannot account for balance changes without transfers. Pitfall: neither token is mechanically fixed at 1 ETH—use the current share/wrapper rate and account for rounding.

prompts.promptText: What does EigenLayer restaking add on top of Ethereum staking, and what is the new risk?
prompts.answerHint: Restaking reuses staked ETH/LSTs to opt into securing additional services (AVSs); stakers delegate to operators who run AVS software and earn extra rewards, extending Ethereum's pooled crypto-economic security to oracles/bridges/DA layers. The new risk is ADDITIONAL, AVS-specific slashing on top of Ethereum's — each AVS defines its own fault conditions. Pitfall: stacking many AVSs multiplies slashing surface and can create correlated-failure risk if operators over-commit the same stake across risky services.

prompts.promptText: Write a scaled-balance balanceOf so an aToken accrues interest without transfers.
prompts.answerHint: function balanceOf(address u) public view returns (uint) { return scaledBalance[u].rayMulFloor(liquidityIndex()); } // mint stores amount.rayDivFloor(index); burn/transfer convert assets to scaled balances with ceil rounding

prompts.promptText: Write Hyperliquid's funding-rate and payment kernel from an averaged premium index.
prompts.answerHint: int adjustment = clamp(interestRate8hWad - averagePremiumWad, -5e14, 5e14); int rate8hWad = averagePremiumWad + adjustment; int hourlyRateWad = clamp(rate8hWad / 8, -4e16, 4e16); int payment = int(positionSize) * int(oraclePrice) / 1e18 * hourlyRateWad / 1e18; // positive: long pays short; use oracle notional

prompts.promptText: What is the funding rate on a perpetual future, and which direction does it push?
prompts.answerHint: A periodic peer-to-peer payment between longs and shorts that helps tether the perp to spot. On Hyperliquid, impact bid/ask prices form a premium normalized by the spot oracle; sampled premiums are averaged, adjusted by a clamped interest term, and capped. Positive funding makes LONGS pay SHORTS; negative funding reverses it. Payment uses position size * oracle price * funding rate, not mark-price notional. Pitfall: funding is not a protocol fee, and weak oracle or impact-price inputs can distort it.

prompts.promptText: In a GMX V2 GM pool, what side do liquidity providers take, and how are trades priced?
prompts.answerHint: A GM market holds long and short backing tokens and references an index price feed; it need not hold the index token. LPs earn fees and are counterparty to aggregate trader PnL, so trader profit reduces pool value. Orders use oracle mark prices instead of a reserve curve, but configured price impact is applied separately from slippage based on imbalance. Two-phase execution commits the order before oracle prices arrive. Pitfall: GM liquidity is market-specific counterparty and token exposure, not risk-free yield.

prompts.promptText: How does Hyperliquid's liquidity model differ from an AMM, and what backstops it?
prompts.answerHint: HyperCore runs fully on-chain order books on Hyperliquid's purpose-built L1; resting orders match by price-time priority rather than a bonding curve. Liquidations first submit market orders to that book. If a position remains deeply below maintenance margin, it can be transferred to the liquidator vault, a component strategy of HLP. Pitfall: HLP is not the matching rule or sole source of ordinary liquidity—the public order book matches all resting orders.

prompts.promptText: State the ERC-4626 share/asset conversion and the two rounding rules that keep the vault solvent.
prompts.answerHint: Ignoring virtual terms, convertToShares = assets*totalSupply/totalAssets and convertToAssets is the inverse; both convert functions must round down. For state-changing previews, deposit/redeem outputs round down while mint/withdraw required inputs round up. A virtual asset plus virtual shares (optionally with a decimal offset) can make donation attacks unprofitable. Pitfall: that defense is implementation-specific, and totalAssets semantics come from the vault—not an assumption that raw balanceOf is always correct.

prompts.promptText: Write ERC-4626 convertToShares with vault-favorable (round-down) behavior and virtual offset.
prompts.answerHint: function convertToShares(uint assets) view returns (uint) { return Math.mulDiv(assets, totalSupply() + 10 ** _decimalsOffset(), totalAssets() + 1, Math.Rounding.Floor); } // virtual asset + virtual shares; convertToShares rounds down

prompts.promptText: What makes an Aave flash loan safe despite being uncollateralized, and how is repayment enforced?
prompts.answerHint: Atomicity: the pool transfers funds and calls executeOperation; after the callback, flashLoanSimple pulls principal plus the configured premium. If approval or balance is insufficient, the entire transaction reverts. The premium is governance-configurable, so receiver logic must use the callback value or query current pool configuration rather than hard-code 0.05%. Pitfall: flashLoan has multiple assets and can open authorized debt modes, while flashLoanSimple is the repay-with-premium path.

prompts.topicTitle: Flash-loan use cases (arb, liquidation, collateral swap)
prompts.promptText: Name three legitimate flash-loan strategies and the constraint they all share.
prompts.answerHint: Cross-venue arbitrage, liquidations, and collateral swaps or debt refinancing. Each path must end the callback with enough of the repayment asset for principal plus premium, within available pool liquidity, or the transaction reverts. The principal need not be pre-funded, but gas, execution risk, slippage limits, and any shortfall still matter. Pitfall: flash liquidity can amplify oracle manipulation, so consumers must harden price sources rather than assume the primitive can be blocked.

prompts.topicTitle: Flash-loan use cases (arb, liquidation, collateral swap)
prompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Naive Receiver: drain a flash-loan receiver that pays the fee on every call.
prompts.answerHint: The receiver pays a fixed fee for any flash loan and doesn't check who initiated it, so anyone can force it to take repeated (even zero-value) loans until its balance is bled out in fees to the pool. The lesson: a flash-loan receiver must authenticate the initiator and validate loan parameters, not blindly pay on callback.

prompts.promptText: What happens, to state and to gas, when a call frame runs out of gas mid-execution?
prompts.answerHint: The frame halts exceptionally: its state changes are discarded, it produces no output, and its remaining gas becomes zero. Pitfall: EIP-150 caps requested CALL-family gas to all but one sixty-fourth of the gas available after call costs; a value-bearing CALL also adds a 2300-gas stipend, so forwarding is not simply `gasleft()*63/64`.

prompts.promptText: How do signed and unsigned opcodes differ, and what does DIV by zero do?
prompts.answerHint: Unsigned (DIV/LT/GT/MOD) treat words as 0..2²⁵⁶−1; signed (SDIV/SLT/SGT/SMOD) treat them as two's-complement. DIV/SDIV/MOD by zero return 0 — no revert at the opcode level. Pitfall: a raw uint8/address on the stack can carry dirty high bits; compare/mask before trusting it, since opcodes operate on full 256-bit words.

prompts.promptText: Give the raw opcodes that push 3 and 2 and add them.
prompts.answerHint: PUSH1 0x03 PUSH1 0x02 ADD → leaves 0x05 on the stack (ADD pops the two operands, pushes the sum).

prompts.promptText: Why can writing to a high memory offset cost far more than writing near 0x80?
prompts.answerHint: The active range rounds up to 32-byte words, and expansion from a to b words costs Cmem(b)−Cmem(a), where Cmem(x)=3x+⌊x²/512⌋. Pitfall: MSTORE writes 32 bytes, so a write at offset+1 overlaps the preceding word; use MSTORE8 for one byte.

prompts.promptText: Write assembly that stores a value at 0x80 and reads it back.
prompts.answerHint: assembly { mstore(0x80, v) let x := mload(0x80) } — MSTORE writes the 32-byte word at 0x80, MLOAD reads it. Pitfall: 0x80 is the first free byte; don't write into 0x00–0x7f (scratch + free-pointer + zero-slot) without care.

prompts.promptText: How do TSTORE/TLOAD differ from SSTORE/SLOAD in cost and lifetime?
prompts.answerHint: TLOAD and TSTORE each cost 100 gas, have no refund, share contract-owned state across that contract's frames, and are discarded at transaction end; TSTORE is forbidden under STATICCALL. Persistent SLOAD is 2100 cold/100 warm, while SSTORE depends on original/current/new values plus a possible cold surcharge and capped refund. Pitfall: transient writes made by a reverting frame are also reverted.

prompts.promptText: Write a transient-storage reentrancy guard in assembly.
prompts.answerHint: assembly { if tload(0) { revert(0,0) } tstore(0,1) } _; assembly { tstore(0,0) } — sets a transient lock, runs the body, then clears it. TLOAD/TSTORE each cost 100 gas. Transaction-end cleanup is not a substitute for clearing: a stale lock blocks later calls in the same transaction.

prompts.promptText: Contrast CALL, DELEGATECALL, and STATICCALL by storage, msg.sender, and value.
prompts.answerHint: CALL: target's own storage, msg.sender = caller, can pass value. DELEGATECALL: caller's storage, msg.sender & msg.value preserved from the outer call, no value arg. STATICCALL: like CALL but any state change (SSTORE/LOG/CREATE/value) reverts. Pitfall: a call to a codeless address returns success=true with empty returndata — EXTCODESIZE-check when you need real code; delegatecall to untrusted code hands over your storage.

prompts.promptText: Give the address formulas for CREATE and CREATE2 and the practical difference.
prompts.answerHint: CREATE: keccak256(RLP(deployer, deployer_nonce))[12:], precomputable when the nonce is known. CREATE2: keccak256(0xff ‖ deployer ‖ salt ‖ keccak256(init_code))[12:]. Pitfall: init_code includes encoded constructor arguments, so changing one changes the CREATE2 address; successful init code's returned bytes become runtime code.

prompts.promptText: Write the Solidity that computes a CREATE2 address for known salt and init code.
prompts.answerHint: address a = address(uint160(uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(bytes1(0xff), deployer, salt, keccak256(initCode)))))); — take the last 20 bytes of the keccak of 0xff‖deployer‖salt‖keccak256(initCode).

prompts.promptText: How do RETURN and REVERT differ, and what does EXTCODESIZE return during a constructor?
prompts.answerHint: Both return a memory range, but REVERT rolls back the frame and preserves unused gas while RETURN completes normally; STOP returns empty output, and an invalid instruction is an exceptional halt that leaves the frame no gas. Pitfall: EXTCODESIZE is zero while an account's init code is running, so contract-rejection checks based on code size are bypassable from a constructor.

prompts.topicTitle: Building an EVM interpreter from scratch
prompts.promptText: What state does a minimal EVM interpreter track per call frame, and what must JUMP validate?
prompts.answerHint: A program counter, a 1024-deep stack of 256-bit words, byte-addressed memory, gas remaining, and the last returndata — plus references to storage and world state. JUMP/JUMPI must land on a JUMPDEST (0x5b) that is a real instruction, not a byte inside PUSH data. Pitfall: failing to exclude PUSH-immediate bytes from valid jump destinations lets crafted bytecode jump into data.

prompts.topicTitle: Building an EVM interpreter from scratch
prompts.promptText: Pass the w1nt3r evm-from-scratch test ladder through the JUMP group.
prompts.answerHint: Fork the repo, implement STOP/PUSH/arithmetic/DUP/SWAP, then JUMP/JUMPI with JUMPDEST validation; run the provided tests per opcode group.

prompts.promptText: What safety does an assembly block give up compared to Solidity?
prompts.answerHint: No overflow/underflow checks, no array bounds checks, no automatic memory management, and no type checking on values written back to Solidity variables. Pitfall: writing a value with dirty high bits into an address/bool variable from assembly can break later comparisons — mask to the type width yourself.

prompts.topicTitle: Solidity memory layout & the free memory pointer
prompts.promptText: What lives at 0x00–0x3f, 0x40, and 0x60 in Solidity's memory model?
prompts.answerHint: 0x00–0x3f is scratch space; 0x40 stores the free-memory pointer, initially 0x80; 0x60–0x7f is a zero slot that must not be written. Pitfall: compiler temporaries can use space at the free pointer without advancing it, so unallocated memory is not guaranteed zero and manual allocations must update 0x40.

prompts.topicTitle: Solidity memory layout & the free memory pointer
prompts.promptText: Write assembly that allocates 32 bytes using the free memory pointer.
prompts.answerHint: assembly { let p := mload(0x40) mstore(0x40, add(p, 0x20)) mstore(p, v) } — read the pointer at 0x40, bump it by the size, then use the region.

prompts.promptText: Where do a function's arguments start in calldata, and what does an out-of-range calldataload return?
prompts.answerHint: Arguments start at offset 4 (after the 4-byte selector); each static arg is a 32-byte word, dynamic args store a 32-byte offset in the head with length+data in the tail. Pitfall: calldataload past calldatasize returns zero-padded bytes (not a revert), so hand-decoding short calldata can read attacker-friendly zeros as valid args — solc's ABI decoder adds the bounds checks you lose.

prompts.promptText: Write Yul that loads the first uint256 argument from calldata.
prompts.answerHint: let a := calldataload(4) — the selector occupies bytes 0–3, so the first 32-byte argument word begins at offset 4 (the second is at 0x24).

prompts.promptText: How do you bubble a child call's exact revert reason back up in assembly?
prompts.answerHint: returndatacopy(0, 0, returndatasize()) then revert(0, returndatasize()) — copy the callee's returndata into memory and revert over it. Pitfall: revert(0,0) discards all error data (opaque failure); to raise your own custom error, store shl(224, selector) plus encoded args and revert over that range.

prompts.promptText: Write assembly that reverts with a 4-byte custom-error selector.
prompts.answerHint: assembly { mstore(0x00, shl(224, 0x12345678)) revert(0x00, 0x04) } — put the selector in the top 4 bytes of the word at 0x00 and revert over those 4 bytes.

prompts.promptText: How is a standalone Yul object structured, and what does its init code do?
prompts.answerHint: An outer object = creation/init code with a `code{}` and a nested sub-object ("runtime") whose `code{}` is the deployed code; the init code datacopy's the runtime and RETURNs it. Pitfall: forgetting to RETURN the runtime from the constructor deploys empty code, and dataoffset("runtime") must match the sub-object's name.

prompts.promptText: What do takes/returns mean in a Huff macro, and what enforces them?
prompts.answerHint: They annotate the macro's intended number of consumed and produced stack items. You still manage actual item order and DUP/SWAP behavior against the inlined opcodes. Pitfall: treating the annotation as a substitute for tracing all control-flow paths can leave a caller with the wrong stack shape.

prompts.promptText: Write a Huff macro that adds one to the top stack item.
prompts.answerHint: #define macro ADD_ONE() = takes(1) returns(1) { 0x01 add } — pushes 1 and ADDs it to the existing top-of-stack value.

prompts.topicTitle: Huff jump tables & when Huff pays off
prompts.promptText: How does a hand-written Huff dispatcher route a call, and what must not be forgotten?
prompts.answerHint: Load the selector (calldataload(0), shr 0xe0), then for each function `dup1 __FUNC_SIG(f) eq <label> jumpi`, else fall through to a revert. Pitfall: omit the final fallback revert and an unknown selector falls into the first function's body — the manual control that makes Huff cheap also makes this your responsibility.

prompts.topicTitle: Huff jump tables & when Huff pays off
prompts.promptText: Practice hand-writing Huff macros and dispatch on the RareSkills Huff puzzles.
prompts.answerHint: Work the huff-puzzles ladder: implement each macro so its test passes, managing the stack and selector dispatch by hand.

prompts.promptText: How is a function selector computed, and what breaks it?
prompts.answerHint: bytes4(keccak256(canonicalSignature)) — first 4 bytes of the keccak of e.g. "transfer(address,uint256)" (= 0xa9059cbb), using canonical types, no names, no spaces. Pitfall: writing "uint" instead of "uint256", adding spaces, or including argument names hashes to the wrong selector; 4 bytes also means collisions exist.

prompts.promptText: Write the Solidity expression for the selector of transfer(address,uint256).
prompts.answerHint: bytes4(keccak256("transfer(address,uint256)")) == 0xa9059cbb — canonical signature string, first 4 bytes of the keccak256.

prompts.promptText: How does the compiled dispatcher extract and route the selector?
prompts.answerHint: A generated dispatcher can guard calldatasize < 4, use shr(0xe0, calldataload(0)) to right-align the selector, compare selectors, and jump to a matching body; no match follows the generated fallback/receive/revert path. Pitfall: the exact comparison tree depends on compiler version, pipeline, optimizer, and interface, so infer it from the pinned build's disassembly, not a universal heuristic.

prompts.promptText: Write the two-op sequence that extracts the selector from calldata.
prompts.answerHint: shr(0xe0, calldataload(0)) — load the first 32 bytes of calldata and shift right by 224 bits to leave the 4-byte selector right-aligned.

prompts.topicTitle: Calldata layout, fallback & receive at bytecode level
prompts.promptText: Which of receive/fallback runs for empty vs unmatched calldata?
prompts.answerHint: Empty calldata with receive() present → receive(); if receive is absent, a payable fallback may handle it. Any calldata whose selector matches no function (including non-empty data shorter than 4 bytes) → fallback() when present. Pitfall: fallback must be payable to accept value; proxies deliberately use the unmatched-call path to delegate.

prompts.promptText: How does solc assign storage slots, and what is fatal for an upgradeable contract?
prompts.answerHint: With the default base, variables follow C3-linearized order from slot 0; value types pack into lower-order bytes when they fit, while structs and arrays start a new slot and pack internally. Constants and immutables use no storage slot. Pitfall: an upgrade must preserve existing layout; reordering, changing types, or inserting before existing fields can reinterpret proxy state.

prompts.promptText: Where does mapping value m[k] (m at slot p) and dynamic-array element i live?
prompts.answerHint: m[k] starts at keccak256(h(k) . p): h pads value-type keys to 32 bytes but uses raw unpadded data for bytes/string keys; nested mappings hash recursively. A dynamic array normally stores length at p and data from keccak256(p); 32-byte element i is at base+i, while smaller elements can pack. Short bytes/string (≤31 bytes) store data and length in p itself.

prompts.promptText: Write assembly that computes the storage slot of mapping entry m[key], m at slot p.
prompts.answerHint: For a `mapping(uint256 => ...)`: assembly { mstore(0x00, key) mstore(0x20, p) let s := keccak256(0x00, 0x40) } — the two mstores produce padded key ‖ slot. For bytes/string keys, h(k) is the raw unpadded key data, so this fixed 64-byte kernel does not apply unchanged.

prompts.promptText: What problem does ERC-7201 solve, and how is its base slot derived?
prompts.answerHint: It roots an annotated module struct at keccak256(abi.encode(uint256(keccak256(bytes(id))) − 1)) & ~bytes32(uint256(0xff)). The subtract-one seed is outside the ordinary tree, the second hash keeps the multi-slot namespace disjoint under the ERC's assumptions, and the mask aligns to 256 slots. Pitfall: the annotation is not enforced; unique IDs and correct assembly slot assignment remain the author's job.

prompts.promptText: Write the ERC-7201 base-slot computation for a namespace string.
prompts.answerHint: bytes32 slot = keccak256(abi.encode(uint256(keccak256(bytes("my.namespace"))) - 1)) & ~bytes32(uint256(0xff)); — hash the namespace, subtract 1, ABI-encode+hash, clear the low byte.

prompts.promptText: What is an EIP-1167 clone's runtime, and why can't it be upgraded or run a constructor?
prompts.answerHint: ERC-1167 standardizes a fixed 45-byte deployed runtime that copies calldata, delegatecalls a fixed 20-byte implementation with all gas, and returns or reverts with returndata; deployment bytecode is explicitly outside the ERC. Pitfall: the implementation constructor never initializes clone storage, so deploy and initialize safely—an uninitialized clone may be taken over.

prompts.promptText: Give the EIP-1167 runtime bytecode template with the implementation placeholder.
prompts.answerHint: 363d3d373d3d3d363d73<20-byte-impl>5af43d82803e903d91602b57fd5bf3 — 45 bytes: calldatacopy, delegatecall to <impl> with all gas, returndatacopy, then RETURN on success or REVERT.

prompts.promptText: Where does an ERC-1967 proxy store the implementation address, and why the odd slot?
prompts.answerHint: At bytes32(uint256(keccak256("eip1967.proxy.implementation")) − 1) = 0x360894…382bbc, with sibling beacon and optional admin slots; the fallback can sload it and delegatecall. The label hash and −1 convention avoid compiler-allocated state. Pitfall: the slot does not provide upgrade authorization or implementation-layout compatibility—both must be enforced separately.

prompts.promptText: Write the constant for the ERC-1967 implementation slot and how the proxy reads it.
prompts.answerHint: bytes32 constant SLOT = 0x360894a13ba1a3210667c828492db98dca3e2076cc3735a920a3ca505d382bbc; // = keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation') - 1; read via sload(SLOT) then delegatecall.

prompts.promptText: How did metamorphic contracts work, and how did EIP-6780 stop them?
prompts.answerHint: CREATE2 pins an address to deployer, salt, and init-code hash, while init code may return runtime obtained from mutable dependencies. Pre-6780, code could be deleted in one transaction and different runtime redeployed later with the same CREATE2 inputs. EIP-6780 leaves code/storage intact for later-transaction SELFDESTRUCT. The same-creation-transaction exception still cannot destroy and recreate at that address within one transaction because creation collision rules apply.

prompts.promptText: What can symbolic execution prove that fuzzing cannot, and what is its main limit?
prompts.answerHint: Fuzzing samples concrete inputs and can find a counterexample but does not exhaust the domain. Symbolic execution forks on symbolic path conditions and can prove an assertion for the modeled domain when every relevant path is discharged, or produce a counterexample. Pitfall: bounds, abstractions, unsupported behavior, path explosion, and timeouts may yield an incomplete run—'no counterexample' alone is not proof.

prompts.promptText: How does Halmos turn a Foundry test into a proof, and what should you watch?
prompts.answerHint: Halmos symbolically executes check_ parameters over their types after setUp and can report assertion counterexamples; svm cheatcodes add symbolic values. Pitfall: dynamic arrays need fixed chosen lengths, vm.assume narrows the domain, and non-assertion reverts are ignored by default. A PASS must be stated with those setup, domain, timeout, and supported-semantics boundaries.

prompts.promptText: What does a CVL spec contain, and how can a spec falsely 'verify'?
prompts.answerHint: A .spec can declare method summaries, rules over symbolic env/args, and invariants. Rules check assertions under their requires; invariants prove a constructor base case and preservation by included state-changing methods. Pitfall: over-strong requires, filtered methods, reverting invariant expressions, preserved assumptions, or unresolved-call modeling can exclude real behavior or make an invariant result unsound.

prompts.promptText: Study worked CVL specs and rules in the Certora Examples repository.
prompts.answerHint: Read and run specs in Certora/Examples: pick a contract, inspect its .spec (methods/rule/invariant), and reproduce the prover reporting verified.

prompts.promptText: What makes Kontrol's guarantees strong, and what remains your responsibility?
prompts.answerHint: Kontrol compiles Foundry artifacts into KEVM helper modules and symbolically executes selected Solidity tests against KEVM's K semantics. `build`, `prove`, `list`, and KCFG inspection expose the workflow and proof state. Pitfall: storage abstractions, bounds, lemmas, loop invariants, or manual steps become part of the claim; any open or stuck branch remains unproven, not safe.

prompts.promptText: What makes an invariant genuinely proven rather than just tested?
prompts.answerHint: Use induction over reachable states: prove the constructor establishes the invariant, then assume it before an arbitrary included state-changing method and prove that method preserves it. Repeat for the complete transition set. Pitfall: filtering a method, adding an unjustified preserved require, allowing the invariant expression to revert, or under-modeling external calls can make a reported result unsound.

prompts.promptText: What does PBS separate, and what does the proposer actually commit to?
prompts.answerHint: Builders assemble execution payloads and bid; the proposer chooses a blinded header before body reveal. Today MEV-Boost implements this out of protocol through trusted relays, while EIP-7732 is only a draft for enshrined PBS. The commitment prevents same-slot unbundling of a revealed builder payload.

prompts.topicTitle: The MEV supply chain: searchers, builders, proposers
prompts.promptText: Trace MEV through its actors and say where most of the value ends up.
prompts.answerHint: Searchers submit bundles/private transactions → builders combine them with public flow → relays validate and escrow candidate payloads → proposers choose header bids. Competition can move much of an opportunity's value to the proposer, but the realized split varies by opportunity and market structure.

prompts.promptText: What does sending a bundle through Flashbots (vs the public mempool) give you, and what's the systemic cost?
prompts.answerHint: eth_sendBundle privately sends an ordered bundle for a target block; transactions revert the bundle unless listed in revertingTxHashes, and inclusion is not guaranteed. Losing sealed bids need not land onchain, but builders and relays can see or censor the order flow. MEV-Boost lets proposers choose competing builder headers through relays.

prompts.promptText: How does a sandwich attack profit, and what defeats it?
prompts.answerHint: Frontrun the victim's swap to push price against them, let them execute at the worse price, then backrun to unwind. The victim's size and permitted price movement bound the opportunity; fees, gas, competition, and execution determine realized profit. A tight minAmountOut can make the controlled example revert or unprofitable, while loose slippage creates more room for extraction.

prompts.promptText: Why do searchers race to liquidate, and how can a flash loan fund the transaction?
prompts.answerHint: On Aave V3, health factor below 1 permits liquidationCall: repay eligible debt and receive corresponding collateral plus the configured bonus. A flash loan can front the debt asset, but principal, premium, swap slippage, gas, and inclusion competition all must fit inside the realized bonus.

prompts.promptText: Practice building a flash-loan-funded liquidation bot (Damn Vulnerable DeFi puppet-style / real Aave).
prompts.answerHint: Flash-borrow the debt asset, call liquidationCall, seize collateral, swap enough to repay principal plus premium, and keep only the net remainder — all atomically in a pinned local fixture.

prompts.promptText: How does an order-flow auction return MEV to users?
prompts.answerHint: MEV-Share's mev_sendBundle can disclose selected privacy.hints so searchers compose backruns, then validity.refund and refundConfig allocate percentages after inclusion. More hints improve searchability but leak more; selected builders still receive the full submitted bundle.

prompts.promptText: How does an intent differ from a transaction, and what must the signature bound?
prompts.answerHint: A transaction prescribes execution, while an intent authorizes constraints/outcomes that a solver may satisfy with a chosen path. The signed domain must bind the account, chain(s), assets, limits, deadline, and replay policy. Authorization and settlement security depend on the chosen intent standard; there is no universal intent envelope.

prompts.promptText: What does the current ERC-7683 draft standardize, and what does it leave protocol-specific?
prompts.answerHint: The current ERC-7683 draft standardizes opaque payload resolution into steps, variables, payments, and named assumptions through a vetted resolver called offchain with eth_call. It does not require a common open/fill interface or secure settlement; those remain protocol-specific.

prompts.promptText: Contrast UniswapX, CoW, and Across on price discovery and risk.
prompts.answerHint: UniswapX uses chain-specific competitive auctions, including Dutch output decay; CoW uses fair combinatorial batch auctions with coincidence-of-wants matching; Across relayers front destination capital and are repaid through bonded optimistic bundle settlement. Compare who sets price, fronts capital, and bears settlement/finality risk.

prompts.promptText: When do V4's swap hooks fire, and what must a hook return?
prompts.answerHint: beforeSwap and afterSwap run around PoolManager.swap only when their address bits are set. Return-delta permissions are separate bits; beforeSwap may also return a per-swap LP-fee override for a dynamic-fee pool. Every callback returns its exact selector, and wrong selectors or malformed return data revert.

prompts.promptText: How does a V4 pool get a dynamic fee?
prompts.answerHint: Initialize with LPFeeLibrary.DYNAMIC_FEE_FLAG (0x800000); the hook may update the stored LP fee with updateDynamicLPFee or return a valid beforeSwap override carrying OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG. Dynamic capability is immutable, and LP fees are distinct from protocol and hook fees.

prompts.topicTitle: V4 hook permission flags & address mining
prompts.promptText: How does the PoolManager know which hooks to call, and why must you mine the hook address?
prompts.answerHint: Fourteen low address bits encode callback and return-delta permissions, so CREATE2 salt mining finds an address with the intended mask. BaseHook validates getHookPermissions against that address during construction; PoolManager later uses the bits to decide which callbacks to invoke.

prompts.promptText: What must a production V4 hook get right, and why is gas-leanness non-negotiable?
prompts.answerHint: Extend BaseHook, make getHookPermissions match the mined address, restrict privileged entry points, and prove every returned delta settles under PoolManager accounting. Review callback inputs, nested actions/reentrancy, price manipulation, gas/DoS, and upgrade/admin risk; custom hook safety is not guaranteed by v4 core.

prompts.promptText: Build and test a Uniswap V4 hook from the official template (Hook Incubator style).
prompts.answerHint: Extend BaseHook, implement getHookPermissions + the callbacks you need, mine the address, and prove a swap triggers your logic in the v4-template test harness.

prompts.promptText: What is an AVS, and who are the three parties in EigenLayer?
prompts.answerHint: An AVS (Autonomous Verifiable Service) uses EigenLayer operator sets to make verifiable commitments; operators run its software backed by stake that restakers delegate and operators allocate. Pitfall: slashing is only meaningful if the AVS specifies an objectively attributable fault condition — otherwise stake can be destroyed subjectively.

prompts.promptText: What is the core tradeoff of restaking the same stake across many AVSs?
prompts.answerHint: Restakers delegate shares to one operator; for each strategy, that operator splits magnitude across operator sets, and total encumbered magnitude cannot exceed current max magnitude. A slash reduces the targeted allocation, delegated shares, and max magnitude, leaving less future capacity. Pitfall: delegation and allocation are separate, and operator-set allocations cannot each reuse the same 100%.

prompts.promptText: What does EigenLayer's slashing framework require to protect honest restakers?
prompts.answerHint: An operator allocates a bounded magnitude to an operator set, and only that set's configured slasher may slash it; the slash proportionally reduces delegated stake. Core v1.13 delays clearing burnable or redistributable shares after the slash is recorded. EigenLayer enforces authority and allocation bounds, not the correctness of an AVS's evidence. Pitfall: unsafe slasher code or subjective evidence can still destroy honestly delegated stake.

prompts.promptText: What distinguishes cryptographic from crypto-economic verifiability for an EigenCloud service?
prompts.answerHint: Cryptographic verifiability supplies a proof; reproducible execution lets another party recompute; crypto-economic accountability penalizes attributable faults. Pitfall: a product label does not tell you which guarantee applies—identify verifier, evidence, failure model, and any stake actually at risk.

prompts.promptText: Why is a tokenized Treasury only as safe as its off-chain wrapper?
prompts.answerHint: The token represents a legally defined claim on an off-chain portfolio or note; code cannot itself establish legal title, custody, valuation, eligibility, or redemption. Trust rests on the product's issuer/fund, service providers, custody and transfer infrastructure. Pitfall: BUIDL, OUSG, USDY, and rUSDY have different assets and yield mechanics.

prompts.promptText: What must a compliant RWA token add over a plain ERC-20, and what does it break?
prompts.answerHint: ERC-3643 separates identity-registry eligibility from global compliance and adds pre-checks, pause/freeze, recovery, and agent-authorized lifecycle actions such as forced transfer. Pitfall: integrations that assume every address can receive and transfer a plain ERC-20 may revert or become unusable.

prompts.promptText: Why do RWAs need proof-of-reserve oracles, and what's the residual trust?
prompts.answerHint: A PoR feed attests a defined reserve quantity; a consumer can compare normalized reserves with liabilities only after checking units, decimals, sign, and freshness. Pitfall: the feed does not independently prove legal title, redemption rights, NAV, or that its attested asset matches the token liability.

prompts.promptText: Contrast SNARKs and STARKs on setup, proof size, and quantum resistance.
prompts.answerHint: Common pairing-based SNARKs offer small proofs and cheap verification but may use circuit-specific or universal setup and are not post-quantum; STARKs use transparent public randomness and hash assumptions, usually with larger proofs. Pitfall: these are families—state the concrete system before claiming setup, size, or verifier cost.

prompts.promptText: What do ZK systems actually prove, and what is the witness?
prompts.answerHint: A backend proves satisfaction of its compiled field constraints using witness assignments. R1CS and PLONKish systems encode relations differently; DSL branches/loops are compiled or bounded. Pitfall: unconstrained hints add no soundness unless constrained code checks their claimed result, and Field arithmetic wraps modulo the backend field.

prompts.promptText: In a Noir `main`, what distinguishes public from private inputs, and how do you verify?
prompts.answerHint: Inputs marked `pub` are public; unmarked inputs are private witness; `assert` adds constraints. Current Nargo compiles/executes (`nargo execute`) and a backend such as Barretenberg proves/verifies (`bb prove`, `bb verify`). Pitfall: pin compatible versions and remember public values are revealed with the proof.

prompts.promptText: Write and prove a Noir circuit for a hash preimage, then verify it.
prompts.answerHint: Write a valid Noir hash constraint with x private and the digest public; `nargo execute` emits circuit+witness, then `bb prove` and `bb verify`. A wrong preimage must fail execution/proving. Pin Nargo, bb, and the selected hash/proof mode.

prompts.promptText: How does an on-chain SNARK verifier work, and where is its trust anchored?
prompts.answerHint: A generated verifier checks backend-specific proof bytes and public inputs against a verification key tied to one circuit and proving configuration. Pitfall: mismatched circuit, key, backend version, hash mode, serialization, or public-input order invalidates the boundary; not every SNARK verifier uses pairings.

prompts.promptText: Across ZK rollups, privacy apps, and identity proofs, what is the common pattern?
prompts.answerHint: Prove a fact while hiding the witness: rollups prove correct L2 execution to L1 (validity), privacy apps prove a statement without revealing inputs, identity proofs reveal a predicate (over 18, is human) not the data. Pitfall: define public inputs vs private witness precisely — a value accidentally made public defeats the privacy goal.

prompts.promptText: How does a Nitro interactive fraud proof keep L1 cost low?
prompts.answerHint: Nitro supplies deterministic Wasm execution; BoLD organizes competing assertions and narrows the disputed history until L1 verifies a one-step proof. Pitfall: one honest validator must actively participate within the challenge period; BoLD bounds delay from many adversarial claims rather than removing that liveness assumption.

prompts.promptText: What are the two halves of the OP Stack fault-proof system?
prompts.answerHint: The deterministic fault-proof program derives L2 output from agreed inputs; Cannon is an FPVM that generates a trace off-chain and verifies one instruction on-chain, while the dispute game narrows claims. Pitfall: op-program is transitioning to kona-client, so pin the game type and implementation version.

prompts.promptText: Why is data availability, not the state root, the security linchpin of a rollup?
prompts.answerHint: The sequencer creates blocks; the batcher publishes compressed channel frames to Ethereum calldata or blobs; verifiers derive the canonical L2 chain from L1 data. A state root alone cannot reconstruct execution. Pitfall: a validium uses external DA, adding an availability assumption rather than merely 'posting only a root.'

prompts.promptText: How does viem split responsibilities between clients, and what is a Transport?
prompts.answerHint: A Public Client does read-only calls (eth_call, getBalance, logs); a Wallet Client signs/sends (sendTransaction, signMessage); both sit over a Transport (http, webSocket, or injected EIP-1193). Pitfall: trying to sign with a public client (or read via a wallet client you didn't need a signer for) means you wired the wrong client — reads never need a signer.

prompts.promptText: What does readContract need, and how do you get full type inference and fewer RPC calls?
prompts.answerHint: address + ABI + functionName + args; it is a decoded eth_call rather than a transaction. Declare an inline ABI `as const` so viem can infer argument and return types; use multicall for compatible reads in one RPC request. Pitfall: a widened ABI loses precise function and result inference.

prompts.promptText: Why simulate before writeContract, and what's the wagmi hook trio?
prompts.answerHint: simulateContract validates against the state it reads and prepares a request before writeContract signs/sends; waitForTransactionReceipt tracks confirmation. In React, compose useSimulateContract with useWriteContract, then useWaitForTransactionReceipt. Pitfall: simulation reduces avoidable failures but cannot guarantee execution after state changes.

prompts.promptText: How do you get live vs historical events in viem, and what must you handle?
prompts.answerHint: watchContractEvent watches new decoded logs, normally polling a filter and falling back to getLogs; a WebSocket client can use subscriptions. getContractEvents fetches a historical range. Pitfall: a log-backed optimistic UI must reconcile against confirmed state after reorgs rather than treating the first callback as final.

prompts.promptText: What does the wagmi CLI generate, and what class of bug does it eliminate?
prompts.answerHint: From your ABIs (Foundry/Hardhat artifacts or Etherscan) it generates fully-typed React hooks/actions, so a renamed function or wrong arg type is a compile error. Pitfall: forgetting to re-run `wagmi generate` after a contract change leaves stale types that compile but call a signature that no longer exists.

prompts.promptText: What interface does an injected wallet expose, and why does EIP-6963 exist?
prompts.answerHint: An EIP-1193 provider with request({method,params}) and events like accountsChanged/chainChanged; EIP-6963 adds multi-wallet discovery so several extensions don't clobber window.ethereum. Pitfall: caching the account/chain once and never subscribing to the change events leaves your UI acting on a stale account after the user switches.

prompts.promptText: What does WalletConnect add over an injected wallet, and what do RainbowKit/ConnectKit save you?
prompts.answerHint: WalletConnect links to mobile wallets over an encrypted relay session (QR/deep link), no extension needed; RainbowKit/ConnectKit are wagmi-based modals that handle injected + WalletConnect connectors, chain switching, and account UI out of the box. Pitfall: WalletConnect needs a valid projectId — omitting it silently breaks mobile connections.

prompts.promptText: How does SIWE authenticate a user, and why is the nonce essential?
prompts.answerHint: The user signs an EIP-4361 message; the server verifies the signature plus expected domain, URI, version, chain ID, address, nonce, issued-at, and any validity bounds before consuming the nonce and starting a session. EOAs use ERC-191 verification, while contract accounts need an ERC-1271 path on the specified chain. Pitfall: a valid signature and nonce alone do not make the message valid for this relying party.

prompts.topicTitle: Reading event logs on the frontend
prompts.promptText: How do indexed vs non-indexed event params affect querying, and why don't raw log queries scale?
prompts.answerHint: Indexed params become searchable topics you can filter on (e.g. Transfers to an address); non-indexed params sit in the data field. Pitfall: RPCs cap block ranges and reorgs remove logs, so scanning full history from the client is slow and fragile — that's the reason to move to an indexer (The Graph/Ponder).

prompts.promptText: What are the three parts of a subgraph, and what does it give the frontend?
prompts.answerHint: A manifest (contracts/events to watch), a GraphQL schema (entities), and AssemblyScript mappings (event → entity updates); The Graph indexes it and serves a GraphQL API of clean, aggregated data. Pitfall: mappings only see data emitted in events — anything the contract never logged can't be indexed retroactively, so design your events for the queries you'll need.

prompts.promptText: Build and deploy a subgraph indexing an ERC-20's Transfer events into per-account entities.
prompts.answerHint: Write the manifest + schema (Account, Transfer) + AssemblyScript mapping, then deploy to a local Graph node or Subgraph Studio and query balances via GraphQL.

prompts.promptText: How does Ponder differ from The Graph in language and operating model?
prompts.answerHint: Ponder uses TypeScript indexing functions, backfills and live-syncs into Postgres, and exposes HTTP query APIs including generated GraphQL and SQL; you deploy the service. The Graph uses subgraph manifests, schemas, AssemblyScript mappings, and its network. Pitfall: self-hosting means you own indexer availability and operations.

prompts.promptText: What are the two Scaffold-ETH 2 packages, and what does the toolchain auto-generate?
prompts.answerHint: A contracts package (Foundry/Hardhat) and a Next.js frontend pre-wired with wagmi/viem + RainbowKit; deployments generate a typed contract registry the UI reads, plus a burner wallet and an auto-rendered Debug Contracts page. Pitfall: the frontend's typed contract info comes from the deploy step — forgetting to redeploy leaves the UI pointing at an old address/ABI.

prompts.promptText: What do the Scaffold hooks add over raw wagmi hooks?
prompts.answerHint: They resolve ABI/address from deployed contract info, so contractName + functionName drive typed reads, writeContractAsync submissions, and event history/watch hooks without raw wiring. Receipt tracking remains a separate concern. Pitfall: contracts absent from deployed or configured external contract data cannot be resolved by name.

prompts.promptText: Complete the current first Speedrun Ethereum challenge (Crowdfunding).
prompts.answerHint: Implement CrowdFund.sol with contribute (payable), deadline + threshold, execute() to fund FundingRecipient or open refunds, and checks-effects-interactions withdraw; pass checkpoint tests and ship the contribution UI.

prompts.promptText: In the Crowdfunding challenge, why let contributors withdraw rather than pushing every refund?
prompts.answerHint: Each contributor claims their recorded balance after an unsuccessful deadline, avoiding an unbounded refund loop and one recipient blocking everyone. Zero the balance before the external call. Pitfall: guard the state machine so contributions, successful execution, and refunds cannot overlap incorrectly.

prompts.promptText: Complete SpeedRunEthereum Challenge 2 (Token Vendor).
prompts.answerHint: Build an ERC-20 + Vendor with buyTokens (payable, fixed price), sellTokens (approve then transferFrom), and owner withdraw; handle the two-step approve→sell UX in the frontend.

prompts.promptText: Why does selling tokens back to the Vendor need a separate approve step?
prompts.answerHint: sellTokens uses transferFrom, which spends the user's ERC-20 allowance, so the user must first approve the Vendor to move their tokens; buying (payable ETH) needs no approval. Pitfall: forgetting the approve makes sellTokens revert with an allowance error — the classic first-dApp UX bug.

prompts.promptText: Why is the Dice Game's on-chain randomness exploitable?
prompts.answerHint: DiceGame hashes blockhash(block.number - 1), its own address, and a public nonce, then takes modulo 16. RiggedRoll reads the same inputs before calling and plays only for rolls 0–5. Pitfall: deterministic public inputs are predictable; use a VRF or a correctly designed commit-reveal when unpredictability is required.

prompts.promptText: Complete SpeedRunEthereum Challenge 3 (Dice Game / RiggedRoll).
prompts.answerHint: Write RiggedRoll to recompute DiceGame's predictable roll and call rollTheDice only on a winning prediction (funding the contract to pay the fee); pass the challenge tests.

prompts.promptText: Complete SpeedRunEthereum Challenge 4 (Build a DEX).
prompts.answerHint: Implement init liquidity, price via x*y=k with a 0.3% fee, ethToToken/tokenToEth swaps, and deposit/withdraw of LP shares; build a swap UI showing reserves and expected output.

prompts.promptText: In the DEX challenge, how is the output of a swap priced?
prompts.answerHint: The challenge sets inputWithFee = input * 997, then output = (inputWithFee * outputReserve) / (inputReserve * 1000 + inputWithFee). Pitfall: a spot-price quote ignores slippage, and swap functions without a minimum output expose users to sandwiching.

prompts.topicTitle: Speedrun: later challenges (Multisig, SVG NFT, Oracle)
prompts.promptText: How do the three oracle designs in the current challenge trade trust for complexity?
prompts.answerHint: The whitelist oracle trusts approved reporters; the staking oracle decentralizes reporting with stake, rewards, inactivity penalties, and slashing; the optimistic oracle accepts bonded proposals unless disputed, then a decider settles the outcome. Pitfall: each design moves trust rather than eliminating it, so state the authority, incentives, latency, and dispute assumptions.

prompts.topicTitle: Speedrun: later challenges (Multisig, SVG NFT, Oracle)
prompts.promptText: Finish at least one currently published later Speedrun Ethereum challenge.
prompts.answerHint: Complete Oracles: implement the whitelist, staking, and optimistic designs; pass the checkpoint tests and wire the reporting, assertion, proposal, dispute, settlement, and reward-claim UI flows.

topics.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
topics.description: Root of the DSA learning path. Structure: NeetCode roadmap category order, each split into reviewable sub-patterns (the actual scheduling unit), each with curated problems from NeetCode 150 / Blind 75. Prereq edges follow real conceptual dependency, not just roadmap position. Study one sub-pattern at a time; drill into individual problems only when reviewing that sub-pattern.
topics.aiContext: path root, created 2026-07-01; cards authored 2026-07-02

topics.title: Arrays & Hashing
topics.description: Foundation category: hash-based lookup and array manipulation underlie most other patterns. No DSA prereqs — entry point.

topics.title: Hashing fundamentals
topics.description: Use a hash set/map to turn an O(n) membership or lookup check into O(1). Recognize: "have I seen this before", "does X exist", frequency counts.

topics.title: Two Sum / complement lookup
topics.description: For each element, check whether its complement (target - x) was already seen; store as you go instead of nested-looping. Recognize: "pair that sums/multiplies to X", single pass with a map.

topics.title: Grouping by key
topics.description: Bucket elements by a derived key (sorted string, character-count signature) into a hash map of lists. Recognize: "group these into categories", anagram/shape clustering.
