topics.title: Prefix sums
topics.description: Precompute running sums so any range sum is O(1) via subtraction; combine with a hash map of seen prefix sums for subarray-sum problems. Recognize: repeated range-sum queries, "subarray with sum equal to X".

topics.title: Sorting-based array tricks
topics.description: Sort first to unlock two-pointer scans, deduplication, or greedy choices that only work on ordered data. Recognize: problem becomes easy once sorted, needs original-vs-sorted comparison.

topics.title: Two Pointers
topics.description: Two indices scanning data (often after sorting) to avoid nested loops. Builds directly on array/hash foundations.

topics.title: Opposite-direction pointers
topics.description: One pointer at each end of a sorted structure, moving inward based on a comparison. Recognize: sorted array, "pair/triplet meeting a condition", area/capacity maximization.

topics.title: Fast & slow pointers (array)
topics.description: A slow write-pointer trails a fast read-pointer to compact/filter an array in place. Recognize: "remove duplicates in place", "move zeroes", in-place filtering with O(1) space.

topics.title: Three-way partitioning
topics.description: Dutch national flag: low/mid/high pointers partition into three buckets in one pass. Recognize: "sort with only 3 distinct values", partition-around-pivot.

topics.title: Sliding Window
topics.description: A contiguous window over a sequence, expanded/contracted to maintain an invariant. Directly generalizes two-pointer scanning to variable-length ranges.

topics.title: Fixed-size window
topics.description: Window of constant width k slides one step at a time; maintain a running aggregate instead of recomputing. Recognize: "subarray of size k", "average/max over every window of length k".

topics.title: Variable-size window
topics.description: Expand right pointer to grow the window, shrink left pointer while an invariant is violated (or once satisfied, for min-length problems). Recognize: "longest/shortest substring with property X".

topics.title: Monotonic-deque window
topics.description: A deque holding candidate indices in monotonic (increasing/decreasing) order gives O(1) amortized window max/min. Recognize: "max/min of every window of size k" needs better than O(n*k).

topics.title: Stack
topics.description: LIFO structure for matching, undo/backtrack-style state, and deferred-processing patterns. Independent axis from Two Pointers, also array-based.

topics.title: Monotonic stack
topics.description: Keep the stack sorted (increasing or decreasing) by popping elements that violate the order before pushing; popped element's answer is resolved by the pusher. Recognize: "next greater/smaller element", "days until warmer".

topics.title: Valid parentheses / matching pairs
topics.description: Push openers, pop-and-check on closers; stack empty at the end means fully matched. Recognize: nested bracket/tag validity, "remove adjacent duplicates".

topics.title: Expression evaluation
topics.description: Use a stack to hold operands/partial results while scanning an expression left to right, applying operator precedence explicitly. Recognize: calculator problems, Reverse Polish Notation.

topics.title: Min-stack design
topics.description: Track the running minimum alongside each push (auxiliary stack or encoded value) so getMin is O(1). Recognize: "design a stack that also supports X in O(1)".

topics.title: Binary Search
topics.description: Halving a search space by testing a monotonic predicate. Fundamentally an array-scanning technique, independent of stack/pointer categories.

topics.title: Classic binary search
topics.description: Standard lo/hi/mid search on a sorted array for an exact target, careful with off-by-one bounds. Recognize: sorted array, direct value lookup.

topics.title: Binary search on answer
topics.description: Search over the space of possible answers (not the input array) using a monotonic feasibility predicate ("can we do it with value X?"). Recognize: "minimize the maximum", "find the smallest X such that condition holds".

topics.title: Search in rotated arrays
topics.description: At each step determine which half is properly sorted, then decide which half to keep based on where the target falls. Recognize: sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot.

topics.title: Binary search on 2D matrix
topics.description: Treat a row/column-sorted matrix as a flattened sorted array (index math) or walk from a corner exploiting sortedness in two dimensions. Recognize: matrix where each row and/or column is sorted.

topics.title: Linked List
topics.description: Pointer-based sequential structure. Reuses the fast/slow pointer idea from Two Pointers in a context with no random access.

topics.title: Reversal
topics.description: Walk the list rewiring each node's next pointer to the previous node, tracking prev/curr/next explicitly (or via recursion). Recognize: "reverse the list" or a sublist of it.

topics.title: Fast & slow pointers (list)
topics.description: Two pointers advancing at different speeds through a list find cycles, midpoints, or the kth-from-end node without a second pass. Recognize: cycle detection, "find the middle", palindrome check without extra storage.

topics.title: Merge / merge-k-lists
topics.description: Repeatedly take the smaller head across lists (pairwise merge, or a heap for k lists) to build one sorted list. Recognize: "merge sorted lists", building block for merge sort on lists.

topics.title: Dummy-node manipulation
topics.description: A dummy head node before the real head removes edge cases when the operation might affect the head itself. Recognize: "remove/insert near the head", list partitioning.

topics.title: Trees
topics.description: Recursive/hierarchical structure. Iterative traversal reuses Stack; construction/pointer rewiring reuses Linked List concepts.

topics.title: DFS traversals
topics.description: Recurse (or use an explicit stack) into children before returning, in pre/in/post order. This is the base traversal every other tree pattern builds on. Recognize: "visit every node", ordered output of a BST via inorder.

topics.title: BFS / level-order traversal
topics.description: A queue processes nodes level by level, tracking level boundaries by queue-size snapshots. Recognize: "per-level" output, shortest path in an unweighted tree/grid-as-tree.

topics.title: BST validation
topics.description: Carry a valid (low, high) range down the recursion, tightening it at each step, instead of only comparing to immediate children. Recognize: "is this a valid BST", BST-specific search/insert/delete.

topics.title: Lowest common ancestor
topics.description: Recurse into both subtrees; a node is the LCA when the target lives in different subtrees (or is the node itself). BST version uses value comparisons instead of full search. Recognize: "lowest common ancestor of two nodes".

topics.title: Tree construction from traversals
topics.description: Use one traversal to find the root/split point and another to recurse into left/right subtrees, typically with a hash map for O(1) index lookup. Recognize: "build tree from preorder+inorder", "build from sorted array".

topics.title: Path-sum patterns
topics.description: Carry a running value (sum, max, or path list) down the recursion and combine child results on the way back up. Recognize: root-to-leaf accumulation, "diameter/longest path", "max path sum through any node".

topics.title: Serialization/deserialization
topics.description: Encode a tree to a string via a traversal that marks null children explicitly, then rebuild by consuming that string in the same traversal order. Recognize: "design serialize/deserialize", tree-to-string round-trip.

topics.title: Tries
topics.description: A tree specialized for prefix operations on strings; every trie problem is really a Trees:DFS traversal over children keyed by character.

topics.title: Trie construction & search
topics.description: Each node holds a map/array of child edges keyed by character plus an end-of-word flag; insert/search walk one character at a time. Recognize: repeated prefix queries, dictionary-style lookup.

topics.title: Word Search II / prefix matching
topics.description: Build a trie of the target words, then DFS the grid while walking the trie in lockstep, pruning branches with no matching prefix. Recognize: "find all words from a dictionary in a grid".

topics.title: Autocomplete applications
topics.description: Traverse to a prefix's node, then DFS the subtree to collect all completions (often ranked/limited). Recognize: "suggest completions for a prefix".

topics.title: Heap / Priority Queue
topics.description: A binary tree kept partially ordered for O(log n) insert/extract-min-or-max. Depends on Trees for the underlying structure and Arrays & Hashing for the array-backed implementation.

topics.title: Kth largest/smallest
topics.description: Maintain a heap of size k (min-heap for kth-largest, max-heap for kth-smallest) so the root is always the answer, or use quickselect for O(n) average. Recognize: "kth largest/smallest", "top k" without needing full sort.

topics.title: Top-K frequent elements
topics.description: Count frequencies with a hash map, then use a size-k heap (or bucket sort by frequency) to pull out the k most/least common. Recognize: "k most frequent", frequency-ranked output.

topics.title: Merge-k via heap
topics.description: Push the current head of each of k sorted sources into a heap; repeatedly pop the min and push its successor. Recognize: "merge k sorted X", generalizes Linked List's pairwise merge to k-way.

topics.title: Two-heap median-finding
topics.description: A max-heap of the smaller half and a min-heap of the larger half, kept balanced in size, expose the median as the top of one/both heaps. Recognize: "running median", streaming order-statistics.

topics.title: Task scheduling with heap
topics.description: A max-heap of remaining counts (plus a cooldown queue) greedily always schedules the currently-most-needed task next. Recognize: "schedule tasks with a cooldown/gap constraint".

topics.title: Graphs
topics.description: General node/edge structures beyond trees (cycles, multiple parents allowed). DFS/BFS generalize Trees' traversals; Stack underlies iterative DFS.

topics.title: Graph representation
topics.description: Build an adjacency list (hash map of node -> neighbors) or matrix from edge-list/grid input before running any traversal. Recognize: the setup step every graph problem starts with.

topics.title: DFS (connected components)
topics.description: Recurse into unvisited neighbors, marking visited as you go, to enumerate everything reachable from a start node. Recognize: "count islands/regions", "is X reachable from Y".

topics.title: BFS (shortest path unweighted)
topics.description: A queue expands the frontier one edge-hop at a time, guaranteeing the first time a node is reached is via a shortest path (unweighted). Multi-source BFS seeds the queue with several starts at once. Recognize: "minimum steps/hops", "nearest X from any of these sources".

topics.title: Union-Find
topics.description: Disjoint-set structure with path compression and union-by-rank tracks which nodes are already connected in near-O(1) amortized time, without a full traversal per query. Recognize: "are these connected", incremental edge-by-edge connectivity, cycle detection in undirected graphs.

topics.title: Topological sort
topics.description: Order nodes so every edge points forward: Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degree-zero nodes) or DFS with a post-order stack. Recognize: "valid ordering given dependencies", scheduling with prerequisites.

topics.title: Cycle detection
topics.description: Directed graphs: track a recursion-stack/coloring during DFS (white/gray/black) since a back-edge to a gray node is a cycle. Undirected graphs: Union-Find or DFS with parent-tracking (an edge to a visited non-parent node is a cycle). Recognize: "detect if a cycle exists", validating a DAG.

topics.title: Backtracking
topics.description: Systematic recursive exploration with undo, i.e. DFS over an implicit decision tree. Depends on Trees (recursion shape) and Arrays & Hashing (state tracking).

topics.title: Subsets / combinations generation
topics.description: At each recursion level, decide include-or-skip (subsets) or iterate a start index forward (combinations), pushing/popping the current choice. Recognize: "all subsets/combinations of size k".

topics.title: Permutations generation
topics.description: Track which elements are already used (a boolean array or by swapping in place) and recurse until the current permutation is full length. Recognize: "all orderings/arrangements".

topics.title: Constraint satisfaction
topics.description: Place one piece/value at a time, check constraints incrementally (row/col/diagonal or Sudoku box), backtrack immediately on violation rather than validating a full board. Recognize: N-Queens-style placement puzzles.

topics.title: Grid backtracking
topics.description: DFS through grid neighbors, marking visited cells before recursing and unmarking on backtrack, matching a target string/path along the way. Reuses Graphs' grid-DFS shape with the extra step of undoing visited marks.

topics.title: Palindrome partitioning
topics.description: At each start index, try every palindromic prefix as one partition and recurse on the remainder; optionally memoize is-palindrome checks. Recognize: "partition string so every piece satisfies property X".

topics.title: Advanced Graphs
topics.description: Weighted-graph algorithms built on top of core Graphs traversals and Union-Find.

topics.title: Dijkstra's shortest path
topics.description: A min-heap keyed by current best distance greedily expands the closest unvisited node next, relaxing its neighbors' distances. Recognize: "shortest path with non-negative weights".

topics.title: Bellman-Ford
topics.description: Relax every edge V-1 times; if a relaxation still succeeds on pass V, a negative-weight cycle exists. Recognize: shortest path where edge weights can be negative.

topics.title: Floyd-Warshall
topics.description: Dynamic programming over an intermediate-node index k: try routing every pair (i,j) through k and keep the shorter path. Recognize: need all-pairs shortest paths, small dense graph.

topics.title: Minimum spanning tree
topics.description: Kruskal's: sort edges by weight, add each if it doesn't create a cycle (Union-Find check). Prim's: grow one tree, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it (min-heap). Recognize: "connect all nodes with minimum total edge weight".

topics.title: 1-D Dynamic Programming
topics.description: Optimal-substructure problems reducible to a single index/state axis. Builds on Backtracking's recursive decision-tree thinking, but tabulated bottom-up instead of explored top-down.

topics.title: Climbing stairs / Fibonacci recurrence
topics.description: dp[i] depends on a small fixed window of previous states (dp[i-1], dp[i-2], ...); tabulate bottom-up with O(1) rolling variables instead of a full array. Recognize: "number of ways to reach step i", simple linear recurrence.

topics.title: House robber (include/exclude)
topics.description: At each index, dp[i] = max(skip this item: dp[i-1], take it: value[i] + dp[i-2]). Tabulate the two running values forward. Recognize: "can't pick adjacent elements", binary include/exclude decision per index.

topics.title: Longest increasing subsequence
topics.description: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over all j<i with nums[j] < nums[i] (O(n^2) tabulation), or maintain a patience-sorting tails array for O(n log n). Recognize: "longest subsequence satisfying an ordering condition".

topics.title: Coin change / unbounded knapsack
topics.description: dp[amount] built up from smaller amounts, iterating each coin as reusable (unbounded) rather than one-shot. Tabulate amounts 0..target forward. Recognize: unlimited supply of each item, "fewest/most ways to make amount X".

topics.title: Decode ways / string DP
topics.description: dp[i] = ways to decode/process the prefix of length i, combining dp[i-1] (single-char step) and dp[i-2] (two-char step) under validity checks. Tabulate left to right over the string. Recognize: "number of ways to parse/decode a string".

topics.title: Word break
topics.description: dp[i] = true if some j<i has dp[j] true and s[j:i] is a dictionary word; tabulate forward over string prefixes. Recognize: "can this string be segmented using dictionary words".

topics.title: 2-D Dynamic Programming
topics.description: DP over two interacting index axes (two strings, or a grid). Direct extension of 1-D DP's tabulation to a 2-D table.

topics.title: Grid path counting
topics.description: dp[r][c] built from dp[r-1][c] and dp[r][c-1] (or their min/sum), tabulated row by row. Recognize: "number of paths / min-cost path through a grid, moving only right/down".

topics.title: Longest common subsequence
topics.description: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]+1 if chars match, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]); tabulate both strings' prefixes together — the 2-D generalization of Longest Increasing Subsequence's single-sequence recurrence. Recognize: comparing two sequences for shared structure.

topics.title: Edit distance
topics.description: dp[i][j] = min cost to convert prefix i of one string to prefix j of the other, taking the best of insert/delete/replace at each step. Recognize: "minimum operations to transform string A into string B".

topics.title: 0/1 knapsack
topics.description: dp[i][w] = best value using the first i items within capacity w, deciding include-or-exclude item i (each item usable once, contrast with unbounded coin change). Recognize: fixed set of items each usable at most once, capacity constraint.

topics.title: Interval DP
topics.description: dp[i][j] over a subarray/substring range [i,j], built from smaller sub-intervals by trying every split/last-operation point k inside the range. Tabulate by increasing interval length. Recognize: "best way to combine/remove a contiguous range", matrix-chain-style problems.

topics.title: Palindromic subsequence DP
topics.description: dp[i][j] = longest palindromic subsequence/substring within s[i..j], expanding inward from single characters and pairs. Recognize: palindrome-related length/count questions over substrings.

topics.title: Greedy
topics.description: Make the locally-optimal choice at each step and prove (or trust) it leads to a globally optimal result. Independent axis from DP — no overlapping-subproblem memoization needed.

topics.title: Interval scheduling
topics.description: Sort by end time, greedily keep an interval if it starts after the last kept interval ends. Recognize: "maximum number of non-overlapping intervals you can select".

topics.title: Jump game
topics.description: Track the farthest index reachable so far while scanning left to right; feasibility/min-jumps falls out of comparing current index to that frontier. Recognize: "can you reach the end", "minimum jumps to reach the end".

topics.title: Gas station
topics.description: If total gas >= total cost a solution exists; the starting point is right after the point where cumulative tank first goes negative. One greedy pass, no brute force needed. Recognize: circular-array feasibility with a running-total tell.

topics.title: Greedy + sorting
topics.description: Sort by the attribute that makes the greedy choice obvious (deadline, ratio, size), then make one linear pass assigning/selecting. Recognize: matching/assignment problems solvable by sorting one or two lists.

topics.title: Intervals
topics.description: Range-overlap problems; mostly solved by the Greedy category's sort-then-scan approach.

topics.title: Merge intervals
topics.description: Sort by start time, then scan and merge the current interval into the previous one whenever they overlap. Recognize: "merge all overlapping intervals".

topics.title: Insert interval
topics.description: Walk the already-sorted, already-merged list in three phases: copy intervals fully before the new one, merge all overlapping ones into it, copy the rest. Recognize: inserting into a pre-merged interval list.

topics.title: Non-overlapping intervals
topics.description: Sort by end time, greedily keep the earliest-ending non-conflicting interval and count/remove the rest — the same recurrence as Greedy's interval scheduling, phrased as a removal-count problem.

topics.title: Meeting rooms
topics.description: Split into separate sorted start-time and end-time arrays (or a min-heap of end times) and sweep to count how many intervals are simultaneously open. Recognize: "minimum rooms/resources needed to cover all intervals".

topics.title: Math & Geometry
topics.description: Numeric/geometric problems that lean on arithmetic properties rather than a traversal or DP structure.

topics.title: Modular arithmetic & number theory
topics.description: Apply modulo reduction to avoid overflow, and number-theoretic identities (mod distributes over +,-,* but not /) to combine large-number results correctly. Recognize: "answer modulo 1e9+7", divisibility reasoning.

topics.title: Matrix rotation
topics.description: Rotate in place via transpose + reverse-rows (90 deg), or walk concentric layers swapping four cells at a time. Recognize: "rotate the matrix in place", spiral traversal.

topics.title: Prime sieve / GCD-LCM
topics.description: Sieve of Eratosthenes precomputes all primes up to N in O(N log log N); GCD via Euclid's algorithm underlies LCM and fraction-reduction problems. Recognize: repeated primality checks, reducing fractions/ratios.

topics.title: Geometry basics
topics.description: Cross-product sign tells turn direction/orientation of three points; use it for collinearity, convex hull steps, and line-segment relationships instead of trigonometry. Recognize: points/lines/polygons in the problem statement.

topics.title: Bit Manipulation
topics.description: Operate directly on binary representations for O(1)-per-op tricks; conceptually standalone from array/graph/DP structures.

topics.title: Basic bit ops
topics.description: AND to check/clear a bit, OR to set a bit, XOR to toggle, shifts to multiply/divide by powers of two. Recognize: any problem phrased directly in terms of binary representation.

topics.title: Counting bits
topics.description: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) reuses the previously-computed bit count for i/2, avoiding recomputation per number (a 1-D-DP-flavored bit trick). Recognize: "number of set bits for every number up to N".

topics.title: XOR tricks
topics.description: XOR cancels identical values to zero and is order-independent, so XOR-ing an entire array isolates whatever appears an odd number of times. Recognize: "find the single/missing number", pairing-cancellation problems.

topics.title: Bitmask DP
topics.description: Represent a subset of up to ~20 items as an integer bitmask, so dp[mask] tabulates over all 2^n subsets — a bit-encoded generalization of Backtracking's subset enumeration into a memoizable state. Recognize: small n (<=20), state naturally described as "which items have been used/visited".

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a hash set/map as the core of a solution? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "have I seen this before", "does X exist", frequency counting, any O(n^2) membership scan you can make O(n). Pitfall: hashing mutable/unnormalized keys (forgetting to sort or canonicalize the thing you look up). Related: Top K Frequent Elements builds a frequency map first.

prompts.promptText: Write a frequency counter in your language of choice: given an array, build a map value -> count in one pass, then use it to find any value appearing exactly twice.
prompts.answerHint: One loop, map.get(x) defaulting to 0 then +1; second loop (or the same one) checks counts. Invariant: after i iterations the map holds exact counts for the first i elements.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Contains Duplicate (Easy) — return true if any value appears at least twice in the array.
prompts.answerHint: Set of seen values; return true the moment insertion finds the value already present.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Valid Anagram (Easy) — given two strings, return true if one is an anagram of the other.
prompts.answerHint: Character-frequency map of s, decrement over t; all zeros means anagram (or compare two count maps).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Longest Consecutive Sequence (Medium) — length of the longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array, in O(n).
prompts.answerHint: Hash-set all values; only start counting from numbers whose predecessor (x-1) is absent — each element is visited at most twice.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the complement-lookup pattern? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "pair summing/multiplying to X", single unsorted pass where sorting would cost the indices. Pitfall: inserting the current element BEFORE checking its complement (breaks on target = 2x). Related: Two Sum II (sorted input) belongs to opposite-direction pointers; Subarray Sum Equals K is the same idea on prefix sums.

prompts.promptText: Write the single-pass complement lookup in your language of choice: given an array and target, return the indices of a pair summing to target.
prompts.answerHint: Map value -> index built as you scan; check map for (target - x) before inserting x. Invariant: map only ever holds elements strictly left of the cursor.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Two Sum (Easy) — indices of the two numbers adding to target, one valid answer guaranteed.
prompts.answerHint: Check seen-map for complement, then store current value -> index.

prompts.promptText: Solve: 4Sum II (Medium) — count tuples (i,j,k,l) across four arrays with A[i]+B[j]+C[k]+D[l] == 0.
prompts.answerHint: Split into halves: map of all A+B sums with counts, then look up -(C+D) — complement lookup on pair-sums, O(n^2).

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for grouping-by-derived-key? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "group/cluster these", items equivalent under a canonical form (sorted string, count signature, normalized shape). Pitfall: a non-canonical key (grouping anagrams by first letter) or an ambiguous string join (use a delimiter that can't appear in the data). Related: Group Shifted Strings uses a shift-invariant signature.

prompts.promptText: Write the bucket-by-key loop in your language of choice: given a list of strings, group them into lists of mutual anagrams.
prompts.answerHint: key = sorted(word) (or 26-count signature stringified); map key -> list, push each word, return the map's values.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Group Anagrams (Medium) — group a list of strings into anagram clusters.
prompts.answerHint: Sorted string (or char-count tuple) as the bucket key; one pass.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Encode and Decode Strings (Medium) — design encode(list of strings) -> string and decode(string) -> list that round-trip any input.
prompts.answerHint: Length-prefix each string (e.g. "4#word") — delimiters alone can't work because any character may appear in the data.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for prefix sums? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: repeated range-sum queries, "subarray with sum X", running totals compared across positions. Pitfall: forgetting the empty prefix (seed the map with {0: 1}) — it's what lets a subarray starting at index 0 count.

prompts.promptText: Write the prefix-sum setup in your language of choice: build the prefix array for nums, then answer sum(i..j) queries in O(1).
prompts.answerHint: prefix has length n+1 with prefix[0]=0, prefix[k]=prefix[k-1]+nums[k-1]; sum(i..j) = prefix[j+1]-prefix[i].

prompts.promptText: Solve: Range Sum Query - Immutable (Easy) — preprocess an array to answer sumRange(i, j) calls in O(1).
prompts.answerHint: Length n+1 prefix array; subtraction answers each query.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Subarray Sum Equals K (Medium) — count subarrays summing to exactly k.
prompts.answerHint: Running sum + map of seen prefix-sum counts; at each step add count of (running - k). Seed {0: 1}.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Product of Array Except Self (Medium) — output[i] = product of all elements except nums[i], no division, O(n).
prompts.answerHint: Prefix products left-to-right, then a right-to-left running suffix product multiplied in — prefix idea with * instead of +.

prompts.promptText: When is "sort it first" the unlocking move? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: pairing/adjacency becomes meaningful once ordered, dedup, greedy picks by size/deadline, original-vs-sorted comparison. Pitfall: sorting away information you still need (original indices — copy or argsort first). Related: Sort Colors (three-way partitioning), Kth Largest (heap/quickselect), Meeting Rooms and Merge Intervals (intervals category).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Merge Sorted Array (Easy) — merge nums2 into nums1 in place, where nums1 has trailing space for the result.
prompts.answerHint: Fill from the BACK (largest first) with two read pointers — writing from the front overwrites unread values.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Largest Number (Medium) — arrange non-negative integers to form the largest possible number (as a string).
prompts.answerHint: Sort with the custom comparator: a before b iff concat(a,b) > concat(b,a). Watch the all-zeros case ("00" -> "0").

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for converging (opposite-direction) two pointers? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: sorted (or sortable) array, "pair/triplet meeting a condition", maximize area/capacity between two ends. Move the pointer that can only improve the objective. Pitfall: sorting when the problem wants original indices, or failing to skip duplicate values on the inner scan (double-counts triplets). Related: Valid Palindrome converges from both ends on characters.

prompts.promptText: Write the converging two-pointer loop in your language of choice: given a sorted array and a target, return whether some pair sums to the target.
prompts.answerHint: lo=0, hi=n-1; while lo<hi compare sum to target: too small -> lo++, too big -> hi--, equal -> found. Invariant: every pair with one index outside [lo,hi] has already been ruled out.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted (Medium) — return the 1-based indices of the two numbers that add up to target.
prompts.answerHint: Converge from both ends: move lo up when the sum is too small, hi down when too big — no hash map needed since it is sorted.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Container With Most Water (Medium) — pick two lines forming the container that holds the most water.
prompts.answerHint: Width shrinks as you move inward, so always advance the shorter wall — moving the taller one can never increase area.

prompts.promptText: Solve: 3Sum (Medium) — return all unique triplets that sum to zero.
prompts.answerHint: Sort, then for each i run a converging two-pointer scan on the rest; skip equal values at every level to avoid duplicate triplets.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Trapping Rain Water (Hard) — compute how much water is trapped between the bars after raining.
prompts.answerHint: Two pointers tracking leftMax and rightMax; water above a bar is bounded by the smaller side, so advance from whichever side has the lower running max.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the slow-write / fast-read two-pointer compaction? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "remove/filter in place", "move X to the end", O(1) extra space over an array you may reorder. Slow marks the next write slot; fast scans. Pitfall: incrementing slow when you skip an element (only advance it after a write), or clobbering unread data. Related: Remove Element uses the same write-pointer idea.

prompts.promptText: Write the in-place compaction loop in your language of choice: given an array and a keep-predicate, move all kept elements to the front and return the new length.
prompts.answerHint: slow=0; for fast over the array, if keep(arr[fast]) then arr[slow]=arr[fast]; slow++. Invariant: arr[0..slow) is exactly the kept elements seen so far, in order.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (Easy) — remove duplicates in place so each value appears once, return the new length.
prompts.answerHint: Slow write-pointer; write arr[fast] only when it differs from the last kept value (arr[slow-1]).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Move Zeroes (Easy) — move all zeroes to the end in place while keeping the order of non-zero elements.
prompts.answerHint: Write pointer collects non-zeros to the front; fill the remainder with zeroes (or swap as you go).

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for Dutch-national-flag three-way partitioning? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "sort with only 3 distinct values/categories", partition around a pivot into <, ==, > in one pass with O(1) space. Pitfall: advancing mid after swapping with high — the value pulled from high is unexamined, so re-check it before moving on. Related: Kth Largest Element in an Array uses the same partition step in quickselect (carded under Heap / Priority Queue).

prompts.promptText: Write the Dutch-national-flag partition in your language of choice: given an array of values 0/1/2, sort it in a single pass with O(1) extra space.
prompts.answerHint: low, mid=0, high=n-1; while mid<=high: 0 -> swap(low,mid), low++, mid++; 1 -> mid++; 2 -> swap(mid,high), high-- (do NOT advance mid). Invariant: [0,low) are 0s, [low,mid) are 1s, (high,n) are 2s.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Sort Colors (Medium) — sort an array of 0s, 1s, and 2s in place in one pass.
prompts.answerHint: Three pointers (low/mid/high): swap 0s to the front, 2s to the back, leave 1s in the middle; don't advance mid after a swap with high.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a fixed-size sliding window? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "subarray/substring of size k", "average/max/sum over every window of length k" — the width never changes, only the position. Pitfall: recomputing the aggregate over the whole window each step (O(n*k)) instead of adding the entering element and subtracting the one that leaves; watch the off-by-one on which index leaves (right-k). Related: the max-over-window variant can't be add/subtracted — see Sliding Window Maximum (monotonic deque).

prompts.promptText: Write the fixed-size window scan in your language of choice: given an array and width k, produce an aggregate (e.g. the sum) over every length-k window without recomputing from scratch.
prompts.answerHint: Seed the running aggregate over the first k elements. Then for each new right index, add nums[right] and subtract nums[right-k], recording the result. Invariant: after processing index right, the running value equals the aggregate of the window [right-k+1 .. right].

prompts.promptText: Solve: Maximum Average Subarray I (Easy) — the maximum average value of any contiguous subarray of length k.
prompts.answerHint: Keep a running window sum, slide one step by adding the new element and dropping the one that left, track the max sum; divide by k once at the end.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Permutation in String (Medium) — does s2 contain a contiguous substring that is a permutation of s1?
prompts.answerHint: Slide a window of width |s1| over s2 comparing character-count vectors; keep a running count of matched buckets so each slide is O(1) instead of re-comparing all 26.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a variable-size sliding window? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "longest/shortest substring or subarray with property X", where the property is monotone — extending the window can only break it, shrinking can only restore it. Pitfall: shrinking with an `if` instead of a `while` (one removal may not restore the invariant), or recording the answer at the wrong moment — for longest, update after the window is valid; for shortest, update while it is valid, then keep shrinking. Related: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K breaks the simple version (negative numbers) and needs a monotonic deque instead.

prompts.promptText: Write the variable-size window loop in your language of choice: expand a right pointer across the sequence and shrink from the left whenever an invariant is violated, tracking the best window.
prompts.answerHint: For each right, fold nums[right] into the window state; then while the invariant is violated, remove nums[left] and advance left. After the while-loop the window [left..right] is valid — update the answer here (e.g. max length right-left+1). Invariant: left is the smallest index that keeps [left..right] valid.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (Medium) — the length of the longest substring whose characters are all distinct.
prompts.answerHint: Track each character's last-seen index (or a set); when a repeat enters, move left just past its previous occurrence rather than one step at a time, updating the max length each step.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Longest Repeating Character Replacement (Medium) — the longest substring you can make uniform by replacing at most k characters.
prompts.answerHint: The window is valid when (window length − count of its most-frequent character) ≤ k; shrink when that surplus exceeds k. Tracking only a running max-count that never decreases still gives the right answer, because the best length can only grow.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Fruit Into Baskets (Medium) — the longest contiguous subarray containing at most two distinct values.
prompts.answerHint: It is exactly "longest window with ≤ 2 distinct keys": keep a count map and shrink from the left while the map holds more than two keys, tracking the max length.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Minimum Window Substring (Hard) — the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t, counting multiplicity.
prompts.answerHint: Expand right until the window covers all required counts (track a have/need satisfied counter), then shrink from the left while it stays covering, recording the smallest such window seen.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a monotonic-deque window? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "max/min of every window of size k" where a plain fixed-window scan is O(n*k) and you need O(n) — the running extreme can't be add/subtracted because removing the current max leaves no cheap successor. Pitfall: storing values instead of indices (you can't tell when the front has slid out of the window), or forgetting to evict the front once its index falls below right-k+1. Related: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K applies the same monotonic deque to prefix sums.

prompts.promptText: Write the monotonic-deque window in your language of choice: report the maximum of every length-k window in O(n), using a deque of candidate indices.
prompts.answerHint: For each right: pop from the back while the back's value ≤ nums[right] (those can never be the max again), then push right; pop from the front if its index ≤ right-k (slid out of the window); once right ≥ k-1, the front index holds the current window's max. Invariant: deque indices increase left-to-right while their values strictly decrease.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Sliding Window Maximum (Hard) — the maximum of each contiguous window of size k, in O(n).
prompts.answerHint: Maintain a deque of indices with strictly decreasing values so the front is always the current max; evict indices that slid out of the window and any that a newer, larger value dominates.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a monotonic stack? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "next/previous greater or smaller element", "days until a warmer day", spans, or a histogram/skyline where each element's answer depends on the nearest bigger/smaller neighbor. Pitfall: choosing the wrong monotonic direction, or storing values when you need indices (distances/widths require indices) — and forgetting to drain the leftover stack at the end. Related: Online Stock Span is the same pop-while-smaller span count.

prompts.promptText: Write the next-greater-element scan in your language of choice: for each array position, find the next element to its right that is strictly greater (or a sentinel if none).
prompts.answerHint: Stack holds indices of positions still waiting for their answer. For each i, while the stack's top element is smaller than nums[i], pop it and record i (or nums[i]) as its next-greater. Then push i. Invariant: the stack's values stay decreasing top-to-bottom; anything left at the end has no greater element.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Next Greater Element I (Easy) — for each value in nums1, find its next greater element in nums2 (elements of nums1 are a subset of nums2).
prompts.answerHint: Monotonic stack over nums2 builds a value -> next-greater map in one pass; then look up each nums1 value.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Daily Temperatures (Medium) — for each day, how many days until a warmer temperature (0 if none).
prompts.answerHint: Decreasing stack of indices; when today is warmer than the top, pop and the answer is i minus the popped index.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Largest Rectangle in Histogram (Hard) — largest rectangle area fitting under a bar-height histogram.
prompts.answerHint: Increasing stack of indices; when a shorter bar arrives, pop and compute area = popped height times the width between the new left boundary and i. Use a trailing zero-height sentinel to flush the stack.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a push-openers / pop-on-closers stack? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: nested bracket/tag validity, balanced-symbol checks, "remove adjacent duplicates", or any structure where the most recently opened thing must close first (LIFO nesting). Pitfall: forgetting the two failure modes — a closer with an empty stack (or wrong opener on top) AND a non-empty stack at the end (unclosed openers). Related: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String pops when the top equals the incoming char.

prompts.promptText: Write the bracket matcher in your language of choice: scan a string of brackets and decide whether every closer matches the most recent unmatched opener.
prompts.answerHint: Push each opener; on a closer, fail if the stack is empty or its top isn't the matching opener, else pop. Map each closer to its opener. Invariant: the stack always holds the still-open brackets in nesting order; valid means it ends empty.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Valid Parentheses (Easy) — return true if brackets '()[]{}' are correctly opened and closed in order.
prompts.answerHint: Push openers, pop and match on closers; valid iff every close matches and the stack ends empty.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid (Medium) — fewest parentheses to insert so the string becomes valid.
prompts.answerHint: Track open count; a ')' with no open to cancel adds one required insertion. Answer is leftover opens plus those unmatched closers (no actual stack needed, just a counter).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Decode String (Medium) — expand encoded strings like "3[a2[c]]" into "accaccacc".
prompts.answerHint: Stack of partial results: on '[' push the current string and repeat count and reset; on ']' pop and repeat the built segment. The stack holds one frame per open bracket.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a stack to evaluate an expression? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: calculator problems, Reverse Polish / postfix notation, expressions with operator precedence, or parentheses that defer evaluation. Pitfall: mishandling operator precedence and associativity — evaluate '*' and '/' immediately but defer '+' and '-', and watch operand order for non-commutative '-' and '/' (a op b, not b op a). Related: Basic Calculator (Hard) adds parentheses handling on the same stack idea.

prompts.promptText: Write the RPN evaluator in your language of choice: evaluate a postfix expression given as a list of number and operator tokens.
prompts.answerHint: Scan tokens; push numbers, and on an operator pop the top two operands (the second-popped is the left operand), apply, push the result. Invariant: after processing a valid expression the stack holds exactly one value — the answer.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation (Medium) — evaluate an arithmetic expression in postfix form.
prompts.answerHint: Operand stack; pop two on each operator (mind order for '-' and '/'), push the result.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Basic Calculator II (Medium) — evaluate an infix string with + - * / and non-negative integers (no parentheses).
prompts.answerHint: Keep a stack of pending additive terms; apply '*' and '/' immediately against the last pushed number, defer '+'/'-' by pushing (signed) values, then sum the stack.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the min-stack (running-extremum-per-entry) design? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "design a stack that also returns the min/max in O(1)", any LIFO structure needing an auxiliary aggregate that must survive pops. Pitfall: storing only a single global min — it can't be restored after the min is popped; pair each entry with the min-so-far (aux stack or encoded pair) so pops roll it back. Related: Max Stack generalizes this with lazy deletion for arbitrary removal.

prompts.promptText: Write a min-stack in your language of choice: push, pop, top, and getMin all in O(1).
prompts.answerHint: Alongside the value stack keep a second stack whose top is always the current minimum: on push, push min(value, current-min); on pop, pop both. Invariant: the min-stack's top mirrors the minimum of exactly the elements currently present.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Min Stack (Medium) — design a stack supporting push, pop, top, and getMin in O(1).
prompts.answerHint: Pair each pushed value with the min-so-far (aux stack or a tuple) so getMin reads the top and pops restore the previous min.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a classic binary search? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: a sorted (or monotonic) array, an exact-value lookup or first/last-position query, O(log n) expected. Pitfall: the off-by-one triad — pick one convention (inclusive [lo, hi] with while lo <= hi, or half-open [lo, hi) with while lo < hi) and keep mid update and shrink step consistent, or you loop forever / skip the answer. Compute mid as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to avoid overflow. Related: Search Insert Position is the lower-bound variant (return lo when not found).

prompts.promptText: Write the classic lo/hi/mid exact-target search in your language of choice: given a sorted array and a target, return its index or -1.
prompts.answerHint: lo = 0, hi = n - 1; while lo <= hi: mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if a[mid] == target return mid; if a[mid] < target lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid - 1. Invariant: the target, if present, always lies within [lo, hi]; each step strictly shrinks that window so termination is guaranteed.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Binary Search (Easy) — return the index of target in a sorted array, or -1 if absent, in O(log n).
prompts.answerHint: Textbook lo/hi/mid loop; the only trap is inconsistent bounds and mid rounding.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array (Medium) — return the start and end indices of target in a sorted array with duplicates, or [-1, -1].
prompts.answerHint: Run two biased binary searches: one that keeps going left on a match to find the first index, one that keeps going right for the last.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for binary-search-on-the-answer? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "minimize the maximum" / "maximize the minimum", "smallest X such that a condition holds", an answer range you can bound even though the input isn't sorted, and a feasible(X) check that's monotonic (once true, true for all larger/smaller X). Pitfall: wrong search bounds (lo/hi must span from a trivially-feasible to a trivially-infeasible value) or a non-monotonic predicate — verify feasibility only flips once before trusting the halving.

prompts.promptText: Write the binary-search-on-answer skeleton in your language of choice: given an answer range [lo, hi] and a monotonic feasible(x) predicate, return the smallest x that is feasible.
prompts.answerHint: while lo < hi: mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if feasible(mid) hi = mid else lo = mid + 1; return lo. Invariant: feasible(hi) stays true and feasible(lo - 1) stays false, so the loop converges on the boundary. feasible() is problem-specific (e.g. simulate the process at candidate value mid and check it fits the constraint).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Koko Eating Bananas (Medium) — find the smallest eating speed k so all piles are finished within h hours.
prompts.answerHint: Binary-search k over [1, max pile]; feasible(k) = sum of ceil(pile / k) <= h, which is monotonic in k.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (Medium) — find the least ship capacity that ships all packages (in order) within D days.
prompts.answerHint: Search capacity over [max weight, sum of weights]; feasible(cap) = greedily packing days-in-order needs <= D days.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Split Array Largest Sum (Hard) — split the array into k contiguous subarrays minimizing the largest subarray sum.
prompts.answerHint: Binary-search the answer (largest sum) over [max element, total sum]; feasible(limit) = greedy left-to-right split needs <= k parts.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the rotated-array binary search? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: an originally-sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot, still needing O(log n) lookup or the minimum/pivot. Pitfall: at each mid, exactly one half [lo..mid] or [mid..hi] is properly sorted — identify it by comparing a[mid] to an endpoint, then only recurse into the half that could contain the target. Related: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II (with duplicates) breaks the clean a[lo] < a[mid] test and degrades to O(n) in the worst case.

prompts.promptText: Write the decide-which-half-is-sorted step in your language of choice: given a rotated sorted array and a target, return its index or -1.
prompts.answerHint: Standard lo/hi loop; at mid, if a[lo] <= a[mid] the left half is sorted — if target is in [a[lo], a[mid]) go left else go right; otherwise the right half is sorted — mirror the check. Invariant: at least one side is always sorted, and you keep the side whose sorted range brackets the target.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Search in Rotated Sorted Array (Medium) — find target's index in a rotated sorted array of distinct values, or -1, in O(log n).
prompts.answerHint: Each step, figure out which half is sorted and whether target lies inside its range; discard the other half.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (Medium) — find the minimum element of a rotated sorted array of distinct values in O(log n).
prompts.answerHint: Compare a[mid] to a[hi]: if a[mid] > a[hi] the pivot is to the right (lo = mid + 1), else it's at or left of mid (hi = mid).

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for binary search on a 2D matrix? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: a matrix that is fully sorted (each row sorted and each row's first > previous row's last) — flatten to one sorted array; or a matrix sorted per-row and per-column independently — use the staircase walk from a corner. Pitfall: converting a 1D index to (row, col) with the wrong divisor/modulus — use row = idx / numCols, col = idx % numCols — or applying the flatten trick when rows aren't globally ordered (then it's the staircase, not binary search).

prompts.promptText: Write the flattened-matrix binary search in your language of choice: given a fully sorted m×n matrix and a target, return whether it exists, treating the matrix as one sorted array of length m*n.
prompts.answerHint: lo = 0, hi = m*n - 1; mid maps to matrix[mid / n][mid % n]; compare and shrink [lo, hi] as in the 1D search. Invariant: the flattened view is globally sorted, so the same monotonic reasoning holds; the only new part is the index-to-(row, col) math.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Search a 2D Matrix (Medium) — the matrix is row-sorted and each row starts after the previous ends; return whether target is present in O(log(m*n)).
prompts.answerHint: Binary search over 0..m*n-1, decoding mid to matrix[mid / n][mid % n].

prompts.promptText: Solve: Search a 2D Matrix II (Medium) — the matrix is sorted per-row and per-column (but not globally); return whether target is present.
prompts.answerHint: Staircase walk from the top-right corner: too big move left, too small move down — each step eliminates a full row or column, O(m + n).

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for in-place pointer reversal on a linked list? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "reverse the list" (or a sublist / every k nodes), reordering that needs next-pointers flipped rather than values copied. Pitfall: overwriting curr.next before you've saved it — capture next = curr.next FIRST each iteration, or you lose the rest of the list. Related: Swap Nodes in Pairs is reversal with k=2; Reverse Nodes in k-Group tiles this per block.

prompts.promptText: Write the iterative list-reversal kernel in your language of choice: given a head, return the head of the reversed list using three pointers.
prompts.answerHint: prev = null, curr = head; each step: next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next. Loop until curr is null; return prev. Invariant: everything from prev backward is already reversed, everything from curr forward is untouched.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Reverse Linked List (Easy) — reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
prompts.answerHint: Three-pointer prev/curr/next sweep, flipping each next pointer as you go; prev is the answer.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Reverse Linked List II (Medium) — reverse the sublist from position left to right (1-indexed) in one pass.
prompts.answerHint: Dummy head, walk to the node before left, then reverse exactly (right-left) links by repeatedly splicing the next node to the front of the reversed segment.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Reverse Nodes in k-Group (Hard) — reverse the list in consecutive groups of k, leaving a trailing remainder of fewer than k nodes as-is.
prompts.answerHint: First count/check that k nodes remain, reverse that block, then recurse (or iterate) linking the reversed block's tail to the next block's result.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for fast & slow pointers on a linked list? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: detect a cycle, find the middle, find the kth-from-end, or check a palindrome without extra storage. Pitfall: dereferencing fast/fast.next without null-guarding both (odd vs even length) — the loop condition must be `fast && fast.next`. Related: Palindrome Linked List finds the midpoint then reverses the second half.

prompts.promptText: Write Floyd's cycle-detection kernel in your language of choice: given a head, return whether the list has a cycle, and adapt it to also return the midpoint node.
prompts.answerHint: slow = head, fast = head; each step slow moves 1, fast moves 2; if they meet there's a cycle. When fast reaches the end (no cycle), slow sits on the middle. Guard the loop with `fast && fast.next`.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Linked List Cycle (Easy) — return true if the linked list contains a cycle.
prompts.answerHint: Advance slow by 1 and fast by 2; a cycle exists iff they ever point at the same node.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Middle of the Linked List (Easy) — return the middle node (the second middle if the length is even).
prompts.answerHint: When fast walks two steps per slow step, slow lands on the middle as fast falls off the end.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Linked List Cycle II (Medium) — return the node where the cycle begins, or null if there is none.
prompts.answerHint: After slow and fast meet inside the cycle, reset one pointer to head and advance both by 1 — they meet at the cycle's entry (Floyd's second phase).

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the pairwise sorted-merge pattern on lists? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "merge sorted lists", or a divide-and-conquer that needs a merge step (merge sort on a list). Pitfall: forgetting to attach the non-empty remainder after one list runs out, or not using a dummy head so you fumble the first node. Related: Merge k Sorted Lists (carded under Heap / Priority Queue) generalizes this to k-way via a heap.

prompts.promptText: Write the two-list sorted-merge kernel in your language of choice: given two sorted heads, splice them into one sorted list.
prompts.answerHint: Dummy head, tail pointer; while both non-null append the smaller head and advance that list; finally attach whichever remainder is left. Invariant: everything from dummy to tail is sorted and already placed.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Merge Two Sorted Lists (Easy) — splice two sorted lists into one sorted list.
prompts.answerHint: Dummy head + tail; repeatedly link the smaller of the two current heads, then attach the leftover tail.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Sort List (Medium) — sort a linked list in O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space.
prompts.answerHint: Merge sort on the list: fast/slow to split at the midpoint, recurse on each half, then reuse the two-list merge to combine.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a dummy head node? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: an insert/delete that might change the head itself, list partitioning, or building a new list from scratch. Pitfall: returning the original head instead of dummy.next (the real head may have been removed), or a two-pointer gap set to n instead of n+1 off-by-one. Related: Partition List builds two dummy-headed sublists; Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II deletes runs behind a dummy.

prompts.promptText: Write the remove-nth-from-end kernel in your language of choice: given a head and n, delete the nth node from the end in one pass using a dummy head and a gap.
prompts.answerHint: Dummy before head; advance a lead pointer n+1 steps, then move lead and a trail pointer together until lead is null — trail now sits just before the target, so set trail.next = trail.next.next. Return dummy.next.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Remove Nth Node From End of List (Medium) — remove the nth node from the end and return the head.
prompts.answerHint: Two pointers with an n+1 gap behind a dummy head; when the lead falls off the end the trailing pointer is right before the node to unlink.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Add Two Numbers (Medium) — two numbers stored as digit lists in reverse order; return their sum as a list.
prompts.answerHint: Walk both lists behind a dummy head, summing digit + carry each step; keep going while either list or the carry is non-zero.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a DFS tree traversal, and how do preorder, inorder, and postorder differ? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "visit every node", and the position of the node-visit relative to its children fixes the order — preorder (node before children) copies/serializes top-down, inorder (left, node, right) emits a BST in sorted order, postorder (children before node) frees/aggregates bottom-up; pitfall: forgetting the null-child base case and dereferencing a leaf's missing child. Related: Binary Tree Preorder/Postorder Traversal.

prompts.promptText: Write an iterative inorder traversal with an explicit stack in your language of choice: given a binary tree root, return its node values in inorder.
prompts.answerHint: Loop with a current pointer and a stack: while current is non-null push it and go left; otherwise pop, emit that node's value, and set current to its right child. Invariant: the stack holds exactly the unvisited ancestors whose right subtrees are still pending.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal (Easy) — return the inorder sequence of a binary tree's node values.
prompts.answerHint: Recurse left, emit the node, recurse right — or run the explicit-stack loop to avoid recursion.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (Easy) — return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.
prompts.answerHint: A node's depth is 1 plus the larger of its two subtree depths, with a null child contributing 0.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for BFS / level-order traversal? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "per-level" grouping, shortest hop-count in an unweighted tree or grid; pitfall: reading the queue length inside the level loop after you have already enqueued children — snapshot the level size once before draining it. Related: Average of Levels in Binary Tree.

prompts.promptText: Write a level-order BFS with per-level grouping in your language of choice: given a binary tree root, return a list of levels, each a list of values.
prompts.answerHint: Seed a queue with the root, then repeat: snapshot the current queue size as this level's width, dequeue exactly that many nodes emitting their values and enqueuing their non-null children. Invariant: at the top of each iteration the queue holds exactly one full level.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (Medium) — return node values grouped level by level, top to bottom.
prompts.answerHint: BFS with a size snapshot per level so each inner loop drains exactly one level into its own list.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Binary Tree Right Side View (Medium) — return the values visible from the right, top to bottom.
prompts.answerHint: Run level-order BFS and keep the last node of each level (the rightmost).

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for range-carrying BST validation? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "is this a valid BST", or any BST search/insert/delete that leans on the ordering invariant; pitfall: comparing only against a node's immediate parent instead of carrying a tightening (low, high) bound — a deep node can satisfy its parent yet violate a distant ancestor. Related: Insert into a BST, Delete Node in a BST.

prompts.promptText: Write range-carrying BST validation in your language of choice: return whether a binary tree satisfies the BST ordering.
prompts.answerHint: Recurse with an open interval (low, high) starting at (-inf, +inf): each node must lie strictly inside, then recurse left with high tightened to the node's value and right with low tightened to it. Invariant: every node is checked against the full ancestor-derived bound, not just its parent.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Validate Binary Search Tree (Medium) — return whether the tree is a valid BST.
prompts.answerHint: Carry a (low, high) bound down the recursion, tightening one side at each step.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Kth Smallest Element in a BST (Medium) — return the k-th smallest value in the tree.
prompts.answerHint: Inorder traversal yields values in sorted order, so stop at the k-th emitted node.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the lowest-common-ancestor recursion? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "lowest common ancestor of two nodes", the split-point where two root-to-node paths diverge; pitfall: on a plain binary tree, returning eagerly on the first target found instead of letting both subtree searches report back — the LCA is the node where the two targets surface in different subtrees. Related: the BST variant just walks down comparing values.

prompts.promptText: Write the lowest-common-ancestor recursion for a binary tree in your language of choice: given the root and two target nodes, return their LCA.
prompts.answerHint: Return the node itself if it is null or equals either target, otherwise recurse both sides; if both sides come back non-null the current node is the LCA, else bubble up whichever side was non-null. Invariant: a call returns a target it saw, or the LCA once both targets have been seen below it.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree (Medium) — return the LCA of two nodes in a BST.
prompts.answerHint: Walk down from the root; the first node whose value sits between (or equals) the two targets is the LCA.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree (Medium) — return the LCA of two nodes in a general binary tree.
prompts.answerHint: Recurse both subtrees; the node whose left and right searches each surface one target is the LCA.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for splitting traversals to reconstruct a tree? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "build the tree from preorder+inorder" (or postorder+inorder, or a sorted array); pitfall: rescanning inorder for the root each recursion (O(n^2)) instead of pre-hashing value->index, plus off-by-one slicing of the left/right subarrays. Related: Convert Sorted Array to BST picks the middle element as the root.

prompts.promptText: Write preorder+inorder tree construction in your language of choice: given both traversals, rebuild the binary tree.
prompts.answerHint: Consume preorder left-to-right as the stream of roots; for each root find its index in inorder via a prehashed value->index map to size the left and right subtrees, and recurse left before right so the preorder cursor advances correctly. Invariant: the preorder pointer always sits on the next subtree's root.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal (Medium) — rebuild the tree from its two traversals.
prompts.answerHint: Preorder gives the root order; each root's position in inorder splits the remaining nodes into its left and right subtrees.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree (Easy) — build a height-balanced BST from a sorted array.
prompts.answerHint: Pick the middle element as the root and recurse on the two halves so the tree stays balanced.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the down-carry-plus-combine-on-return path-sum recursion? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: root-to-leaf accumulation, "diameter/longest path", "max path sum through any node"; pitfall: conflating the value you carry DOWN (a running prefix) with the value you return UP (the best completed path), and, for through-node problems, forgetting to clamp negative child contributions to zero. Related: Path Sum II collects the actual root-to-leaf paths.

prompts.promptText: Write the combine-on-return path recursion in your language of choice: return the diameter (longest edge count between any two nodes) of a binary tree.
prompts.answerHint: A helper returns each node's height (edges down to its deepest leaf); at every node update a global best with leftHeight + rightHeight (the path bending through this node), then return 1 + max(left, right). Invariant: the returned value is a downward height while the answer tracks the best two-sided join seen.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Path Sum (Easy) — return whether some root-to-leaf path sums to a target value.
prompts.answerHint: Carry the remaining target down the recursion; at a leaf check whether its value finishes the sum exactly.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Diameter of Binary Tree (Easy) — return the length of the longest path between any two nodes.
prompts.answerHint: At each node the candidate diameter is left height + right height; track the max while the recursion returns heights.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (Hard) — return the maximum sum of any node-to-node path.
prompts.answerHint: Each node returns its best single downward branch with negatives clamped to zero, while a global max records the best left + node + right join.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for null-marked traversal serialization? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "design serialize/deserialize", any tree-to-string round-trip; pitfall: omitting explicit null markers (the string can then no longer distinguish different tree shapes) or dropping the delimiter when values are multi-digit or negative. Related: Serialize and Deserialize N-ary Tree, which needs a child-count marker (premium-skip).

prompts.promptText: Write preorder serialize/deserialize with explicit null markers in your language of choice: encode a binary tree to a string and rebuild it.
prompts.answerHint: Serialize by preorder-emitting each value (or a sentinel like '#' for null) into a delimited string; deserialize by consuming that stream left-to-right, building a node from the next token and recursing to fill its left then right child. Invariant: encode and decode walk the nodes in identical order so the cursor never desyncs.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (Hard) — design methods to encode a tree to a string and decode it back.
prompts.answerHint: Preorder with an explicit null marker for each missing child makes the string unambiguous and lets decode rebuild by consuming tokens in the same order.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a trie instead of a hash set of words? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: repeated prefix queries ("does any word start with..."), dictionary-style lookup, autocomplete, shared-prefix storage where a hash set would rescan whole words. Pitfall: forgetting the end-of-word flag — without it "app" looks present just because "apple" was inserted, and prefix-search gets confused with full-word search.

prompts.promptText: Write the trie node plus insert and search in your language of choice: a node with a character-keyed children map and an end-of-word flag, insert walking/creating one node per character, search walking to confirm a full word.
prompts.answerHint: Node = { children: char -> Node, isEnd: bool }. Insert: start at root, for each char descend into children[char], creating the child if absent; mark isEnd on the final node. Search: descend char by char, return false the moment a child is missing, else return the final node's isEnd. startsWith is the same walk without the isEnd check. Invariant: the path from root to any node spells exactly the prefix that node represents.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) (Medium) — support insert(word), search(word), and startsWith(prefix).
prompts.answerHint: One node type with a children map and a boolean end flag; search and startsWith share the descend loop and differ only in whether the end flag must be true.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure (Medium) — addWord and a search where '.' matches any single character.
prompts.answerHint: Store words in a trie; on '.' branch into a DFS/recursion that tries every child, otherwise follow the one matching child — the wildcard turns the linear walk into a small backtracking search.

prompts.promptText: When do you combine a trie with grid DFS instead of running a search per word? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "find all words from a dictionary in a grid/text", many target words sharing prefixes, where per-word search would rescan the board once per word. Pitfall: not pruning dead branches — walk the trie in lockstep with the DFS so a cell path with no matching trie child is abandoned immediately, and de-duplicate found words (or prune matched nodes) so the same word isn't reported twice. Related: Word Break II is the trie-accelerated segmentation variant (skipped here).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Word Search II (Hard) — given a grid of letters and a word list, return every word that can be traced through adjacent cells.
prompts.answerHint: Build a trie of the word list, then DFS each cell walking the trie in lockstep — the trie prunes every path whose prefix no target word shares, collapsing many per-word scans into one board traversal.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a trie's prefix node as the anchor for completions or shortest-prefix lookup? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "suggest completions for a prefix", "replace a word by its shortest matching root/prefix", ranked/limited suggestions off a shared dictionary. Pitfall: re-walking from the root for every query instead of caching the prefix node, and (for shortest-prefix) not stopping at the FIRST end-of-word node on the descent. Related: Design Search Autocomplete System (premium, skipped here) adds ranking by historical frequency.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Replace Words (Medium) — given a dictionary of roots, replace each word in a sentence with the shortest root that is a prefix of it.
prompts.answerHint: Insert all roots into a trie, then for each word descend character by character and stop at the first node flagged end-of-word — that shortest matching prefix is the replacement.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a size-k heap (or quickselect) for kth-largest/smallest? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "kth largest/smallest", "top k" where a full sort is overkill, or a streaming source where new values keep arriving. Use a min-heap of size k so its root is the kth largest (max-heap of size k for kth smallest). Pitfall: picking the wrong heap polarity — for the kth LARGEST you keep a MIN-heap and evict the smallest, so the k survivors are the k largest and the root is the answer. Related: quickselect gives O(n) average when you have the whole array up front (no streaming).

prompts.promptText: Write the size-k-heap kth-largest kernel in your language of choice: given a stream of numbers and k, keep the kth largest seen so far available at all times.
prompts.answerHint: Maintain a min-heap; push each incoming value, then while the heap holds more than k elements pop the smallest. Invariant: after processing each value the heap contains exactly the k largest values seen, so its root is the kth largest. Each push/pop is O(log k).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Kth Largest Element in a Stream (Easy) — a class that returns the kth largest element after each add.
prompts.answerHint: Hold a min-heap capped at size k across calls; add pushes then trims to k, and the root is the running answer.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Kth Largest Element in an Array (Medium) — find the kth largest element in an unsorted array.
prompts.answerHint: Size-k min-heap gives O(n log k); quickselect (partition around a pivot, recurse only into the side holding index n-k) gives O(n) average.

prompts.promptText: Solve: K Closest Points to Origin (Medium) — return the k points nearest the origin.
prompts.answerHint: Max-heap of size k keyed by squared distance (no sqrt needed); evict the farthest so the k survivors are the closest.

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the frequency-map-plus-heap (or bucket-sort) pattern? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "k most/least frequent", output ranked by how often something occurs. Count with a hash map first, then a size-k heap over (count, value) pairs pulls the top k in O(n log k) — or bucket-sort by frequency for O(n) since counts are bounded by n. Pitfall: heaping over the raw elements instead of the (count, value) pairs, or sizing the heap to the number of distinct values instead of k.

prompts.promptText: Solve: Top K Frequent Elements (Medium) — return the k most frequent elements of an array.
prompts.answerHint: Hash map of counts, then a size-k min-heap over the counts (or bucket-sort by frequency, index = count, and read buckets from the top down).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Sort Characters By Frequency (Medium) — rearrange a string so characters appear in decreasing order of frequency.
prompts.answerHint: Count characters, then emit each character repeated count times in descending-frequency order (heap or bucket by count).

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for a k-way merge with a heap? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "merge k sorted lists/arrays/streams", combining many already-sorted sources into one sorted output. Keep a min-heap of the current front element from each source; pop the smallest, append it, then push that source's successor. Pitfall: pushing a source's next element without carrying enough context to find its successor (store the source id / node, not just the value) — and remember to skip exhausted sources. Related: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists rides the same heap-of-heads sweep.

prompts.promptText: Write the k-way merge kernel in your language of choice: given k sorted sequences, produce one merged sorted sequence.
prompts.answerHint: Seed a min-heap with the head of each non-empty source (store value plus which source it came from). Repeatedly pop the minimum, append it to the output, and push the next element from that same source if one exists. Invariant: the heap always holds at most one live element per source — the smallest unconsumed one — so the popped minimum is globally next. O(N log k).

prompts.promptText: Solve: Merge k Sorted Lists (Hard) — merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
prompts.answerHint: Min-heap of the k current head nodes (compare by value); pop the smallest, link it into the result, push its .next. (Pairwise divide-and-conquer merging is the O(N log k) alternative.)

prompts.promptText: When do you reach for the two-heap (max-heap + min-heap) technique? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
prompts.answerHint: Signals: "running/streaming median", order statistics maintained as values arrive one at a time. Keep a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half, sizes differing by at most one; the median is the top of the larger heap (or the average of both tops when balanced). Pitfall: rebalancing without first routing the new value through the correct heap — push, then move one element across to restore the size invariant, or the two halves overlap. Related: Sliding Window Median adds lazy deletion of the element leaving the window.

prompts.promptText: Write the two-heap running-median kernel in your language of choice: support add(value) and getMedian() over a stream.
prompts.answerHint: Keep a max-heap `low` and a min-heap `high`.
